Despite the silent friction inherent in the internet’s design, most non-live experiences on the internet still feel live because the volume of updates sent and requested is high (as in the case of instant messengers), the delivery time is typically rapid and delays often hidden behind design tricks, users don’t necessarily know when information is out of date, and update requests occur more regularly when an application is open and thus under the eye of the user. Unlike web browsing and instant messaging, however, truly live online experiences require a user’s device to establish a sustained or continuous connection to the relevant third-party server. It’s for this reason that video calls, live video streaming, and video games are not always possible, let alone reliable in performance. Yet it’s these experiences, not browsing the New York Times, that best reflect the data needs of the Metaverse. The Metaverse is a live world and live experience and therefore requires both live (i.e., real-time) information and a continuous connection to its source. And unfortunately, neither the internet backbone nor the Internet Protocol Suite was designed for these applications. As an example, TCP/IP’s Border Gateway Protocol, which routes traffic on the internet as it jumps from one network to another, neither routes nor prioritizes traffic that needs to arrive quickly or whose connection must be sustained. Indeed, BGP doesn’t even receive that information.

Making matters more challenging, the Metaverse is imagined as a shared and multiparticipant experience. As such, the information sent by a given user or server must be synchronized across all relevant users, networks, and devices in real time. Again, though, the internet was designed to connect no more than two devices or servers at once, and for only finite periods of time.

This structure has worked fairly well over the past 40 years because there are relatively few shared online experiences. When visiting an office cafeteria, many users are on the company’s corporate Wi-Fi, but their experiences are entirely disconnected and irrelevant to one another. When two users scroll BuzzFeed together on their respective devices, they are sharing a real-world experience, but not a digital one. In some cases, the internet is co-experienced—but these experiences are typically simple, computationally limited, and tolerant of delays. Live text chats, such as those on Twitch, are uncoordinated between users, barely customized, and unaffected by which entry appears above or below another. Google Docs are coordinated, but it’s rare that they are edited concurrently, and even rarer that the same part of the document has several simultaneous authors.† Video calls are an exception to the above as they are both live and, by definition, multiuser experiences. Yet these applications have an important advantage: there is usually just one focal participant at any given moment, with all others serving primarily as spectators, not “collaborators” in the experience.

What makes the Metaverse particularly difficult from a networking perspective is that every additional user or device has a linear impact on the number of required continuous connections—which is already hard—and an exponential impact on the number of interactions that must be synchronized in real time. And unlike a video call or Google Doc, these interactions are not video frames or text, but contribute to a complex and dynamic computer model. Recall that the Street protocol of Neal Stephenson’s could “handle” more than ten million simultaneous users.

A related problem is that of “copies.” The Internet Protocol Suite as it exists today is designed to share copies of files. As such, every message, document, or photo that is sent is ultimately copied to various recipient devices. When a user sends a photo from their iPhone using Gmail, a copy exists on their device and Gmail account, as well as the recipient’s email service, and any number of devices they use to download it on or view it. Both users’ iCloud accounts may also store a copy of the photo, too, which may or may not sync with whether the device keeps or deletes the photo. There is no mechanism in TCP/IP that establishes, let alone manages or enforces, the canonical version of a file, ownership of it, or various access and permission rights. Instead, these properties and rights are possible—on a limited basis—only when the content remains on a single platform on the internet. If a Roblox user wants to trade an avatar to their friend, Roblox can ensure the friend receives it, the sender loses access to it, and so on. If that user were to export the avatar, then the copy problem begins. To use a “real-world” analogy, Chase Bank can reassign the rights to a $100 bill across its customers’ bank accounts, but neither Chase nor the US Treasury can control who has it, takes it, or might try to forge it when it leaves Chase Bank.

There are some bodies that administer the “canon” of the internet. The domain system managed by ICANN is a literal database which enables various agents (e.g., GoDaddy or Name.com) to register domains on behalf of private individuals and shift their websites from one domain to another, or sell their domain to another person or company. The DNS record is singular, authoritative, and dynamic, having expanded from only 7 top-level domains in 1998 (.com,.org,.net,.edu,.gov, .int, .mil) to more than 1,500 a quarter century later, but neither technical systems nor governance structures of ICANN can scale to manage infinitely expanding inventories of virtual goods worth trillions per year.

The Metaverse does not mean securitizing or canonizing all content on the internet. It’s not just okay, it’s good that many copies of a photo might exist, and that User A cannot alter a photo they sent to User B after User B received it, or take it back. But for the Metaverse to have a network-level economy for any virtual goods, or any creations, that spans more than a single platform, it requires altogether new systems for object rights and exchange.

To summarize: a basic definition of the Metaverse might be a “shared, live, and 3D version of the internet that supports an open economy of virtual goods.” Part II of this book will progress from this definition to a description that better illuminates the Metaverse and its technological needs. But for the time being, this stated definition should suffice to explain the “next internet” in contrast to the current one.

What the Metaverse Is Not

Having established a baseline, if still simplified, understanding of both the internet and the Metaverse, it’s helpful to address common Metaverse myths and misunderstandings. Several points should now be obvious to readers, but it’s helpful to address them directly.

Error #1: Using the singular article “a” Metaverse, plural form “Metaverses,” or possessive construction such as “Company A’s Metaverse”

Companies such as Amazon, Apple, Facebook, Google, and Microsoft are not “the internet,” do not operate “the internet,” control the protocols of the “internet,” or have their own “internets.” Instead, these companies operate large, hardware- and software-based, horizontal and vertical platforms that are on the internet, help users access the internet, and provide things to do with the internet. And as vast and mighty as these various platforms are, they represent just a small portion of the overall internet—even when combined. This is the right way to think about the Metaverse, too.

Like the internet, the Metaverse is not any one network, platform, device, application, or even group of them. It is instead a network of myriad interconnected and interoperable networks, platforms, devices, applications, and so on. While it’s common to hear that Company A or B is building “the” Metaverse or building “a” Metaverse, they are typically just building hardware and/or applications (and maybe contributing to development of a Metaversal Internet Protocol Suite). Now, there are some important nuances to this taxonomy and philosophy.

First, there are rival efforts to build the foundational technologies of the Metaverse. Company A and Company B, for example, may envision and advocate for competing protocols and standards for the Metaverse, which would in turn affect how the Metaverse operates or is commercialized. As such, it could be argued that these two companies are contributing to the development of Metaverses (certainly, Web3 developers would say they are building a very different Metaverse than the likes of Facebook and Microsoft). History suggests that separate initiatives can endure for some time, before eventually merging or establishing a single winner. From the 1970s to 1990s there were many proposed and operating working alternatives to the internet, some of which were supported by different US federal departments even though the Department of Defense had created and still spearheaded much of the internet. Few technologists at the time expected that a single global winner would emerge from these so-called “protocol wars,” but the utility of a unified digital economy was too great, and holdouts eventually switched or integrated into the internet. It’s even less likely that over the coming decades, the common foundations of the current internet would split into multiple Metaverses.

Second, there is likely to be some regional fragmentation across “the” Metaverse. The so-called “Chinese internet” uses the same Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP) as the rest of the world, yet the experience of using the internet in China is unmistakably different due to various regulations, firewalls, software giants, and cultural norms. If the Metaverse proves as essential and valuable as many predict, it’s likely the Chinese Metaverse will be even more distinct from that of the rest of the world than the internet is today (as mentioned in the introduction, the Chinese government has already stated that its domestic Metaverse should be “independent” and “controllable”). Still, the Chinese Metaverse will be built on top of the Internet Protocol Suite, likely leverage many of the same technologies that are also used for the Metaverse outside China, and interoperate into parts of the non-Chinese Metaverse. As such, the “Chinese Metaverse” is best described as a regional expression or variation of the Metaverse, rather than a wholly different Metaverse.

Third, one company may still establish effective control over the Metaverse by designing and/or operating its protocols or access devices. Though the foundations of the internet are both open and without an owner, it has become increasingly closed and commercialized over the past 40 years—and the Metaverse is likely to exacerbate this trend, rather than reverse it. This dynamic is discussed throughout this book and is a point of focus in Chapters 3 and 10.

Error #2: Conflating the Metaverse with a virtual or augmented reality headset, operating system, or experience

Technically, the term “virtual reality” refers to computer-generated simulations of three-dimensional objects or environments with seemingly real, direct, or physical user interaction.9 The underlying mechanics of processing and rendering computer-generated simulations do not fundamentally differ based on the type of screen they’re viewed through, or how the user’s inputs are collected. In current usage, however, virtual reality refers to a computer-generated simulation that is rendered on a screen contained within a headset, rather than a TV screen or monitor, with the user interacting with the simulation using a mix of facial or body movements, rather than typing on a keyboard or operating a controller. VR headsets provide a greater sense of immersion inside a computer-generated simulation, and greater ease of use, as the user’s senses (i.e., their eyes and ears) are enveloped in the device, and they can interact as they do in the real world (e.g., look right to shift the camera angle right, turn body right to turn the character right).

In contrast to VR devices, augmented reality devices layer computer-generated simulations on top of the real world, rather than replace it altogether. For example, an AR device worn in a supermarket might layer floating, 3D labels above produce that identify various items and estimate their ripeness. As with VR, AR does not require a headset. Many applications provide rich AR experiences today through a standard smartphone camera and screen. Popular examples include Snapchat (which enables users to capture videos wearing AR costumes and makeup), Pokémon Go (which enables users to “see” and interact with Pokémon that appear to exist in the real world), and Google Maps (which can help users find their way by placing directional arrows on top of landmarks and streets). As with VR, it is assumed that wearable headsets are the most intuitive way to use AR functionality, just as glasses are easier to use than monocles stored in pockets.

VR and AR devices are often conflated with the Metaverse because of their role in novels such as Neuromancer, Snow Crash, and Ready Player One, as well as their centrality to Facebook’s Metaverse strategy. There is also a widely held belief that VR/AR headsets will eventually become the “best,” “most popular,” and “preferred” way to access the Metaverse. Regardless, the Metaverse is not a device, nor a specific interface or type of experience.

To better understand the relationship between VR/AR devices and the Metaverse, consider the relationship between touchscreen smartphones and the internet. Neither the internet nor even the mobile internet requires either a touchscreen or the use of apps—users could, if they preferred, use BlackBerry-style clickwheels and physical keyboards. In fact, no part of using the internet even requires a visual interface; billions of people globally can and do occasionally access the internet simply by saying “Siri” or “Hey Google” or “Alexa.” Apps are another good example. Though the most popular way to access digital content and experiences, users could mostly just use a single app to engage with the internet: a web browser.

Though the internet does not require touchscreens, smartphones, or apps, it’s generally recognized that they are the best way to access it and have been key to expanding who uses the internet, for what, and how often. Without a touchscreen, keyboards would take up half of a smartphone’s display and there would be little ability to tailor any interface to a specific application—whether the user was playing a game, accessing a medical record, or scrolling TikTok, they would need to use an alphanumeric keyboard, a half dozen symbol-based keys, and some form of trackwheel or thumbpad, rather than benefit from a tailor-made touch user interface (UI). This limitation would have made general-purpose smartphones ill-suited to many specialized tasks and kept many children and senior citizens from adopting the devices in the first place. Though most internet products and services are available via web browser, most users prefer to access these products and services via apps, which are purpose-built for these products and services and therefore offer substantial performance, stability, and interface-related improvements. VR/AR headsets will likely play a similar role to touchscreens and apps in the Metaverse.

All that said, traditional or “flat 2D” devices have proved surprisingly capable at enabling users to interact in 3D spaces. In 2022, Neal Stephenson wrote a series of tweets intended to answer a commonly asked question: Did the Metaverse he envisioned require an AR or VR headset?

The assumption that the Metaverse is primarily an AR/VR thing isn’t crazy. In my book [Snow Crash] it’s all VR. And I worked for an AR company [Magic Leap]—one of several that are putting billions of dollars into building headsets. But I didn’t see video games coming when I wrote Snow Crash.… Thanks to games, billions of people are now comfortable navigating 3D environments on flat 2D screens. The UIs that they’ve mastered [keyboard and mouse for navigation and camera] are not what most science fiction writers would have predicted. But that’s how path dependency in tech works. We fluently navigate and interact with extremely rich 3D environments using keyboards that were designed for mechanical typewriters. It’s steampunk made real. A Metaverse that left behind those users and the [developers] who build those experiences would be getting off on the wrong foot.… My expectation is that a lot of Metaverse content will be built for screens (where the market is) while keeping options open for the future growth of affordable headsets.10

Error #3: Conflating the Metaverse with a video game platform such as Fortnite, Minecraft, or Roblox

As with AR/VR, this mistake is understandable. Nearly all of the top popular multiplayer video games of 2024 are shared, live, and 3D and boast some form of internal goods economy. In addition to these attributes, Fortnite, Minecraft, and Roblox each operate networks of tens of millions of virtual worlds, all of which are underpinned by an extensive technology suite that covers identities, avatars, virtual currencies, and communications, and can be accessed through nearly every mainstream computing device globally, are used for both work and play, and have millions of individual contributors supporting hundreds of millions of users as part of their multibillion-dollar economies.

Though there is a structural similarity between the Metaverse and these platforms, characterizing the former as the latter would be akin to saying Facebook is the World Wide Web. Yes, Facebook is a large, device-agnostic platform that spans billions of interconnected pages, with standardized identifiers (accounts rather than IP addresses), formats, conventions, and so on. And for some users, Facebook is most of what they do on the internet. Yet Facebook is a fraction of the overall internet, predominantly leisure focused, and entirely separate from the actual protocols of the internet. Roblox, Minecraft, and Fortnite are likely to be part of the Metaverse, resemble much of it, and pioneer some of its standards and user behaviors, but they are not a Metaverse, let alone the Metaverse.

Error #4: Conflating the Metaverse with Web3, blockchains, cryptocurrencies, or NFTs

A recurring theme in this book is the difficulty of fully separating various technological eras, waves, or models. Nevertheless, technologists, sociologists, and investors typically differentiate between the early stage of the internet, so-called “Web 1.0,” which began with the creation of the World Wide Web in 1989, and “Web 2.0,” which started around 2004 or 2005, following the launch of Facebook and YouTube. Webs 1.0 and 2.0 can be broadly differentiated in terms of content, user activity, the role of platforms, and the technologies used.

During the Web 1.0 era, content was not strictly limited to text, but limitations in broadband speeds and computer processing power meant that images were scarce and low resolution, while audio was typically available only in excerpts and low quality, and video was hard to find and even harder to watch. The content creator typically hosted this content themselves on servers they owned, and these ran open-source operating systems such as Linux. The content itself was usually produced or displayed using common standards (e.g., JPEG, GIF, JavaScript, HTML), and distributed through open platforms (the World Wide Web, web browsers, Microsoft Windows, email protocols, etc.). Although the Web 1.0 era was the first time most people could widely distribute their content—and without intermediation by a publisher, producer, retailer, and so on—almost no internet users created content during Web 1.0. They just consumed it.

During Web 2.0, it became common to create, distribute, and access high-quality media formats, including live video and interactive media. Billions of users also established comprehensive internet-based identities (e.g., a Facebook account), as well as their own internet-based networks (e.g., adding friends on Facebook). The advent of cloud data centers meant a developer or user could easily hire a company like Amazon or Microsoft to host and manage their website or app versus buying, setting up, and maintaining their own server. Apple, Google, and Facebook, among other technology companies, made it easier for individuals to create, discover, share, or monetize a piece of content, page, application, and so on. These many advances led to a surge in online creation. Rather than just view the internet, as was the case in Web 1.0, nearly all users of the Web 2.0 internet also contribute to the internet. Some of these contributions are just an occasional social media post, but millions of independent developers and creators now earn a living through their social media pages, video channels, apps, and websites, while millions more work in the digital “gig economy.”

Despite these benefits, many in the tech community worried about the underlying trade-off of Web 2.0: though more prosperous and participatory, it was also becoming more closed and privately owned. Identities and networks were established not on TCP/IP (e.g., email or IP addresses) or other open protocols but instead on private databases and systems (e.g., Facebook log-ins). If a developer published a website to the World Wide Web, they could freely shift it from one host to another, change their domain, or shift their customer and mailing lists to a different provider, but on Facebook or YouTube, most of the user’s content, identity, and followers were stuck. The major mobile operating systems also dictated what sorts of apps could be distributed, using which technologies, and through which business models they could be monetized—and took 15%–30% of an app’s digital revenues, too. Though nominally still “open,” the World Wide Web was intermediated by web browsers that were also tightly controlled by mobile operating systems (i.e., iOS and Android); a search engine with 95% market share and a desire to foster its ecosystem, collect data, and sell ads (Google); and algorithmic social feeds that were even more opaque and represented the majority of time spent online for billions of users (Facebook, Twitter, TikTok, etc.).

The overarching goal of Web3 is to continue to expand and enrich the number of contributors to the internet, while also returning the internet to the decentralized principles upon which it was founded, and reducing the power of big-tech platforms and aggregators. The supposed result would be a “healthier” internet that gives more rights to the individual user, offers more profits to the independent developer, and reduces the influence and controls of the various big-tech platforms that typically sit between users and developers.

Specifically, Web3 advocates argue this dream is best enabled by (or at least most likely through) blockchains, which also use cryptocurrencies and tokens to compensate users who help “run” these blockchains. In this sense, a Web3 internet is one in which regular users not only consume the internet and create content on the internet, they also help to operate it and have an economic stake in it, too. Advocates of “Web 3.0” (note the small terminological difference from “Web3”) share similar aims, but do not see blockchains as necessary (or even useful) to achieving them—or to the need to securitize the internet’s operations. Vint Cerf says he has some skepticism about blockchains and the Metaverse, but believes that revising and expanding the Internet Protocol Suite, which has gone largely unchanged since the early 1990s, is key to the internet’s long-term health.11 Sir Tim Berners-Lee, who believes the Metaverse is “going to be part of the future,” has called Web3 a “marketing hijack” that should be “ignored,” but insists that “Web 3.0” is “the real thing … a mid-course correction to take [the internet] back.”12

The confusion between “Metaverse” and “Web3/Web 3.0” has several causes. Most obviously, the two terms rose to prominence at the same time and both are considered “successor states” to the internet as it’s known today. The evolution of online media formats from Web 1.0 to Web 2.0 also suggests that the embrace of a 3D/spatial internet would mean transitioning to Web3/Web 3.0. Some also believe blockchain technologies are required to actually run the Metaverse (though some Metaverse pioneers believe blockchains have no future at all), while others believe the Metaverse must emerge for the many blockchains and cryptocurrencies to justify their multitrillion-dollar combined valuation.

Despite their occasional similarities, the Metaverse and Web3/Web 3.0 remain definitionally distinct. The former does not require further decentralization of the internet (in fact, it would likely emerge more slowly as a result), while the latter does not require the development of a 3D internet. Regardless, the principles of Web3/Web 3.0 would likely produce a healthier Metaverse, even if it’s not technically required.

Error #5: Considering the Metaverse a “replacement” to today’s internet, applications, and devices

Believing in the Metaverse does not require one to believe that society will stop using PCs or smartphones, abandon 2D applications and interfaces, or perform all digital labor and leisure inside 3D or spatial simulations.

Consider usage of the internet today. Though the “mobile and cloud” era of computing and networking is doubtless here, non-mobile devices such as laptops and PCs are still in use, “traditional” phone calls are common, most files are stored on local devices, billions still work “in person,” and restaurant, live sporting, and concert revenues have never been higher. And while more than half the traffic on the internet both originates and terminates on a mobile device, and over two-thirds of data is stored in the cloud, nearly all transmission of this data occurs via wired, not wireless, infrastructure, using a version of the Internet Protocol Suite that remains mostly unchanged since its formalization decades ago.

As was the case with the rise of both mobile networking and computing and cloud networking and computing, the Metaverse will likely result in new software, services, behaviors, use cases, and even hardware. In some cases, these new technologies will fully substitute for their predecessors. But more often, they will complement existing behaviors.

  1. * At the time of Apple’s unveiling of its Vision Pro device, the company eschewed the term “virtual reality,” too, instead saying “fully immersive experiences.”

  2. † Google Docs actually does work as though it were an instant messaging client, with each user receiving updates on a frequent but not real-time or continuous basis, and sending updates back on a frequent but not real-time or continuous basis.

Chapter 3 WHY NOW?

If the ideas behind the Metaverse are nearly a century old, if the Metaverse evolves from a technology more than a half century old, and if the term itself is 30 years old, it’s natural to wonder why the Metaverse came into focus in 2021—and to wonder when it might arrive.

New technological eras do not have launch dates. It’s possible to identify when a certain technology began development, when that technology first performed a given task, completed a public demonstration, or passed a sales milestone. But eras? They lack a singular starting moment. Instead, they emerge and are named only when the maturation of ecosystems proceeds to the point where sociologists, technologists, and regular people can identify widespread change. A great way to understand this dynamic is by considering the history of mobile computing.

Dialing Back

The first mobile (i.e., cellular network) phone call was placed in New York City in 1973 using a Motorola cellphone. It’s difficult to argue the mobile computing era began that year, but the development of the two-and-a-half-pound prototype Motorola DynaTAC is nonetheless an essential starting point, in retrospect. To build its device, Motorola had to not just establish a new category but also make advances in portable, miniaturized, and rechargeable batteries and help establish new standards for long-range wireless data transmission. And the success of the first phone call, which was placed by Motorola researcher Martin Cooper as he walked between 53rd and 54th Streets on Sixth Avenue in Manhattan, also prompted companies such as Bell and NTT to build the wireless towers and networks that device manufacturers would need to be able to sell usable phones and, later, smartphones too.

In 1991, Norway launched the first “2G” network—the first network to support wireless data, rather than just voice communications (which powers SMS). The following year, IBM unveiled the first smartphone, the IBM Simon, which was made available for sale in 1994. That year also saw the release of Apple’s first portable computer, the Newton, though the device lacked a mobile networking chip and predated the creation of Wi-Fi by three years and, as such, could receive and send data only through physical cables and chips. By the late 1990s, Research in Motion’s various BlackBerry models had begun to take hold in governments, large enterprises, and information-focused businesses (e.g., finance, healthcare), with RIM going public in 1998. In 1999, the Wireless Application Protocol, or WAP, debuted, enabling a primitive version of the World Wide Web to be accessed from most phones—smart or not.* Though not part of the Internet Protocol Suite, WAP was the first mobile-specific protocol to see widespread adoption and facilitate widespread access.

In October 2001, a year and a half after the dotcom crash, Japan premiered the first commercial 3G network. The speeds enabled by 3G made it practical for smartphones to download more than text-based emails and WAP webpages, which in turn expanded the device’s appeal to consumers rather than just business users, and led to the development of the first major mobile-only media companies. December 2002, for example, is considered the start of the “ringtone” industry, after a Japanese wireless carrier launched its “Chaku-Uta” service, which let customers pay to download 45 clips of select songs, which could then be used instead of a traditional phone ringer. Mobile game downloads followed soon after.

As 3G internet speeds and coverage expanded, and more mobile services and games debuted, smartphone sales began to surge. From 1991 through 2003, roughly 70–80 million total smartphones were sold worldwide. In 2004 and 2005, nearly 100 million more were sold.

Although smartphone sales hit additional records in the years that followed, there’s a reason that most industry observers and smartphone owners consider the smartphone era to have truly begun sometime between the second half of calendar year 2007 and the end of 2008. In July of 2007, the first iPhone launched, with Apple releasing an updated 3G model as well as its now-famous App Store in the summer of 2008. In September of 2007, Google released the first version of Android, which would later become the most popular operating system in human history. Two months later, the International Telecommunication Union unveiled 4G, which offered speeds practical for video, just as 2G enabled text and 3G enabled audio and images. These many convergent innovations established a brand-new curve for smartphone adoption, which grew from 100 million units sold in 2007 to over 250 million in 2010, 500 million in 2012, and a billion in 2013.

Still, it’s strange to say mobile had “arrived” in 2007, in 2008, or even by 2012. It took until 2014 for half of Americans to own a smartphone and it wasn’t until 2020 that half of the world had one. Until these milestones, most Americans and most people globally were not part of the mobile era. And during the interim years, there was an increase not just in the number of people using smartphones but in what smartphones could do, how often they were used, and for what purposes.

How Many Years Does It Take to Turn On a Lightbulb?

Another case study—a personal favorite—is the process of electrification, which began in the late 19th century and ran into the mid-20th century, and focused on the adoption and usage of electricity, skipping past the centuries-long effort to understand, capture, and transmit it. Electrification was not a single period of steady growth, nor a process through which any one product was adopted. Instead, it consisted of two separate waves of technological, industrial, and process-related transformation. The first wave began around 1881, when Thomas Edison stood up electric power stations in Manhattan and London. Yet while Edison was quick to commercialize electricity—he had created the first working incandescent light bulb only two years earlier—demand for the resource was low. A quarter century after the first stations, an estimated 5% to 10% of mechanical drive power in the United States came from electricity (two-thirds of which was generated locally, rather than from a grid). But then, rather suddenly, the second wave began. Between 1910 and 1920, electricity’s share of mechanical drive power quintupled to over 50% (nearly two-thirds of which came from independent electric utilities). By 1929, it stood at 78%.1

The difference between the first and second waves was not the portion of American industry that used electricity but the extent to which that portion did—and designed around it.2

When factories first adopted electrical power, it was typically used for lighting and to replace the on-premises source of power (usually steam). Owners did not rethink or replace the legacy infrastructure that would carry this power throughout the factory and put it to work. Instead, they continued to use a network of cogs and gears that were messy and loud and dangerous, were difficult to upgrade or change, were either “all on” or “all off” (and therefore required the same amount of power to support a single operating station or the entire plant, and suffered from countless “single points of failure”), and struggled to support specialized work.

But eventually, new technologies and understandings gave owners both the reason and the ability to redesign factories end to end for electricity, from replacing cogs with electric wires to installing individual stations with bespoke and dedicated electrically powered motors for functions such as sewing, cutting, pressing, and welding.

The benefits were wide-ranging. The same factory now had considerably more space, more light, better air, and less life-threatening equipment. What’s more, individual stations could be powered individually (which increased safety, while reducing costs and downtime), and they could use more specialized equipment, such as electric socket wrenches.

Factory owners could configure production areas around the logic of the production process rather than hulking equipment, and even reconfigure production areas on a regular basis. These two changes meant that far more industries could deploy assembly lines (which had first emerged in the late 1700s), while those that already had such lines could extend them further and more efficiently. In 1913, Henry Ford created the first moving assembly line, which used electricity and conveyor belts to reduce the production time per car from 12.5 hours to 93 minutes, while also using less power. According to the historian David Nye, Ford’s famous Highland Park plant was “built on the assumption that electrical light and power should be available everywhere.”3

Once a few factories began this transformation, the entire market was forced to catch up, thereby spurring more investment and innovation in electricity-based infrastructure, equipment, and processes. Within a year of its first moving assembly line, Ford was producing more cars than the rest of the industry combined. By its 10 millionth car, it had built more than half of all cars on American roads.

The “second wave” of industrial electricity adoption didn’t depend on a single visionary making an evolutionary leap from Thomas Edison’s core work. Nor was it driven merely by an increasing number of industrial power stations. Instead, it reflected a critical mass of interconnected innovations, spanning power management, manufacturing hardware, production theory, and more. Some of these innovations fit in the palm of a plant manager’s hand, others needed a room, a few required a city, and all depended on people and processes. In aggregate, these innovations enabled the “Roaring Twenties,” which saw the greatest average annual increases in labor and capital productivity in a hundred years, and helped power the Second Industrial Revolution.

Back to the Future

In June of 2021, Epic Games’ founder and CEO Tim Sweeney tweeted a screenshot of code from Epic’s first 3D game, Unreal, with the caption “October 1997.” In a pair of follow-up tweets, Sweeney wrote, “[Users] could go into portals and travel among user-run servers when Unreal 1 was released in 1998. I remember a moment where folks in the community had created a grotto map with no combat and were standing in a circle chatting. This style of play didn’t last for long though. Epic has had Metaverse aspirations for a very, very long time … but only in recent years have a critical mass of working pieces started coming together rapidly.”4

At the time of Sweeney’s post, the Metaverse was already years behind not only the fictional forecasts of Snow Crash, which supposed that the Metaverse was fully operational and inhabited by more than a hundred million people by the early 2010s, but also the real-world hopes of many tech entrepreneurs. But as the histories of mobile computing and electrification remind us, eras begin when many different technologies converge and ecosystems are built up around them. And by the early 2020s, there was growing consensus that the Metaverse was about to hit its version of the 1910s in electricity or the 18-month period that followed the iPhone’s debut in 2007. The modern history of virtual worlds, real-time graphical simulation, head-mounted displays, human culture and pastimes, and AI also helps to explain this belief, too.

Pre-Release Code from Epic Games’ 1998 Video Game Unreal

Synthetic Worlds

Most accounts of the history of the Metaverse begin in the 1970s, with the advent of Multi-User Dungeons (or MUDs), a sort-of software-based version of the role-playing game Dungeons & Dragons, but which was experienced purely through text and the internet. Using text-based commands that resembled human languages, MUD players could interact with one another, explore a fictional world populated by non-playable characters and monsters, attain power-ups and knowledge, and eventually retrieve a magical chalice, defeat an evil wizard, or rescue a princess.

The growing popularity of MUDs inspired the creation of Multi-User Shared Hallucinations (or MUSHs) and Multi-User Experiences (MUXs). Unlike MUDs, which asked players to carry out specific roles in the context of a specific and usually fantastical narrative, MUSHs and MUXs enabled participants to collaboratively define the world and its objective. Players might choose to set their MUSH in a courtroom, while taking on roles such as defendant, attorney, plaintiff, judge, and members of the jury. One participant might later decide to transform the relatively mundane proceedings into a hostage situation—which would then be defused by a poem mad-libbed by the other players. As late as 1993, traffic analysis suggested that 10% of data transmitted on the internet was for MUDs, MUSHs, and MUXs—a remarkable figure given that these simulations transmitted little data in each message compared to emails, financial files, and research reports.5

The next great advance came in 1986 with the release of the Commodore 64 online game Habitat, published by Lucasfilm, the production company founded by Star Wars creator George Lucas. Habitat was described as “a multi-participant online virtual environment” and, in a reference to Gibson’s novel Neuromancer, “a cyberspace.” Unlike MUDs and MUSHs, the world of Habitat was graphical, thereby allowing users to actually see virtual environments and characters, though only via pixeled 2D. It also afforded players far greater control over the in-game environment. “Citizens” of Habitat were in charge of the laws and expectations of their virtual world, and had to barter with each other for necessary resources and avoid being robbed or killed for their wares. This challenge led to periods of chaos, after which new rules, regulations, and authorities were established by the player community to maintain order.

Though Habitat is not as widely remembered as other 1980s video games, such as Pac-Man and Super Mario Bros., it transcended the niche appeal of MUDs and MUSHs, ultimately becoming a commercial hit. The title was also the first game to repurpose the Sanskrit term avatar, which roughly translates to “the descent of a deity from heaven,” to refer to a user’s virtual body. Decades later, this usage has become convention—in no small part because Stephenson reapplied it in Snow Crash.

In the 1990s, virtual world platforms began to transcend the flatness of 2D text and imagery. Web World, released in 1994, was the first open-ended virtual world platform that was rendered in “2.5D.”6 This graphics approach produced the illusion of 3D through the use of isometric art styles,† mathematically precise distortions in the virtual world’s map and objects, and tilting the virtual world’s map and/or the camera angles a player used to see it. In 1995, Worlds, Inc., brought true 3D to the category and was expressly focused on all forms of virtual socializing, rather than game-like objectives.7 That same year saw the debut of Activeworlds, the first virtual world platform that enabled multiple users to build a given world at the same time using 3D drag-and-drop objects, rather than just commands and code.8 Notably, Activeworlds also had the express purpose of building Stephenson’s Metaverse and asked players to both enjoy its virtual world and help expand and populate it.9 In 1998, OnLive! Traveler launched with spatial voice chat, allowing users to hear where other players were positioned relative to other participants, and for an avatar’s mouth to move in response to the words spoken by the player.10

In 1999, Intrinsic Graphics, a 3D gaming software company, completed the spin-off of Keyhole, whose titular product was a virtual production of the entire planet earth. Five years later, Google acquired the company after concluding that more than a quarter of Google Search queries were for geospatial information, such as the location of a supermarket or the directions to it.11 In 2005, Google renamed Keyhole “Google Earth” and made it available for free to consumers worldwide. In the ensuing 20 years, Google’s many upgrades to Google Earth brought the product ever closer to the “Earth” application of Stephenson’s Snow Crash, which had inspired at least one of Keyhole’s founders to start the business. In 2007, Google began its Google Street View project, which eventually enabled Google Maps users to view 360-degree photos staged every few feet (in cities) or dozen meters (rural areas) on nearly every street in the world. By 2020, Google was updating these photos every year (cities) or three (rural areas). In 2008, Google added live traffic information across its mapping products. At first, Google’s data set relied on licenses to traffic sensors owned by various governments and private infrastructure operators, but the company eventually factored in data generated by the billions of smartphone-based Google Maps users, which provided greater insight into real-time transit, scheduled transit, and typical patterns. In 2012, Google Earth launched a 3D mode for select cities, such as Manhattan and Paris.

For many, especially those in Silicon Valley, the idea of a parallel virtual existence was not seriously contemplated until the arrival of the aptly named Second Life in June 2003 (two months before the debut of the 2D social network MySpace). In its first year, Second Life attracted over one million regular users, and shortly thereafter, numerous real-world organizations rushed to add their own businesses and presences inside the platform. This included for-profit corporations such as Adidas, BBC, and Wells Fargo, as well as nonprofits such as the American Cancer Society and Save the Children, and even universities, including Harvard, whose law school offered exclusive courses inside Second Life. In 2007, a stock exchange was launched on the platform with the aim of helping Second Life–based companies raise capital using the platform’s Linden Dollars currency.

Unlike most virtual worlds before and after Second Life, its developer Linden Labs did not intermediate transactions between players, nor actively manage what was made or sold. Instead, transactions were made directly between buyers and sellers and based on perceived value and need. Overall, Linden Labs operated more like a government than a game maker. The company did provide some user-facing services, such as identity management, ownership records, and an in-world legal system. But its focus wasn’t on building out the Second Life universe directly. Instead, it enabled a thriving economy via ever-improving infrastructure, technical capabilities, and tools that would attract more developers and creators who would then create things for other users to do, places for them to visit, and items for them to buy—attracting more users and therefore more spending, which would in turn attract more investment from developers and creators. To this end, Second Life also offered users the ability to import virtual objects and textures made outside the platform. By 2005, just two years after it launched, Second Life’s annualized GDP exceeded $40 million.12 By 2009, it exceeded half a billion dollars, with users cashing out $55 million into real-world currency that year.13 Over Second Life’s first decade, a total of $3.2 billion in player-to-player transactions took place, with an average of more than 1.2 million individual transactions per day.14

For all the success of Second Life, it was the rise of virtual world platforms Minecraft and Roblox in the 2010s that brought Linden Labs’ ideas to mainstream audiences. In addition to offering significant technical enhancements compared to their predecessors, Minecraft and Roblox were far easier to use, too, due to their focus on children and teenage players. The results have been astounding.

By the end of 2021, more than 150 million people were using Minecraft each month—more than six times as many as in 2014, when Microsoft bought the platform—with the title also becoming the best-selling game in history. Despite this, Minecraft was far from the size of the new market leader, Roblox, which had grown from fewer than 5 million to 225 million monthly users over that same period. Put together, the two platforms were averaging more than 6 billion hours of monthly usage, with more than 100 million different virtual worlds having been created, and more than $1 billion in royalties paid to Roblox developers alone. The second most popular virtual world on Roblox, Adopt Me!, was created in 2017 by two hobbyist players under the age of 25; in 2021 alone, Adopt Me! received more than 10 billion visits—more than seven times the average number of global tourism visits in pre–COVID-19.15

In addition to being popular, the virtual worlds of Roblox and Minecraft consistently achieved new creative highs and made their presence felt in the “real world,” too. On a recurring basis, fans of franchises such as Game of Thrones or Star Wars, or sports teams such as Real Madrid or Manchester City, would spend weeks reproducing major locations brick by brick—such as the Santiago Bernabéu Stadium or even the 500 square miles of the fictional King’s Landing. One video game streamer, Aztter, constructed an original cyberpunk city out of an estimated 370 million Minecraft blocks, having worked an average of 16 hours per day for a year.16 In 2015, Verizon built a cellphone inside Minecraft that could browse the web and even complete live (though blocky) video calls with people in the “real world.”17

As the COVID-19 virus spread across China in February 2020, a community of Chinese Minecraft players rapidly re-created the 1.2-million-square-foot hospitals built in Wuhan as a tribute to the “IRL” (“in real life”) workers, receiving global press coverage.18 One month later, Reporters Sans Frontières (also known as Reporters Without Borders) commissioned the construction of a museum within Minecraft that was composed of over 12.5 million blocks assembled by 24 virtual builders in 16 different countries over some 250 hours combined.19 The Uncensored Library, as it was called, allowed users in countries such as Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt to read banned literature, as well as works promoting free speech and detailing the lives of slain journalists such as Jamal Khashoggi.

Despite the enormous growth in Minecraft’s and Roblox’s audiences and developer communities, many other platforms emerged and grew in the second half of the 2010s. In the summer of 2016, Niantic released Pokémon Go, which shared the core mechanics of most Pokémon titles—finding, capturing, training, and battling Pokémon—but required players to leave their homes and traverse a virtual map layered atop the real world. To catch a Pokémon that swam in the ocean, for example, a player would need to visit an ocean-side beach; to find a bumblebee-styled Pokémon, they would need to wander a local park in the summer. Once the Pokémon Go application noticed the player was close to a Pokémon, a battle would trigger, in which the user could see a 3D version of the creature through their smartphone screen and camera, then throw an animated pokéball to capture the creature, which would also try to evade the player. By visiting various virtual locations set around physical landmarks, the user could also train their Pokémon, and battle other players at “gyms” based on key locations such as museums or statues. After six months, Pokémon Go amassed more than half a billion downloads and half a billion in revenue. By its sixth anniversary, lifetime revenue exceeded $6 billion with monthly players averaging between 75 and 150 million. The title was praised for its promotion of physical activity, helping local businesses grow as a result of increased foot traffic, and fostering in-person connection among players who didn’t know one another. Notably, Niantic was a spin-off from Google’s Geo division, which oversaw Google Maps, Google Earth, and Google Street View. Niantic’s CEO, John Hanke, had run the division until the spin-off, having joined with the sale of Keyhole, where he was co-founder and CEO.

In 2017, Epic Games launched Fortnite, which quickly established itself as a platform for mass culture, rather than just a virtual pastime. In 2018 and 2019 (the last years with publicly available data), Fortnite collected more than $9 billion in net revenue—mostly through the sale of virtual apparel that had no performance-related or competitive value. These sales exceeded those of storied fashion houses and brands such as Dolce & Gabbana, Saint Laurent, J.Crew, Prada, and Lacoste. Unlike these physical labels, however, Fortnite had only design costs, rather than manufacturing and shipping/fulfillment expenses, making Epic one of the most profitable apparel makers globally. By the end of 2023, brands such as Nike, Balenciaga, LVMH, Moncler, and Ralph Lauren had released exclusive virtual apparel inside Fortnite, as well as complementary physical editions with prices that ran into the thousands. Before passing away from cancer at the age of 41, Virgil Abloh, the founder and CEO of Off-White and creative director of Louis Vuitton menswear, announced the creation of a virtual-only fashion label, saying, “I want to make virtual clothes to paint pictures physical clothes cannot, and let buyers access a new dimension of their personal style—no matter who they are, where they live, and the virtual worlds they love.”20

In 2018, Epic launched Fortnite Creative, its own riff on Minecraft’s and Roblox’s world-building modes, with brands such as Nike and Coachella, as well as the Estate of Martin Luther King Jr., establishing a presence. The following year, Fortnite hosted a live, interactive, and canonical prologue to the Star Wars film The Rise of Skywalker, which also included a live interview with director J. J. Abrams. The year after that, hip-hop star (and Kardashian family member) Travis Scott hosted a concert that was attended live by over 12 million players, with millions more watching live on social media. As a point of contrast, fewer than 9 million Americans attended The Avengers: Endgame, which holds the record for highest single-day ticket sales in American history, during its first 24 hours of release. The track Scott premiered during the concert, which featured Kid Cudi, debuted at #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 charts a week later, was Cudi’s first #1 track, and finished 2020 as the third-largest US debut of the year. In addition, several of the tracks Scott performed from his two-year-old Astroworld album returned to the Billboard charts after the concert, with the official event video accumulating more than 200 million views. Fortnite would go on to host live shows with artists such as Steve Aoki, Ariana Grande, and J Balvin; exclusively premiere trailers to films such as Christopher Nolan’s Tenet; host film festivals; and tie in with the 75th anniversary of the NBA.

In the history of the Metaverse from MUDs to Fortnite, a few points are clear. Efforts to build a parallel virtual existence span decades rather than just a few buzzy years. As graphical capability, experiential diversity, and the number of internet users grew, so did the popularity of the top virtual worlds. Moreover, growth seems likely to continue in the years to come. But to understand why so many companies declared for the Metaverse in 2020–22, it’s necessary to examine the technical side of the history detailed above. Recall Sweeney’s 2021 observation: not only has a “critical mass of working pieces started coming together,” it is “coming together rapidly.” The best place to start is with live graphical simulation technologies.

Real-Time Graphical Simulation

The first attempts to build a “computer game” or “video game” emerged in the 1940s. The 1947 “cathode-ray tube amusement device” is considered the first interactive electronic game, but it did not use a computer or any form of memory device or program. Instead, the player adjusted various knobs to change the trajectory of a CRT beam so that it would align with plastic targets overlaid on the device’s screen.21 In 1948, the celebrated mathematician, computer scientist, and cryptanalyst Alan Turing began development of Turochamp, which was intended to play a full game of chess with a human player, but the code proved too complex for even military computers of the era.

In 1950, the Canadian inventor Josef Kates unveiled Bertie the Brain, a nearly four-meter-tall computer that, for all its immensity, could play just a single game that spanned only two different inputs and nine total decisions: tic-tac-toe. Bertie was incapable of producing computer graphics; the moves of both the player and Bertie’s AI were represented by the turning on and off of various lightbulbs.‡ OXO, a 1952 tic-tac-toe title which was developed at the University of Cambridge as part of a research study, added on-screen computer graphics and ran on a general-purpose computer rather than purpose-built one (though this meant the computer was the size of the room, rather than an everyday storage cabinet).

Until 1958’s Tennis for Two, all “video games” had been made to test computer-programming capabilities or evaluate human-computer interactions rather than for entertainment. Still, Tennis for Two had no leisurely origin story—and it still required several hundred pounds of professional equipment.22 The title was created by William Higinbotham, an American physicist working at Brookhaven National Laboratory, which had been established by the US Atomic Energy Commission following World War II, and was based on research used to simulate the trajectory of missiles under various wind conditions. Specifically, Tennis for Two’s display ran on an oscilloscope, which graphically displayed voltage-based signals as waveforms. Higinbotham programmed his oscilloscope for three different voltage inputs—one each for the tennis court, its net, and a ball—that cycled so rapidly that a human player would see all three at the same time. The ball, meanwhile, was adapted from the missile arcs. As the name suggests, Tennis for Two was also a multiplayer title—the first in history. It was also the first video game whose graphics were in a constant state of change. Earlier titles with computer-generated graphics, such as OXO, changed only when a move was made.

The video game sector shifted from its infancy to childhood in 1962 following the release of the multiplayer combat title Spacewar! Originally created at MIT by Steve Russell and fellow members of the school’s Tech Model Railroad Club, Spacewar! became the first video game that was playable outside a single research institute and to be installed on multiple computers. In fact, Russell promptly open-sourced the title’s codebase, inspiring other computer scientists and hobbyists to use his creation to build their own.

The 1970s saw four major innovations in graphics-based simulations. The first was the release of the first video game console, 1972’s Magnavox Odyssey. For only $99.95 (equivalent to roughly $750 in 2024), a family could purchase an easy-to-use, shoebox-sized computer designed to play 28 games, including Pong, each of which was limited to white shapes on blank black screen and no sound. The second and third innovations came via MUDs and MUSHs, which pioneered both user-generated virtual world creation and the ability for multiple users to co-experience that world over the internet. The fourth advance was “3D,” though these early efforts focused on producing the sensation of 3D rather than “true 3D.” The first such example was Maze, which debuted in 1973 and was made by high school students Steve Colley, Greg Thompson, and Howard Palmer during a study program at NASA’s Ames Research Center.23 Maze was a first-person-perspective title in which players navigated through a labyrinth of seemingly endless, identically designed hallways. Though users could move forward or backward, or take a left or right to travel down an intersecting hallway, their perspective was always straight ahead, with no ability to look up or down (vertical axis) or to the side (horizontal). When the player did make a turn, the very next frame would place them in the center of the new hallway, rather than show the user’s eyeline as it shifted across a doorframe and from one pathway to another. And if the player wanted to move forward or backward, they could do so only in fixed one-step increments. In truth, the maze didn’t even have a 3D model. Instead, it was composed of coordinate-based intersections of green lines that provided the illusion of angles and three dimensions.

In 1980, Atari released Battlezone, which let users take control of a tank viewport as they navigated a large two-dimensional map, that included various pyramid- and block-shaped obstacles, and fought enemy combatants. In contrast to Maze, players could look right and left, but the underlying mechanics were similar. Opponents and obstacles looked like they were 3D thanks to their geometric green outlines and 360-degree rotations, but this was an illusion similar to that produced by quickly flipping through a stack of papers that, sheet by sheet, portrayed a tank rotating from left to right. And while enemy tanks and hazards were often wider at the base than at their top, the tank could only ever shoot straight ahead and its shells, unlike the balls of 1958’s Tennis for Two, had no gravity-like arcs. As such, the varying widths were of purely aesthetic value (in fact, the game could have been played with only a single horizontal row of pixels). Battlezone’s background hills, meanwhile, would enlarge and shrink as the players moved backward or forward, but could never be reached.

A Reproduction of the 1973 Game Maze (also known as Maze War)

In 1991, John Carmack, Adrian Carmack (no relation to John Carmack), Tom Hall, and John Romero founded id Software, which released the groundbreaking Catacomb 3-D in 1991, Wolfenstein 3D in 1992, and Doom in 1993. Though these titles seemed to be 3D—and offered full-color maps and models—they are not typically described as “true” or “full” 3D.

Imagine playing the classic Pac-Man arcade game, but with the camera (and all in-game assets) swung down 90 degrees from a bird’s-eye view into first person. The player, as Pac-Man, would see hallways dozens of feet long, several feet tall, and several feet wide, and be able to travel freely forward and backward, while also turning right or left at an intersection. Though this might seem 3D, the game’s ghosts, pellets, and fruit would still be flat 2D models with no sides or backs, let alone angles. These objects would sit squarely in the center of view at all times, too, and could not be ducked under or jumped over when moving forward. Meanwhile, the level itself would remain flat, with no stairs, hurdles, or even inclines or declines, with the player also unable to tilt their camera up or down. And because tilting the camera angle does not add any more detail to the map, moving forward or backward would, from a visual perspective, resemble zooming in or out from a given perspective (not unlike zooming in or out on a Google Street View image, which either tightens or widens the view, with the image blurring or sharpening accordingly).

id’s Catacomb 3-D effectively pioneered the Pac-Man example described above and, in doing so, created a thrill ride that felt not only 3D but new. The title was a fast-moving action shooter with large maps, swappable guns, depleting health and ammo meters that could be replenished through in-game items, secret doors the player could push through to reveal hidden pathways, and the ability for players to move “naturally” across its map, rather than jump across preset chess- or checkers-like positions.

In 1992, id debuted Doom, which maintained the 3D approach of 1991’s Catacomb 3-D, but seemed to offer players the ability to travel to higher and lower levels. Mechanically, it was akin to visually elevating half of a Pac-Man maze. The titular hero might seem to fall down from or jump up to this higher level, but there would be no real interaction between the two layers, and the process of moving from one to another was just an in-game animation. In the case of Doom, a player sitting on the top of a ledge would still be shooting straight, but their bullets would hit an enemy down below as though they were standing side by side. And if the player were below the ledge, they could not “shoot” up, just straight into the wall. And above the wall was just more wall that looked like the top of the ledge. Though these were tricks, the result was still stunning—especially given that Doom, unlike Catacomb 3-D, supported local and internet-based multiplayer.

In 1996, id released its “first true 3D” game, Quake, which boasted full 3D models, uneven terrain, the ability to look up and shoot artillery that would follow gravity-like arcs when shot—and even as these explosives ricocheted among walls, columns, and other obstacles. Though Quake was another landmark for the gaming industry, id’s earlier achievements had already convinced many of its peers that the era of real-time 3D had arrived. One of the first to subscribe to this view was Epic Games.

Epic had been founded by Tim Sweeney in 1991, the same year as id, but the company initially focused on 2D games, such as ZZT, Jazz Jackrabbit, and Jill of the Jungle. According to Sweeney, the release of “Wolfenstein and DOOM … changed everything. The titans were busy building huge 2D games and Epic took a huge leap of faith on 3D.”24 In the months after Wolfenstein’s release, one of id’s business leads, Mark Rein, joined Sweeney as a co-founder, and by 1995, Epic had merged all of its smaller teams working on 2D games into one focused on a true 3D game—1998’s Unreal.

Like Quake, Unreal was a “true 3D” sci-fi multiplayer shooter and an instant hit. It achieved an 89% average review on GameRankings (the predecessor to Metacritic),25 was the 14th-best-selling PC game of the year,26 sold 1.5 million units by its fourth anniversary,27 and led to a direct sequel in 2003, as well as four multiplayer-focused spin-offs (Unreal Tournament in 1999, Unreal Tournament 2003, Unreal Tournament 2004, and Unreal Tournament 3 in 2007). As discussed at the start of this chapter, Unreal was also Epic’s first effort to build a “proto-Metaverse,” though it was limited to “text chat” and “300-polygon strangers.” Despite the success of the game, Unreal’s greatest legacy was the technology that powered it.

Unreal had cost about $3 million to produce ($6 million in 2024 dollars), most of which was spent on its engine, dubbed “Unreal Engine,” rather than gameplay or artwork. Most game developers at the time could not afford such investments and those that could weren’t guaranteed an equally useful result, either. And so in 1996, two years before Unreal was even released to the public, Sweeney bet he could build a business around its engine. Though licensing UE meant aiding Epic’s rivals, some of whom produced directly competitive titles such as Duke Nukem, it netted the company $250,000–$350,000 in up-front payments and 5%–7% in royalties in each case.28 It also enabled Epic to further its investment in UE and to benefit from the R&D of its licensees, too. In September of 1998, Sweeney told Maximum PC: “The big goal with the Unreal technology all along was to build up a base of code that could be extended and improved through many generations of games.”29

In 1996, id had begun selectively licensing its Quake Engine, too—and saw early success when Valve produced its 1998 blockbuster title Half-Life using a modified version of the Quake Engine—but most developers opted to build on UE. And while Unreal was inspired by the early 3D games of id Software, the Unreal Engine’s source of inspiration was Epic’s very first game, the 2D puzzler ZZT.

In 1989, Sweeney had begun building a text editor,§ because he didn’t like those available on PCs at the time. Eventually, he transformed the cursor into a smiley face, then designed and inserted other characters into the application, followed by labyrinth-like walls, the ability to collect ammo and shoot enemies, discovery keys used to unlock doors, and so on, until he had produced a colorful 2D action-adventure puzzle game. After encouragement from friends, Sweeney decided to release ZZT publicly in January 1991.30 By November, the 20-year-old Sweeney was generating over $3,000 in monthly sales from ZZT (equivalent to $6,700 in 2024 prices). Less than a year later, monthly sales exceeded $25,000 ($58,000).31

A Screenshot of the Homescreen for Epic Games’ ZZT

Due to its origins as a text editor, ZZT’s “graphics” were actually just made up of the 256 characters that constituted the ASCII standard, each of which was one byte in size, and spanned the numbers 0–9, lower- and uppercase versions of all 26 English letters, various mathematical symbols such as π and + as well as select punctuation like !, shading blocks like or , and other signs like ↑ and . While ASCII had been popular in the 1960s and 1970s, it had largely fallen out of style as computers gained the ability to render individual pixels, which led to the rise of more specialized in-game art. As such, ZZT’s visuals were inferior to those of titles as old as 1978’s Space Invaders or other maze-focused games like Pac-Man—and the title fell particularly short of other 1991 releases, such as Sonic the Hedgehog and The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past. Yet ZZT’s technical foundations provided the title with a key advantage.

In addition to its fun and intuitive gameplay, ZZT thrived because of Sweeney’s decision to include a customized version of the very software he used to make it, thus allowing users to build their own levels using his ZZT-OOP scripting language. ZZT was not the first video game to support or encourage “user-generated content”—MUDs were based on that very premise and dedicated game-creation software had been released throughout the 1980s for consoles such as the Commodore 64 or Atari ST. However, ZZT’s origins as an editing program and Sweeney’s interest in such functionality meant that ZZT’s tools were far easier to use than those afforded by other titles. In contrast with other game creators, ZZT was also downloaded over the internet, rather than purchased via cartridge or disk. Accordingly, users could easily (and freely) share their mazes with other users online, which helped grow awareness of ZZT while also deepening its gameplay.

Eventually, Sweeney announced a contest in which users could submit their mazes to his company, then known as Potomac Computer Systems. The winning entries were then packaged in the 1992 sequels Best of ZZT and ZZT’s Revenge, with their creators receiving gift certificates and/or honorable mentions in the game’s credits (six creators even won jobs at the newly renamed Epic MegaGames).32

Sweeney credits ZZT with convincing him to start a gaming company and setting its “core philosophy.… We both build games ourselves and we share all the results of our work with the world to build their own games.”33 And as the company shifted its focus to 3D in the mid-1990s, Sweeney aspired to produce a 3D engine that was as easy to use as it was powerful, thereby enabling creative teams to spend more of their time making a game, not building the tools needed to do so, or learning how to use those same tools. To Sweeney, ZZT was “sort of a prototype Unreal Engine 0.”34

The development of easy-to-use, cross-company tools such as UE are key to establishing the Metaverse. Previously, building a virtual world required a developer/creator to acquire deep technical expertise and design their own tools, just like Epic Games or id Software, or build within a platform, such as Second Life or ZZT. The former approach constrained how many virtual worlds were created, and led to technical fragmentation that made interoperation difficult. The latter approach, meanwhile, produced networks within an application, rather than a network of applications.

In the quarter century since its debut, the Unreal Engine (now UE5) has become the most widely used “high-fidelity” engine for 3D games. Unity, a rival engine that launched in 2005, powers more than 50% of mobile games. And these engines are increasingly used outside of gaming, too.

Although the first few dozen virtual worlds were designed for scientific purposes, such as Turochamp, Bertie the Brain, OXO, Tennis for Two, Spacewar!, and Maze, nearly all of those created since were designed for video games. This skew is partly why so many liken the Metaverse to such experiences. It’s also a contrast with the traditional adoption curve for advanced computing and networking technologies.

The first computers were too large, expensive, and power intensive for anyone but governments and major enterprises to afford, let alone use. Moreover, these devices were too difficult for the average person to use and their utility was limited to (slowly) solving complex calculations that were relevant only to research labs and governments. Accordingly, it was more than 50 years until half of computers were owned by consumers and longer still for most usage to be noncommercial. The arc of the internet was similar. Over its first 20 years, bandwidth was too limited and latency too great for the internet to support consumer use cases such as photo sharing, let alone video calls or streaming, but it was more than capable of sharing word documents, spreadsheets, and messages, which were of immense value to the “information economy” and far superior to using couriers and postal services. And while early smartphones could barely play Snake, let alone support color displays, businesses and governments considered push email to be orders of magnitude more helpful than pager notifications or live phone calls.

In contrast to the path of computers and the internet, 3D simulations have limitations that historically prevented their adoption by industry and government services and instead confined them to consumer-focused implementation. All a “game” needs from simulation is to create a sense of fun; the physics of a building on fire, a car crash, or a shotgun pellet do not need to be realistic—and are sometimes better because they’re fantastical. Military personnel, surgeons, and infrastructure operators, meanwhile, need far greater fidelity. And it’s only over the past few years that this has been possible.

By the start of the 2020s, a company that had access to enough computing power could run large-scale, real-time simulations down to the particle level, enabling precise readings of heat absorption, transference, and dissipation, the effects of vibrations, the flow of sound, the reflection of light, the accumulation of radiation, and so on. The engines behind these simulations recently became “deterministic,” too—able to generate the identical outcome each time they were run, rather than nondeterministic, in which outcomes are largely but not precisely alike.

The many advances in real-time 3D simulation have resulted in new usages. In 2019, the Hong Kong International Airport produced a digital twin using the Unity Engine that simulates critical airport activity in real time, from passenger movement to planes and vehicles on the runway, as well as inbound traffic and their dependencies. This information is then used to predict and address potential backups and gate changes, and to prepare for and respond to emergency situations. In other cases, entire cities have been re-created and then connected to real-time data feeds for vehicular traffic, weather, and civic services, such as police, fire, and ambulance response. The goal of a digital twin is to enable city planners to make more informed decisions about zoning, construction approvals, and more. How would a new commercial mall affect travel times for emergency medical or police services? How might a specific building design adversely affect wind conditions, urban temperatures, or downtown light?

A good way to understand the practical potential of city-scale digital twins, unsurprisingly, came from video gaming. In December 2021, Epic Games released The Matrix Awakens, a playable technical demonstration that was intended to show off the functionality of the forthcoming Unreal Engine 5 when running on the newly released PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S|X, which kicked off the “ninth generation of video game consoles” (the 1972 Magnavox Odyssey was first gen). Matrix Awakens was set in a procedurally generated and photorealistic city that was 16 square kilometers in area, spanning 7,000 buildings, 260 kilometers of drivable roads with 1,250 intersections, 50,000 cars (nearly all of which could be walked up to and driven), and 40,000 pedestrians.35 “Players,” if one could call them that, could change the city’s time of day in real time and watch the sun’s rays shift and bounce across various buildings and windshields, as well as modify the number of pedestrians and cars, and then watch how the flow of traffic and people altered as a result. Some masochistic users even orchestrated traffic accidents so severe that hours later, they could observe how traffic jams had spread throughout the city.

In September of 2022, job postings at Tesla revealed the company was working to make Epic’s demonstration a reality by producing a live 3D model of the city of San Francisco using the Unreal Engine.36 Unlike Epic’s demo, Tesla’s simulation doesn’t need to run on a single, consumer-brand video game console. Instead, it can be operated on Tesla’s private supercomputer cluster, or on the data centers of cloud computing giants such as Amazon and Microsoft. And Tesla’s virtual San Francisco is not made by designers or generative models, but assembled and maintained using the myriad real-time lidar scans and positional pings generated by the network of San Franciscan Teslas. The resulting simulation would aid city planning, autonomous driving software, and human navigation.

Tesla wasn’t the only tech giant to imagine a living Metaverse version of Google Street View; Google, too, was hard at work. In June of 2023, the company launched its Geospatial Creator tool, which let users create 3D/augmented reality experiences that could be “anchored” to real-world locations inside Google’s various mapping programs for other users to see and experience. To commemorate the launch, Google announced an AR-based reinvention of the 1978 hit video game Space Invaders. Unlike the arcade classic, however, the titular enemies would rain down not from the top of a CRT-display but from the skies of major cities such as Rio de Janeiro and New York, and they would be repelled not through joysticks and buttons but by smartphone-wielding citizens throughout the city. Nvidia, meanwhile, announced it was building “Earth-2,” a live digital twin that would model “the physics, chemistry and biology of the atmosphere, waters, ice, land and [aggregate] human activities” of the earth down to the “meter-scale resolution [that] is needed to simulate [as an example] clouds that reflect sunlight back to space.”37

Head-Mounted Displays

As the field of graphical simulation progressed, so too did efforts to build “head-mounted displays” capable of realizing “Pygmalion’s Spectacles.”

In 1955, the American cinematographer Morton Heilig wrote a famous paper, “The Cinema of the Future,” declaring that “pandemonium [reigned] supreme in the film industry,” with studios “hastily converting to its own ‘revolutionary’ system—Cinerama, Colorama, Panoramic Screens, Cinemascope, Three-D, and Stereophonic Sound,” which were used to “lure” customers with (false) promises of a “sensational new experience.”38 Worse still, Heilig argued, “art” had fallen behind “science” and “industry” in using contemporary technology and research into the human mind to make its products more “effective.”39 In many cases, art failed to achieve “active participation” from a spectator—and without it “there can be no transfer of consciousness, no art.”40
