The remedy, to Heilig, was to activate four of the human species’ five primary senses (sight, hearing, smell, and touch), which contemporary research suggested “monopolized man’s attention” to 99% (respectively, 70%, 20%, 5%, and 4%, with taste making up the remaining 1%).41 Due to sight’s share, he also argued that all of a spectator’s visual field must be filled with a screen, rather than the 5% offered by contemporary movie theaters, the 7.5% of widescreen-equipped theaters, the 18% of Cinemascope, or the 25% of Cinerama.42 Ideally, the screen would offer “true and not illusory depth … another essential element of man’s consciousness” which would be achieved by “electronic and optical means,” rather than the tricks of polarized glasses, which first emerged in the late 1800s and were popularized by the 1930s.43 Not long after his paper, Heilig got to work.

In 1960, the cinematographer-turned-inventor patented the “Telesphere Mask,” which would give spectators “a complete sensation of reality, i.e. moving three dimensional images which may be in colour, with 100% peripheral vision, binaural sound, scents and air breezes.”44 The device looks astonishingly similar to modern HMD patents and supported stereoscopic (3D) and widescreen TV and true stereo sound (though no motion capture).45

Two years later, Heilig patented the Sensorama, an “Experience Theater” designed to fully realize his vision of the Cinema of the Future.46 This time, the “device” was an arcade-sized cabinet equipped with a screen, surround-sound system, fans, odor emitters that reproduced smells such as that of pizza and petroleum, and a moving chair—all of which were timed to specific events in movies that had also been produced by Heilig. Though the Sensorama was considered a marvel for decades after its unveiling, Heilig, like Professor Ludwig, was unable to find backers for his pioneering device and returned to traditional filmmaking by the 1970s.

Morton Heilig’s Telesphere Mask

In 1961, the Philco electronics company developed the first head-mounted display, the Headsight, which had a dedicated screen for each eye, as well as a magnetic motion detector that was connected to an external camera that moved with the user’s head. Though notable for its form factor, the Headsight was never intended to represent virtual reality, but instead to allow military users a live, first-person view of areas that were too dangerous to physically access.47

In 1965, Ivan Sutherland detailed “The Ultimate Display,” a concept document that continues to guide VR research decades later. Sutherland’s objectives included the creation of a synthetic digital world that was photorealistic, supported 3D sound, provided haptic feedback, was fully interactive, and endured beyond the user’s personal experience inside the display. Moreover, Sutherland imagined this display being worn in a physical location that complemented his virtual world but was also controlled by the same computer. As he wrote, “A chair displayed in such a room would be good enough to sit in. Handcuffs displayed in such a room would be confining.” More alarmingly, Sutherland imagined “a bullet displayed in such a room would be fatal,” though “with appropriate programming,” he argued, the room and display paired together “could literally be the Wonderland into which Alice walked.”48 By 1968, Sutherland had converted his theorizing into a real HMD, commonly known as the “Sword of Damocles.”¶ Sutherland’s device could not control a physical space, but it is considered the first HMD able to generate its imagery via computer, rather than just relay the live video feed from a camera or play back prerecorded video. As one might expect, the Sword of Damocles did not have an onboard computer, but instead connected to a computer that was nearly as large as a typical American bedroom.

Morton Heilig’s Sensorama

Through the 1970s and 1980s, HMDs continued to progress, with a particular focus on simulating flight for professional pilots and other aviators. In 1989, NASA created project VIEW (Virtual Interface Environment Workstation), an HMD that could display an “artificial computer-generated environment or a real environment relayed from remote video cameras.”49 In addition to the display, operators would wear a “DataGlove” that used fiber-optic cables and sensors that could reproduce their hands inside the VIEW, as well as a similarly functional “DataSuit,” which was also programmed to understand gestures.50 The 1990s saw both Nintendo and Sego release VR headsets and gloves, though neither was a success.

After decades of unsuccessful tinkering from toy makers, inventors, and public research labs, big tech began to plow billions into the HMD field in the early 2010s. In 2010, Rony Abovitz, who previously founded MAKO Surgical Corp., which designed and manufactured robotic arms to aid live patient surgery, launched Magic Leap, which designed and manufactured mixed-reality devices primarily aimed at industrial and governmental applications. By the time Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund acquired a majority stake in Magic Leap in 2022, the company had raised more than $4 billion (though reports suggested it sold for less than that sum). Also in 2010, Microsoft started development of HoloLens AR platform,# which also focused on enterprise usage, with the first model releasing in 2016 and a follow-up in 2019, and Google kicked off its Google Glass smart glasses, which were designed for consumer users. The first Google Glass Explorer was released in 2013, with an enterprise-focused unit launching in 2019 and a reconceived and rebranded design publicly field-tested in 2022. Google’s Cardboard VR platform debuted in 2014, with Google’s second VR platform, Daydream, coming two years later. Sony PlayStation began development of its VR platform in 2011, and the PS VR came to market in 2016. In 2014, Snap acquired Vergence Labs, an AR glasses start-up that had been founded in 2011, and served as the foundation for the Snap Spectacles, which premiered in 2016, with the Spectacles 2, Spectacles 3, and Spectacles 4 releasing over the following five years. Amazon began development of its Alexa-based AR glasses sometime in 2016 or 2017. The first Echo Frames were released in 2019; the second edition arrived two years later.

NASA’s Project VIEW and DataGlove

As Magic Leap, Microsoft, and Google started their HMD divisions, Palmer Luckey, an HMD designer at the University of Southern California Institute for Creative Technologies, began developing a VR device that later became known as the Oculus. At the time, Luckey was rumored to own the largest personal collection of HMDs in the world, and his goal for the Oculus was to build a device more capable than any other available in the market at the time but also cheaper. At the time, John Carmack, the id Software founder, had also been investigating the HMD field and heard about Luckey’s work. After trying a prototype Oculus in late 2011, Carmack began to help Luckey with his research, and at the 2012 E3 video game convention in Los Angeles, the “father of 3D graphics” gave the first public demonstration of the Oculus (which was visibly held together by duct tape) and announced Doom 3 would be ported to the device. The following year, Carmack joined Oculus as chief technology officer and left id shortly thereafter. A year after that, Facebook purchased Oculus VR for $2 billion, with Carmack staying on until 2022, when he left to found Keen Technologies, an artificial general intelligence start-up.

Despite the tens of billions spent on VR and AR HMDs by mid-2020, the lifetime sales of these devices were fewer than $30 million combined.51 But then, suddenly, these investments seemed to mature.

In June 2020, neurosurgeons at Johns Hopkins performed America’s first and second surgeries on a live patient using an FDA-approved AR device. The first was a spinal fusion surgery, during which six screws were inserted into the patient’s spine, while the second concerned the removal of a cancerous tumor on another patient’s spine. In both cases, the surgeon used a head-mounted AR device that rendered a 3D model based on a CT of the patient’s spinal column and internal bone structures, which displayed, in real time, the surgeon’s tools and insertions, plus the patient’s vitals. By the end of 2022, Dr. Timothy Witham, who performed Johns Hopkins’s AR surgeries and is the director of the hospital’s Spinal Fusion Laboratory, had completed more than 150 live patient surgeries using an AR device, with dozens of other such surgeries taking place across the United States.52

In September of 2020, Mercedes-Benz announced it would deploy Microsoft’s HoloLens 2 AR device across its nearly 400 dealerships throughout the United States to local technicians performing complex repairs.53 Specifically, the device would provide technicians with on-screen schematics, automatically highlight the parts that needed testing or repairs, and guide installations and removals, while also warning of key risks, such as the potential for a burn. Technicians could also use the device to video-call Mercedes’s own centralized experts, who would be able to instruct the local technicians while watching their efforts in real time from the HoloLens’s front-facing camera.

Throughout 2020 and 2021, each of the ten largest upstream oil and gas companies began to incorporate VR devices into their training programs, especially for those who would be stationed on oil rigs and platforms. Not only are these facilities entirely foreign to most new hires, but they are in remote locations and dangerous; in the United States, oil rig and platform fatality rates are 25–30 per 100,000 (45–50 for drill workers), more than seven times the national average.54 One oil and gas executive reported that beyond reduced training time and accident rates, the use of VR devices in workplace onboarding had even led to new safety signage, placements, and instructions after eye tracing revealed that many trainees struggled to locate (or otherwise missed) emergency information in test scenarios.

In March 2021, the US Army announced a deal to buy up to 120,000 customized AR HoloLens devices from Microsoft over the following decade. This contract was valued at $22 billion—nearly $200,000 per headset (this sum includes hardware upgrades, repairs, bespoke software, and other Azure cloud computing services). In a press release, Master Sergeant Marc Krugh, who supported the army-Microsoft AR partnership since its inception, said the device would enable soldiers “to rehearse and train in more realistic scenarios.”55 The army-specific HoloLens unit, called IVAS (Integrated Visual Augmentation System), used HoloLens’s technology, while adding thermal imagery, additional sensors, GPS, and night vision to provide situation inputs and live training data to soldiers. Users could see where they were on the battlefield, as well as what and who was around them, by “projecting holographic images, three-dimensional terrain maps and a compass onto their field of vision.” Microsoft boasted that IVAS would enable users to shift their view to the simulated “vantage point of combatants” and evaluate not just their prospect for success but how they might be affected by daylight, moonlight, rain, and so on. The army was particularly keen on the ability to minimize the risk of friendly fire and improve the ability to escape a firefight. When paired with a weapon sight, IVAS allowed soldiers to see as their rifle might see, thereby providing the ability to “safely look around corners.”

Alongside the rapid deployment of commercial HMDs was an equally sudden, and even larger, surge in consumer demand. In May of 2019, Facebook released the Quest 1, the sixth VR device released by its Oculus division. Over its first 14 months on sale, fewer than 1 million total units were shipped. The Quest 2, which released in October 2020, sold 1 million units in under 100 days and crossed 10 million by its one-year anniversary. Moreover, the Quest 2’s sales figures were comparable to those of Microsoft’s Xbox S|X console, which had sold roughly 12 million units since its debut in November 2020, and not far off from the 16 million units sold by PlayStation 5, which also came to market in November 2020. The Quest 2’s growth over the Quest 1 also recalled the second iPhone, which outsold the first iPhone three to one and ushered in the smartphone era. In 2022, Mark Zuckerberg revealed that it was the success of the Quest 2 that inspired him to publicly unveil Facebook’s Metaverse ambitions and rename the company.56 By the end of 2022, annual spend on VR applications was estimated at more than a billion dollars per year, three-quarters of which was billed through Facebook’s Quest Store.57

For many, the clearest signal that the age of mixed-reality headsets was imminent came on June 6, 2023. At its Worldwide Developers Conference, Apple unveiled its long-awaited Vision Pro headset at its Cupertino, California, headquarters, with an average of 725,000 people watching the more than two-hour-long video.58 The Vision Pro represented Apple’s most significant product launch since 2007’s iPhone, with tens of billions in R&D invested and more than 5,000 patents behind what the company called “the most advanced personal electronics device ever” and the start of a “new era of computing … spatial computing.”59 Among the many use cases demonstrated were virtual movie theaters, mixed-reality school lessons, and immersive 3D “memories.”

Given the attention paid to the new 3D-focused devices, it has been easy to overlook the investments that added spatial functionality to traditional 2D form factors. In 2016, Apple released its first iPhone model with two rear cameras, enabling apps to focus on two fields of depth at the same time. Starting in 2017, the standard-issue iPhone came equipped with two rear cameras, with that year’s model also adding infrared (IR) sensors to the front-facing camera that could track and recognize 30,000 points on a user’s face in real time. To support this new hardware, Apple introduced ARKit, a software frame that helped developers build AR apps using the iPhone’s many cameras, computer and graphics processors, and motion sensors. The results were immediate.

In 2015, Snap launched AR filters, which used a phone’s camera and processor to understand a face and contextually layer on top a 3D effect, such as sunglasses, a beard, or blue eyes, all in real time. At the time, all filters were produced by Snapchat. Two months after the 2017 launch of Apple’s ARKit and IR-enabled iPhone X, Snap launched Lens Studio, which enabled third-party developers and eventually users to create their own lenses. Two years later, the company reported that users had created more than 600,000 AR lenses, with 142 million using at least one AR lens daily;60 by April 2021, Snap said it had 200 million daily users of its AR lenses, with over a million AR lenses having been created.61

Apple’s AR investments, which were rapidly replicated by Google’s Android operating system and ecosystem of device manufacturers, also enabled Pokémon Go to embrace “true AR.” Upon its release in July 2017, Pokémon Go’s “AR” was really just a 3D character or object layered overtop whatever the user’s camera was pointed to and without reference to what it saw, or its implications. A Pikachu might be seen on top of a user’s back lawn, but if the user tilted their camera to the sky or underground, Pikachu would still be there and not seem to know that fact, either. But starting three months after Apple’s ARKit and iPhone X, Niantic began a series of contextual AR upgrades. Now, Pikachu would be layered correctly on top of the user’s backyard, and if the user looked elsewhere, Pikachu would stay where it was. By 2020, Niantic had begun to roll out “occlusion,” whereby Pokémon might even hide behind a tree in the backyard, and a Pokéball thrown at Pikachu would appear to hit the tree and bounce away, rather than pass through it to the popular character.

In 2019, Apple added a third rear camera to its iPhone Pro line and also began to include ultra-wideband (UWB) transmitters and receivers into its full iPhone line, which enabled the devices to “see” through sound—just as a bat might. Specifically, Apple’s UWB transmitters were capable of emitting and processing up to a billion radar pulses per second. In doing so, these devices could generate spatial maps of a user’s home or workplace, precisely place itself within any preexisting map (whether generated by the user or available through a mapping app, such as those of Google or Apple), identify the location of other UWB devices within a few centimeters, and enhance the accuracy and safety of proximity-based smart home functionality (e.g., automatically unlock a home door when the user was approaching from outside but not when they were walking by inside the home).

Beginning with 2020’s iPhone 12 Pro, high-end iOS devices were also equipped with lidar scanners that enabled users to create high-fidelity 3D models by photographing real-world objects (a process called photogrammetry). The iPhone’s lidar-based photogrammetry capture is so powerful that many design and engineering professionals now use the device instead of $20,000–$30,000 dedicated lidar cameras. By the end of 2022, tens of thousands of private owners had used the device to produce high-resolution, immersive models of their homes, with the models then uploaded to real estate sites to better attract home buyers, or to furniture websites to help with interior decorating.

In May of 2021, Google announced Project Starline, the company’s efforts to reinvent the stodgy telepresence booth using photorealistic 3D models and machine learning software. The “magic” of traditional telepresence hardware, which first emerged in the early 1990s, was rooted in hardware and context. A corporate executive would feel as though their peers were sitting across from them in the boardroom because they (as well as their peers) were staring at a series of life-size monitors stationed on the other side of a circular table that had been cut in half. Moreover, the camera trained on each participant would be angled according to their placement on-screen (e.g., someone on the far right screen would sit to the left of the camera pointed at them, rather than head-on). As with its spiritual predecessors, Starline depended on hardware—in this case, a dozen depth sensors and cameras (together producing seven video streams from four viewpoints and three depth maps), four spatial audio speakers, and a fabric-based, multilayered light-field display. These many components, mixed with Google’s suite of computer vision and machine learning AI technologies, enabled participants to be captured and then rendered using volumetric data, rather than flattened 2D video.62 In effect, viewers were looking at a live 3D model (or a “photorealistic avatar”) of their family member, friend, or colleague, rather than 30 still images played per second. Though Google did not make Starline publicly available, the company’s internal research boasted about Starline’s improvements over traditional video calls. Starline users focused 15% more on those they were speaking to (based on eye-tracking data), displayed significantly greater nonverbal forms of communication (e.g., ~40% more hand gestures, ~25% more head nods, and ~50% more eyebrow movements), and had 30% increases in memory recall when asked to remember details from their conversation or meeting.63 In testing against the peer-reviewed Zoom Exhaustion & Fatigue Scale, Google found Starline users had 31% lower fatigue compared to those on traditional 2D calls, and exhibited 12% faster response times when completing cognitive tasks after the call.64 For those skeptical of why the internet needs broad 3D, or who have found Zoom, Microsoft Teams, or Google Meets exhausting or alienating, Starline offers one answer.

An Annotated Look at the 2021 Google Starline without Its Enclosure

Human Culture and Pastimes

While simulation technologies and devices increased in number and effectiveness, so too did the cultural embrace of 3D environments and socialization. As the world moved on from the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022, supposed “pandemic darlings” such as Zoom, Shopify, and Peloton began to shrink. Although many had predicted their categories were forever “pulled forward” by the global lockdowns of 2020 and 2021, this acceleration was illusory. In 2019, e-commerce constituted roughly 10% of total US retail spend and 15% of addressable retail spend. This share had grown in a fairly linear fashion from approximately 3.5% and 6% since 2009, gaining an average of 0.65 and 0.9 percentage points annually. In 2020, those sums surged to about 17% and 23% (+7 percentage points and +8 percentage points year over year). By 2023, however, e-commerce’s share was well below the level experienced in both 2020 and 2021, with roughly 15.5% and 22% (representing a decline of 1.5 and 1 percentage points over a three-year period). Furthermore, e-commerce’s share of retail sales in 2023 was almost exactly where pre-COVID trendlines would have predicted.65 Digital’s share of ad spend looks similar. Roblox, in contrast, continued to see new highs. Every quarter since the pandemic, Roblox exhibited year-over-year (if not quarter-over-quarter) increases in users and usage. Moreover, Roblox was adding more users and user hours each quarter than ever before.

It’s likely that Roblox experienced smaller-scale pullbacks as the pandemic eased. Some users probably played less frequently, or for less time, or stopped playing altogether. Yet the platform was benefiting from generational changes, too. Each year, 140 million people globally turn nine, entering the Roblox demographic for the first time. This generational shift, which e-commerce began to experience in the 1990s, also helps to explain why Roblox, a platform that launched in 2006, took a decade to take off.

Think back to the first two years following the release of the iPad. As the device’s sales grew, it became common to see press reports and viral YouTube videos of infants and young children who would pick up an “analog” magazine or book and try to “swipe” its nonexistent touchscreen. Today, those one-year-olds are thirteen to fourteen. A four-year-old in 2010 is well on her way to adulthood. These media consumers are now spending their own money on content—and some are already creating content themselves. And while these once unintelligible young people now understand why adults found their futile efforts to pinch-to-zoom a piece of paper so comic, older generations are not much closer to understanding how the worldviews and preferences of the young differ from their own. Most adults look at Roblox and see an uninteresting and rudimentary “game.” Kids see something much different: a milieu. Just as prior generations grew up talking on the phone for hours after school and loitering in malls, or on text chats and message boards or, later still, social media, younger Gen Zs and all of Gen Alpha look to platforms such as Roblox to socialize and make friends. Certainly, Roblox benefited from various technological improvements since its release, not the least of which was the launch of consumer-friendly portable computers, but it’s no coincidence that Roblox’s core users are the very children who grew up “iPad native” and expect everything they touch to be fully interactive. Fortunately for Roblox, this cohort grows by nearly 400,000 people every day.

Although many Metaverse pioneers believe blockchain and cryptocurrency technology have no place in the Metaverse (and potentially no future at all), the growth in these technologies during 2020, 2021, and 2022 reinforced society’s embrace of virtual existence.

In 2021, the combined value of all cryptocurrencies crossed $2.9 trillion,** with the Bitcoin blockchain processing a remarkable $4.7 trillion in bitcoin transaction value that year, and Ethereum managing $3.6 trillion in Ether.66 Though these sums fell short of credit card giants Visa ($10.4 trillion) and MasterCard ($6 trillion), they were more than American Express ($1.2 trillion), and more than the combined payments volume of Stripe, PayPal, Square, and Shopify ($1.3 trillion)—even though nearly all crypto payments are for virtual-only assets, currencies, securities, and tokens, rather than groceries, cars, travel, and so on. In 2022, Bitcoin and Ethereum transfer value declined (−13% and −56% respectively), but average daily transfers were largely flat (−3.3% and +3.7%), with the gap largely due to the declining price of bitcoin and ether throughout the calendar year.67 In contrast, the US dollar inflated by an average 8% in 2022. Throughout 2021, over $40 billion was spent buying Ethereum-based NFTs alone,68 only 11% shy of the $50 billion spent on physical art globally,69 with 2022 sales hitting roughly $25 billion70 against $68 billion.71 MetaMask, the most popular crypto wallet, reported that its monthly active users grew from fewer than 500,000 in September 2020 to 10 million a year later, crossing 30 million by March of 2022.72

Included in these multibillion- and multitrillion-dollar headlines were a number of significant cultural achievements, too. In July of 2021, the state of Wyoming legalized blockchain-based decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) as a corporate entity, having also been the first state to recognize the LLC business structure back in 1977.73 The following month, several thousand outdoor enthusiasts used a DAO to purchase a 40-acre plot of land near Yellowstone National Park, which the collective promptly turned into a public park funded and operated by its membership.74 Three months later, a crypto collective named ConstitutionDAO was formed after Sotheby’s announced that one of 13 surviving first editions of the United States Constitution was set for auction and expected to sell for between $15 and $20 million. Though ConstitutionDAO lost to Ken Griffin, the billionaire founder of the multinational hedge fund Citadel, it raised roughly $47 million in cryptocurrency from nearly 20,000 anonymous contributors in less than a week—none of which required a legal contract, lawyer, or even bank account.

Artificial Intelligence

A final area that saw sudden, multifaceted advances at the end of the 2010s and the early 2020s was artificial intelligence, which had been in active development longer than not just the Metaverse but the internet, too.

As early as the 1930s, philosophers and mathematicians began to debate whether a machine that processed logic through shuffling symbols as basic as 1 and 0 could be said to “deduce” or “reason.” In 1948, the University of Manchester unveiled the Manchester Mark 1, one of the first computers capable of storing (and thus recalling) a program, prompting the press to refer to the device as an “electronic brain.” As discussed earlier in this chapter, it was possible to play games such as tic-tac-toe against an AI by 1950, with checkers following in 1951.

In 1955, American computer scientist John McCarthy coined the term “artificial intelligence,” and in 1956, IBM researcher Arthur Samuel created one of the first adaptive computer programs, the Samuel Checkers-Playing Program, which improved its checkers performance by playing against itself. The year 1956 also saw the debut of Logic Theorist, the first automated reasoning program, which was developed by Allen Newell, Herbert A. Simon, and Cliff Shaw and is considered the first “true” AI. To test the device, its creators had Logic Theorist attempt to prove the first 52 theorems of Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell’s Principia Mathematica. It successfully proved 38 (or 74%) of them, and even established several new—and shorter—proofs than had been created by any human mathematician at the time.75 In 1958, McCarthy began development of the LISP programming language, which spent decades as the preferred language in the AI field, and is now the second-oldest high-level programming language still in use.††76 In 1959, Samuel coined the term “machine learning.”

The first industrial robot, Unimate, was invented in 1950 by George Devol and debuted on a General Motors assembly line in 1961. Five years later, Unimate joined Johnny Carson’s Tonight Show to hit a golf ball (which, tragically, lipped out) and pour a beer (done to perfection). In 1966, MIT computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum unveiled ELIZA, the first publicly demonstrated “chatbot” that understood natural human language and could credibly attempt the Turing Test.‡‡ Weizenbaum named his program after the ingenue Eliza Doolittle in George Bernard Shaw’s Pygmalion, which took its name from the same Greek myth Stanley Weinbaum had referenced in “Pygmalion’s Spectacles.” In Shaw’s play, the working-class Doolittle is successfully trained to pass as a member of high society, after which the phonetician Henry Higgins§§ deems her a successful experiment.

In 1986, the German professor Ernst Dickmanns unveiled the first autonomous car, a reengineered Mercedes-Benz van called VaMoRs, equipped with cameras, sensors, and a computer capable of real-time computer vision as well as steering, throttling, and braking. By 1987, the Benz’s computer vision was capable of processing enough imagery to drive at 60 miles per hour.77

In 1996 and 1997, the IBM chess computer Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov across two six-game matches, winning 4–2 and 3½–2½. Deep Blue’s victories came nearly a half century after Turing had tried to create a program that could just play a game of chess but could not find a computer powerful enough to even test Turochamp’s code. The year 1997 also saw the release of British programmer Rollo Carpenter’s Jabberwacky (named after the famous nonsense poem “Jabberwocky” from Lewis Carroll’s Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There), which became the first popular internet-based chatbot. The express purpose of Carpenter’s Jabberwacky was to develop artificial intelligence by learning from interactions with humans rather than just applying a predefined ruleset and finite knowledge base. Later that year, Dragon Systems unveiled NaturallySpeaking 1.0, the first consumer product to offer continuous speech recognition, and by the end of the decade, various speech-recognition systems had surpassed the vocabulary of the average American.

In 2001, ActiveBuddy, Inc., launched SmarterChild, the first natural language chatbot that was integrated into messaging platforms such as AOL Instant Messenger (AIM) and MSN Messenger and given a distinct personality. Within its first year, nine million users added SmarterChild to their friend list (roughly 2% of all internet users at the time), with a quarter of a million engaging with it daily to look up information, play word games, and pass time.78 Six years after the launch of SmarterChild, Microsoft acquired ActiveBuddy.

By 2011, information-based bots had progressed to the point where IBM’s Watson was able to handily defeat all-time Jeopardy! champions Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings in a live competition. That same year, Apple launched its Siri digital assistant across its hundreds of millions of iOS devices, which users could access simply by holding down the home button. Apple had acquired the start-up behind Siri in 2010; its origins could be traced to a DARPA-funded AI project led by the nonprofit Stanford Research Institute. Siri’s speech recognition engine was provided by Nuance Communications, which had acquired Dragon Systems four years after the launch of NaturallySpeaking (Microsoft would go on to buy Nuance in 2021 for nearly $20 billion). Google’s Siri competitor, Google Now, launched in 2012, with Microsoft’s Cortana and Amazon’s hardware-centric Alexa coming in 2014. Google’s self-driving car investments had begun in 2009 and by 2012, its Waymo division had passed the Nevada driver’s test. In 2015, Tesla began to roll out its self-driving capabilities, the same year Elon Musk helped to co-found OpenAI. A year later, Musk announced another start-up, Neuralink, which focuses on implantable brain-computer interfaces.

Sales and usage of digital assistants continued to grow in the second half of the 2010s, with Amazon’s Alexa line selling an estimated 250–300 million units that decade, and iOS and Android users making billions of voice-based queries each year through smartphones. However, these AI rarely provided much intelligence. Instead, they primarily reported the weather or time, put on a song, or answered a trivia question. But during the first years of the 2020s, AI seemed to cross a key threshold—especially in natural language processing.

In 2017, eight computer scientists and researchers who worked at (or who would soon join) Google released a paper, “Attention Is All You Need,” which proposed a new deep learning architecture they called a “transformer model.”79 According to the Financial Times, the paper “kick-started an entirely new era of artificial intelligence: the rise of generative AI.”80 Within a year, OpenAI had refocused its development on transformers and released its first attempt, a large language model dubbed the “generative pre-trained transformer,” or GPT for short. In 2019, OpenAI released GPT-2, with GPT-3 following a year later, GPT-3.5 debuting in March 2022, and GPT-4 launching publicly a year later.

OpenAI’s models demonstrated substantial improvements with each release. The company’s GPT-3 was first detailed in May 2020, with the enhanced GPT-3.5 submodel unveiled in March 2022 in advance of OpenAI’s public release. A year later, GPT-4 was launched and boasted comprehensive improvement over its predecessor. According to OpenAI, GPT-4 ranked in the 88th percentile in the US Law School Admission Test (LSAT) versus GPT-3.5’s 40th percentile, and 90th percentile in the Uniform Bar Exam versus 10th.81 In an independent study performed by researchers at Cornell University, on the 2022 Plastic Surgery In-Service Training Exam GPT-4 ranked 99th percentile, up from GPT-3.5’s 3rd percentile placement, and 88th percentile on the 2021 exam, up from 8th.82 On a custom oncology exam, the Cornell researchers found that GPT-3.5 averaged 53%, human medical physicists averaged 63%, and GPT-4 managed 75%.83

In the lead-up to GPT-4’s public release, OpenAI released ChatGPT in November of 2022, a chatbot based on its GPT-3.5 model. Within 40 days, the product surpassed 10 million daily active users—the fastest a new consumer application had ever crossed that threshold—and became the 17th-most-visited website in the world, ranking alongside quarter-century-old brands such as Amazon.com and Yahoo, and passing Netflix and Microsoft Office. Although its popularity was partly due to novelty, it also reflected the unprecedented utility of OpenAI’s transformer model, which could not just engage in factual and detailed conversations but also carry out complex requests intended to aid actual work creation rather than just information retrieval. For example, a user might ask a GPT model to “write a 1,500-word essay outlining the top five causes of World War I” (as well as variations on that question), or detail the 17 precedential cases relevant to a legal dispute around agricultural water rights in California and why. ChatGPT’s sister product DALL-E, which had released a few months earlier, also let users instantly translate their thoughts into a vivid high-resolution image that could imitate specified styles (e.g., pointillist, impressionist, charcoal) and be automatically updated on command (e.g., change the black roof to brown, remove the clouds, cut the lawn). In April 2022, OpenAI released DALL-E 2, which substantially enhanced the realism and accuracy of its generative imagery, with DALL-E 3 following in September 2023 and available inside the ChatGPT application. OpenAI’s Codex, which rolled out during 2021 and 2022, enabled users to ask for the code required to carry out specified tasks (e.g., make a Pong game, copy the headline article text from NewYorkTimes.com every hour and paste it into a spreadsheet) in the specified language (C#, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, SQL). In February 2024, OpenAI unveiled Sora, an adaptation of its DALL-E image technology but which generated high-definition videos based on a user’s text prompts. Many technologists believe Sora has been trained primarily on Unreal Engine–based simulations, with Sora receiving considerable praise for its ability to simulate complex particle interactions such as waves crashing through a building, snow bouncing off puppies as they wrestled, and light bouncing between windows and puddles in a nighttime street in Tokyo.84

Remarkably, OpenAI was not alone in its advances. Many considered the text-to-image capabilities of Midjourney, a ten-person start-up founded in 2021, superior to those of OpenAI’s DALL-E. Several other start-ups, such as Cohere (co-founded in 2019 by Aidan Gomez, one of the eight authors of the “Attention Is All You Need” paper) and Anthropic (founded in 2021 by OpenAI’s former vice president of research), were also gaining on OpenAI’s GPT models. Facebook’s GPT competitor, meanwhile, LLaMa (Large Language Model Meta AI), was another powerful and potentially more efficient model. And unlike the models of OpenAI, Facebook opted to open-source LLaMa 2 in 2023 and make it available free of charge—even for commercial usage—thereby democratizing access to powerful AI tools. Not long after, Nvidia publicly launched its suite of generative AI solutions and integrations that could create 3D objects and even the foundations of entire 3D worlds, rather than just memos and 2D images. In December 2023, artificial intelligence start-up Runway announced it was adding “general world models” to its audio-visual offering.¶¶ “A world model is an AI system that builds an internal representation of an environment, and uses it to simulate future events within that environment,” Runway’s co-founder and CTO Anastasis Germanidis wrote. “Research in world models has so far been focused on very limited and controlled settings, either in toy simulated worlds (like those of video games) or narrow contexts (such as developing world models for driving). The aim of general world models will be to represent and simulate a wide range of situations and interactions, like those encountered in the real world.”85

Alongside the leaps in transformer-based AI were equally impressive, if less heralded, achievements in neural networks. One example is neural radiance fields (NeRFs), which were originally developed at Google in 2019 and 2020. NeRFs use neural computing networks to produce large-scale, realistic immersive models out of a few dozen 2D photos, with the network filling in the many unseen angles and elements, such as the underside of a wood table or a partly obscured stove. In 2023, Google announced its NeRF system would be used to supplement its Google Maps and Street View solutions with full immersive models of major cities, and the interiors of popular destinations such as particular restaurants or museums, as well as the ability to “time slide” through different weather and traffic conditions in order to aid trip planning.

As is reviewed in detail throughout Chapter 12, AI is a critical aspect of the Metaverse and serves several functions. From a philosophical perspective, it reflects and accelerates the multidecade trend toward synthetically aided existence. It is also required to overcome many of the physics-related challenges to building the Metaverse. In May 2023, for example, Google announced that advances in AI had enabled it to shrink its two-year-old Starline device from the size of an enclosed restaurant booth to that of a midsize TV sitting atop a minifridge, while also shifting from a dozen high-end cameras and sensors to only a “few standard” ones.86 As a result, Google promised, the device would be both easier and cheaper to deploy but would still maintain its performance benefits versus traditional 2D displays. In other instances, improvements in AI will enable computer processors to “beat” the speed of light and better contend with unreliable and low-capacity networks (detailed in Chapters 5 and 6) by predicting what transmitted data will tell it to do before it arrives.

AI will also enable there to be more and better virtual worlds across the Metaverse. In 2022, Roblox’s roughly 275 million average monthly users created nearly 5.5 million worlds, though nearly all fall short of what users imagined. Roblox co-founder and CEO David Baszucki believes generative AI will enable users to type or speak entire worlds into existence by 2028.87 And difficult though the creation of purely fictional worlds is today, it’s even more difficult to translate the ever-changing “real world” into virtual assets. With solutions such as NeRF and photogrammetry, it may soon be possible to produce an “Earth 2.0” that covers nearly every square meter seen by humankind.

Just as AI can help generate and operate virtual worlds, it will also help interoperate between them—enabling otherwise incompatible file formats, coding conventions, and systems to seamlessly interconnect with one another without needing human developers to conform to a single standard or produce endless permutations of every world, asset, or data set they built.

Another related role for AI is in populating virtual worlds. Transformer models from companies such as OpenAI and Facebook are now being used to create virtual agents, characters, and entire communities with detailed personalities that grow with their experiences and can serve as friends, colleagues, or mentors. Lastly, humanity will rely on AI systems to operate large-scale digital twins and simulations, as they can process more information and make more decisions than any human could, and guide users through them.

Why the Metaverse Matters

When Ray Bradbury, Isaac Asimov, and Philip K. Dick began to build upon the ideas of Stanley Weinbaum and Vannevar Bush, virtual worlds were limited to single-purpose computers, played by single users, rendered in barely changing 2D monochrome, and were accessed by no more than a dozen scientists and researchers a year. Today, there are vast cloud-based networks that span tens of billions of dynamic virtual worlds that reach more than half a billion people on a regular basis and operate multibillion-dollar economies. And in the decades to come, these worlds will continue to grow in realism, diversity, functionality, economic value, and cultural influence. Meanwhile, the technologies behind these worlds will improve in capability, expand in deployment, and more deeply integrate into the physical. Precisely when “the Metaverse” arrives is a philosophical question; that it’s coming faster than ever can be said with certainty.

Another certainty is the many wars for supremacy in and over this new computing era. They will be fought between tech giants and insurgent start-ups via hardware, technical standards, and tools, as well as content, digital wallets, and virtual identities. The wars will be motivated by more than just revenue potential or the need to survive the “pivot to Metaverse.”

In 2016, a year before his company’s release of Fortnite and long before the term “Metaverse” entered public consciousness, Epic’s Tim Sweeney told reporters: “This Metaverse is going to be far more pervasive and powerful than anything else. If one central company gains control of this, they will become more powerful than any government and be a god on Earth.”88 It is easy to find such a statement hyperbolic.## The history of the internet, however, suggests that it may not be.

The foundation of today’s internet was built over several decades and through a variety of consortiums and informal working groups composed of government research labs, universities, and independent technologists and institutions. These mostly not-for-profit collectives typically focused on establishing open standards that would help them share information from one server to another, and in doing so make it easier to collaborate on future technologies, projects, and ideas. The internet’s decentralized design also reflected the philosophies of individuals such as Vannevar Bush, who hoped to exchange rather than control data, and the necessities of the era during which it was built, the Cold War, which prompted the adoption of transmission protocols and technologies that could operate even if substantial portions of the network were destroyed or commandeered.89

The benefits of this approach were far-ranging. For example, anyone with an internet connection could build a website in minutes and at no cost using pure HTML, and even faster using a platform like GeoCities. A single version of the site could be accessed by every device, browser, and user connected to the internet. In addition, no user or developer needed to be disintermediated—they could produce content for, and speak to, anyone they wanted. The use of common standards also meant that it was easier and cheaper to hire and work with outside vendors, integrate third-party software and apps, and repurpose code. The fact that so many of these standards were free and open-source meant that individual innovations often benefited the entire ecosystem, while placing competitive pressures on paid, proprietary standards, and helping to check the rent-seeking tendencies of platforms sitting between the web and its users (e.g., device manufacturers, operating systems, browsers, and internet service providers).

Importantly, none of this prevented businesses from making a profit on the internet, deploying a paywall, or building proprietary technology. Rather, the “openness” of the internet enabled more companies to be built, in more areas, reaching more users, and achieving greater profits, while also preventing pre-internet giants (and, crucially, telecom companies) from controlling it. Openness is also why the internet is largely considered to have democratized information, and why the majority of the most valuable public companies in the world today were founded (or were reborn) in the internet era.

It’s not difficult to imagine how different the internet would be if it had been created by multinational media conglomerates to sell widgets, serve ads, harvest user data for profits, or control users’ end-to-end experience (something AT&T and AOL both tried but failed to pull off). Downloading a JPG could cost money, and a PNG could cost 50% more. Video calls might have been possible only through a broadband operator’s own app or portal—and only to those who also had that same broadband provider (imagine something like, “Welcome to your Xfinity Browser™, click here for Xfinitybook™ or XfinityCalls™ powered by Zoom™; Sorry, ‘Grandma’ is not in our network, but for $2, you can still call her …”). Imagine if it took a year or a thousand dollars to make a website. Or if websites worked only in Internet Explorer or Chrome—and users had to pay a given browser an annual fee for the privilege of using it. Or maybe the user would have to pay their broadband provider an extra fee to read certain programming languages or use a given web technology (“This website requires Xfinity Premium with 3D”). When the United States sued Microsoft in 1998 for alleged antitrust violations, it centered its case on Microsoft’s decision to bundle Internet Explorer, the company’s proprietary web browser, with the Windows operating system. Yet if a corporation had created the internet, is it conceivable that it would have even allowed a competing browser? If so, would it have allowed users to do whatever they wanted on these browsers, or access (and modify) whichever sites they chose?

A “corporate internet” is the current expectation for the Metaverse. The internet’s nonprofit nature and early history stem from the fact that government research labs and universities were effectively the only institutions with the computational talent, resources, and ambitions to build a “network of networks,” and few in the for-profit sector understood its commercial potential. None of this is true when it comes to the Metaverse. Instead, it is being pioneered and built by private businesses, for the explicit purpose of commerce, data collection, advertising, and the sale of virtual products.

What’s more, the Metaverse is emerging at a time when the largest vertical and horizontal tech platforms have already established enormous influence over people’s lives as well as the technologies and business models of the modern economy. Their power is bolstered by the profound feedback loops of the digital era. Metcalfe’s Law, for example, states that the value of a communication network is proportional to the square of the number of its users, a relationship that helps to keep large social networks and services growing and presents a challenge to upstart competitors. Any business based on artificial intelligence or machine learning benefits from similar advantages as its data sets grow. The primary business models of the internet—advertising and software sales—are also scale-driven, as the companies that sell another ad slot or app encounter almost no incremental cost from doing so, and both advertisers and developers focus primarily on where consumers already are, rather than where they might be.

But to secure their user and developer bases while also expanding into new areas and blocking potential competitors, the tech giants have spent the past decade closing their ecosystems. They’ve done this by forcibly bundling together their many services, preventing users and developers from easily exporting their own data, shutting down various partner programs, and stymying (if not outright blocking) for-profit and even open standards which might threaten their hegemony. These maneuvers, mixed with the feedback loops that come from having comparatively more users, data, revenue, devices, and so on, have effectively closed much of the internet. Today, a developer must essentially receive permission and provide payment. Users have little ownership of their online identity, data, or entitlements.

It is here that fears of a Metaverse dystopia seem fair, rather than alarmist. The very idea of the Metaverse means an ever-growing share of people’s lives, labor, leisure, time, wealth, happiness, and relationships will be spent inside virtual worlds, rather than just extended or aided through digital devices and software. It will be a parallel plane of existence for millions, if not billions, of people, that sits atop the digital and physical economies, and unites both. As a result, the companies that control these virtual worlds and their virtual atoms will likely be more dominant than those who lead in today’s digital economy.

The Metaverse will also render more acute many of the hard problems of digital existence today, such as data rights, data security, misinformation and radicalization, platform power and regulation, abuse, and user happiness. The philosophies, cultures, and priorities of the companies that lead in the Metaverse era, therefore, will help determine whether the future is better or worse than the current moment, rather than just more virtual or remunerative.

As the world’s largest corporations and most ambitious start-ups pursue the Metaverse, it’s essential that we—users, developers, consumers, and voters—understand that we have agency over our future and the ability to reset the status quo. Yes, the Metaverse can seem daunting and scary, but it also offers a chance to bring people closer together, to transform industries that have long resisted disruption and that must evolve, and to build a more equal global economy. Everything depends on how it’s built.

Part II BUILDING
THE METAVERSE

Chapter 4 A GUIDE TO THE “FULL-SPEC” METAVERSE

Part i of this book is dedicated to the history of the Metaverse, as well as its current state. Part II focuses on its future. These chapters explore the various technologies, solutions, and agreements that will be needed to build the Metaverse—and the individuals and companies, philosophies and hypotheses, and complexities and histories that are behind each one.

With the above in mind, it’s helpful to move beyond the high-level definition of the Metaverse provided in Part I and instead provide a description of a “fully realized” Metaverse. The Metaverse is …

“A massively scaled and interoperable network of real-time-rendered immersive virtual worlds that can be experienced synchronously and persistently by an effectively unlimited number of users with an individual sense of presence, and with continuity of data, such as identity, history, entitlements, objects, communications, and payments.”

The rest of the chapter explains this description in detail.

“Virtual Worlds”

The Metaverse is made up of virtual worlds. The term “virtual worlds” refers to any computer-generated simulated environment. A virtual world can be presented in 2D (e.g., Pac-Man) or 3D (Fortnite), be purely virtual (Super Mario) or layered on top of the “real world” via augmented reality (Pokémon Go), or even be text-based (as in the case of a MUD). Some argue a virtual world need not be graphically rendered at all and instead can be limited to code (think of Neo viewing the Matrix in The Matrix). Stylistically, a virtual world can reproduce the “real world” exactly (this is typically called a “digital twin,” “virtual twin,” or “3D twin”) or represent a fictionalized version of it (e.g., the fantastical, quarter-scale Manhattan of PlayStation’s 2018 game Marvel’s Spider-Man), or represent an altogether fictional reality in which the impossible is commonplace (Fortnite). The graphics of this world may be “photoreal,” cartoonish, or stylized to imitate the works of Vincent van Gogh, Picasso, or any other artist, including one’s infant daughter.

The purpose of a virtual world can be “game-like,” which is to say there is an objective such as winning, killing, scoring, defeating, or solving, or the purpose can be “nongame-like” with objectives such as educational or vocational training, commerce, socializing, meditation, fitness, or operating physical spaces using a digital twin. In some cases, a virtual world has no individual users (as in the case of a Pixar film or when virtually simulating a closed ecosphere in a biology class), a single user (The Legend of Zelda), or many concurrent ones (Call of Duty).

The devices used to affect a virtual world vary: a keyboard controller, or motion sensor, network of cameras, voice, and more. The virtual world may run only on specialized hardware (e.g., a high-end supercomputer), a subset of broadly available computing platforms (e.g., PlayStation, but not Xbox), or across most possible endpoints (which likely involve large variations in the user’s experience by device).

Operationally, a virtual world may have a predefined run-time, after which it is fully reset (a level of Super Mario) or run in perpetuity (EVE Online), or it may operate somewhere in the middle, with only part of its world reset after a game or event (World of Warcraft). As with the real world, governance models vary widely. Most virtual worlds are centrally controlled by the person or group that developed and operates the world, which means they have unilateral control over its economy, policies, and users. In other instances, users self-govern through various forms of democracy. Some blockchain-based games aspire to operate as close to autonomously as possible after launch.

All virtual worlds face constraints. The most obvious is the difficulty and cost of development, operation, and updates. Any reduction to these barriers results in more worlds, with greater diversity, and more potential applications, which leads to a larger, more valuable, and more used Metaverse. Another constraint, which underpins much of this chapter, is the availability of computing resources (local or in the cloud). Naturally, an increase in these resources affects the virtual world’s cost structure, but it also determines the sophistication of its underlying simulation. In a simplified sense, one can think of a virtual world as having a maximum number of available “operations per second.” These operations can be used on graphical detail (i.e., shifting from low-fidelity graphics to photorealism), physics (e.g., simulating precise light reflections or damage to a car), environmental complexity (increasing the number of cars in an intersection from two to ten), the number of simultaneous users (which leads to more interactions produced per second), increasing the world’s level of persistence (discussed later in this chapter), computer vision (to understand the “real world” or a user’s hands), and so on. The “full-spec” Metaverse will simulate and include anything that an individual user or business might want to simulate and in whatever quality or fidelity is desired.

Immersive (or 3D or Spatial)

The Metaverse is an immersive medium that enables users to do more than just surf “on” a page or look at an app. Instead, they will exist within it. As discussed in Chapter 2, these experiences do not require the user to adopt new form factors, such as a headset, but such devices would probably be an aid to adoption, usage, and functionality. Billions may be adept at using keyboards and controllers to navigate 3D spaces, but billions of others find those inputs impossible to use—and these inputs cannot match the precision, ease of use, or flexibility of a human hand or eye. Accordingly, companies such as Apple and Facebook are developing devices as wide-ranging as motion-tracking cameras and tracking rings, even sensors that can detect electrical signals traveling across skeletal muscles, and neural implants to read brain activity. Regardless, today’s devices, from smartphones to smartwatches, will also need additional and better sensors. The world will too. While digital twins and city-scale simulations can transform the world into the greatest software development platform in the world, fleets of Internet of Things (IoT) sensors and data pipelines will be required to both track the world in real time and translate it into 3D reproductions.

New development suites (such as the aforementioned iOS ARKit), software languages, and standards (discussed later in this chapter) will also be needed. Google’s Starline device is a great illustration of the utility of 3D, but it requires novel software and AI not just to create a realistic live avatar but also to share it. Starline creates many gigabits of data per second, several times greater than the average US household can download per second. Accordingly, Google developed a new compression algorithm that rapidly shrinks this data by more than 100 times and is still compatible with the common WebRTC standard. And to use with 3D interfaces, developers will need to create new interaction models and design principles, just as Apple pioneered user experience (UX) elements such as “pinch-to-zoom” and “swipe-to-unlock.”

Not all use cases or applications will benefit from spatial, immersive, or 3D implementations, nor will those that do benefit do so in all cases. Yet many examples are already clear, including Google’s Starline, VR training for dangerous work environments, and AR-assisted surgery or repairs. It’s also evident that among those native to devices such as the iPad or video game consoles, 3D/AR socializing is often preferred to 2D alternatives whether based on text, image, or video. But there is particular hope that a 3D internet will enhance categories that have historically resisted digital disruption.

For decades, theorists have expected education to be transformed by the internet—that Harvard University would offer online-only degrees that rivaled its in-person equivalents in both imprimatur and test scores, yet was available at a fraction of the cost and to far more students. Harvard has abstained from such a model in part due to brand- and legacy-related concerns, but no effective alternative has emerged. Indeed, the COVID-19 pandemic revealed the value of the classroom and peers-based learning just as it demonstrated the inadequacies of learning through large video calls, on-demand videos, multiple choice, and even interactive e-books. Between 2020 and 2023, the National Center for Education Statistics reported that average reading and math scores for American children fell 5 points in their standardized testing rubric (220 to 215), the largest drop since 1990, while math scores fell by 7, the first-ever-reported drop.1 Among 13-year-olds, scores fell by 4 (260 to 256), more than double the largest-ever-recorded drop, and 9 (280 to 271), the second-ever-recorded drop and three times larger than the first.2

The suddenness of the shift to remote education is partly to blame, but for all the power of computers and the internet, the educational sector has seen no measurable productivity improvements since the internet and PCs. Students are not taught in less time, nor are more students taught effectively per instructor. Student outcomes have not seen substantial improvements, either. In comparison to 1999, the average reading score for 9-year-olds had grown only from 212 to 220 and math grew from 232 to 241; scores for 13-year-olds saw even smaller gains, with reading increasing from 259 to 260 and math from 276 to 280.* Since 2012, ACT scores have routinely hit two-or-three-decade lows.3 In fact, no other sector has seen greater increases in costs, with college tuition and fees up more than 825%,4 while the second-closest sector, medical care and services, is up 450%,5 versus 210% for the Consumer Price Index overall.6 Worse still, there have been few improvements in education equality or access.

At-home or at-distance education will never fully substitute for in-person experience, or for the effects of geography or income on learning. But the gap is likely to close for the same reasons VR training is so impactful in industries such as automotive repairs and oil and gas rigging: humans learn best by doing and through physical instruction. Immersive simulations enable virtual classrooms to be accessed worldwide, while also affording participants the ability to be “present” in these classrooms and to make eye contact with a teacher or peer. Furthermore, the virtual classroom can be stocked with infinite and no-cost Bunsen burners to light and frogs to dissect. The classroom need not exist at all, either. Instead, students could learn on the surface of the moon or the right ventricle of the heart. Everything once imagined in The Magic School Bus becomes virtually real—and it will be staffed by live versions of Miss Frizzle, motion-captured recordings of other teachers and instructors, and a suite of personalized AI assistants.

To be clear, education-related use cases are not a necessary part of any Metaverse description (nor are any comparable examples in fields such as healthcare, engineering, and so on). But for the Metaverse to be “the Metaverse,” it needs more than just technological enablers to be in place. Developers must also produce new experiences out of whole cloth for it which are subsequently adopted by society.

Real-Time Rendered

For a virtual world to be visible, it must be “rendered.” Rendering is the process of generating a visible 2D or 3D object using a computer program. The goal of this program is to “solve” an equation made up of many different inputs, data, and rules to determine what should be rendered and when, and by using various computing resources, such as a graphics processing unit (GPU) and central processing unit (CPU). As is the case with any math problem, an increase in the resources available to solve it (in this case, time, the number of CPUs and GPUs, and the power of these CPUs and GPUs) means that more complex equations can be tackled, and more detail provided in the solution.

Take the 2013 Pixar film Monsters University, which not only boasted beautiful graphics and vivid worlds but was designed to look great even on an IMAX screen more than 125 feet tall and 70 feet wide. Even when using a top-of-the-line industrial-grade computing processor, Pixar concluded that the film’s 120,000-plus frames would require an average of 29 hours each to be rendered. In total, the film would therefore require two years to be rendered, assuming no single rendering was redone, let alone any scene changed. In response to this conclusion, Pixar built a data center of 2,000 conjoined industrial-grade computers with a combined 24,000 cores that, when fully assigned, could render a frame in roughly five seconds.7 Most companies, of course, can’t afford such a powerful supercomputer and therefore spend more time waiting. Many architectural and design firms need to wait overnight to render a highly detailed model. An alternative approach is to render a less complex or detailed image, object, or scene.

Prioritizing visual fidelity is sensible if one is creating a Hollywood blockbuster that will be shown on the silver screen, or selling a multimillion-dollar building renovation. However, experiences set in virtual worlds require real-time rendering. Without real-time rendering, the size and visuals of virtual worlds would be severely constrained, as would the number of participating users and the options available to each user. Why? Because experiencing an immersive environment through pre-rendered images requires every possible sequence to have been pre-made—just as a choose-your-own-adventure novel can offer only a handful of choices, rather than infinite ones. In other words, the cost of greater visuals is less functionality and agency.

Compare, for example, navigating the Roman Colosseum in a video game versus doing the same on Google Street View. Both provide 360-degree views and multiple dimensions of movement (look up or down, move left or right, backward or forward), but the former severely limits one’s choices—and if a user decides to look closely at a given stone, all they can do is zoom in on an image not designed for such scrutiny. It will be blurry, and the view angle is fixed.

Although real-time rendering enables a virtual world to be “alive” and to respond to input from a user (or a group of users, for that matter), this requires each visual frame to be rendered in a fraction of a second, rather than several seconds, let alone days. Moreover, more frames per second are needed depending on the screen that’s used and content that’s displayed. Whereas most movies, such as those of Pixar, have only 24 frames per second, most games require at least 30.† Titles that are more dynamic and require more precise input, such as Call of Duty, aspire for a minimum of 60 frames per second. For head-mounted displays (e.g. virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality headsets), many experts believe at least 120 and as many as 240 frames per second are needed to avoid nausea, disorientation, and related sensations.8 According to a study from VRHeaven and compiled by Goldman Sachs, 7 percent of men and 23 percent of women who had tried virtual reality headsets in June 2020 reported that they “Frequently” experienced motion sickness when using these devices, and another 14 percent and 23 percent responded “Sometimes,” and 29 percent and 20 percent said “Rarely.”9 Only 50 percent of men and 35 percent of women said “Never.”10 At the time, nearly all VR headsets were limited to 75 fps or fewer. The incidence of nausea stems from many unique attributes of headset-based experiences, such as proximity of the device’s screen to the wearer’s eyes (2–5cm), the overall sense of immersion in the device (which means the user’s sense of balance is not necessarily “anchored” to the real world), and the use of head and body movements as an input (which can result in a disagreement between the brain’s sense of balance or “inner ear” and the experienced viewed on the display).

In totality, non-real-time-rendered films and real-time-rendered virtual worlds face the same resource constraints, but the latter requires far more, at far greater speeds, and at lower cost than the former. Whereas a Pixar film might have roughly 1,440 frames (24 frames per second × 60 seconds), a real-time-rendered world needs 1,800 (+25%) to 14,400 (+900%). It’s okay for Pixar’s frames to take seconds, minutes, or even days to render, but a real-time-rendered world’s frames cannot be rendered in advance and must therefore be produced between 99.5% and 99.999% faster. Pixar gets to use a world-class supercomputer that costs tens of millions to construct, but to reach the entire smartphone population, a virtual world needs to run adequately on a $100 Android device.

A Pixar film, like a video game, looks better as resolutions increase. A 2K display offers twice the detail of a 1K display, making circles sharper and smiles richer whether they are predetermined or interactive. And in both cases, a doubling in resolution doubles the frames required. But while the math is linear, the difficulty is not, given the aforementioned limitations on time, cost, and available resources. Furthermore, head-mounted displays require even greater resolutions than typical displays because the user’s eyes are only an inch or two away; the pixels of a 2K television are imperceptible from seven feet, but enormous when a user’s nose is pressed up to the screen.

Interoperable Network

As with the internet, the term “Metaverse” does not describe any single system or even a group of systems. It instead describes a network of systems—and these systems are interoperable with one another. “Interoperability” refers to the ability for independent, autonomous, and heterogeneous systems to exchange and make use of one another’s data.

Interoperation requires network participants to adopt common technologies, such as the Internet Protocol Suite. These shared technologies are usually steered by nonprofit groups whose recommendations must then be voluntarily adopted by the various network participants. The Internet Protocol Suite is managed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), a nonprofit with no formal membership or requirements and whose work is funded by its contributors and project sponsors.

Typically, network participants work to establish and/or support additional common standards and working conventions that aid the exchange of data. HTML, for example, is not part of the Internet Protocol Suite and thus does not, strictly speaking, enable the exchange of data. However, the widespread use of HTML ensures that most devices, users, and developers are able to coherently understand, consistently display, and easily use one another’s data. The widespread support of formats such as JPEG and MP3, meanwhile, ensures that most photo and audio files can be used on most websites and applications, irrespective of which website or application created them. Moreover, interchange solutions and frameworks emerged which helped convert between different formats, such as JPEG and PNG. To make the internet easier to use for consumers, rather than just for servers and networks, organizational hierarchies and registries were also established, such as the Domain Name System (which effectively converts an IP address into a text name like www.google.com). HTML is managed by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), a public-interest not-for-profit organization; JPEG by the Joint Photographic Experts Group, a not-for-profit committee in partnership with the United Nations’ International Telecommunication Union; MP3 by the Fraunhofer Society, a for-profit research organization which licenses the MP3 format; and DNS is managed by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), a not-for-profit multi-stakeholder group which also oversees IP and network addresses.

The healthiest instantiation of the Metaverse is likely one in which as many underlying protocols and standards are managed or guided by birds-of-a-feather groups, rather than by corporations or other private entities. This may take time. The easiest pathway to standards development is for a single party, especially one that already operates at scale, to lead said standards’ development and deployment. The IETF was originally established by the US federal government, which also developed the majority of TCP/IP in the first place, but by 1993, the organization had become fully independent. A related concern is how many protocols and standards are established; the internet could operate on fewer, but would likely benefit from more.

Although Neal Stephenson’s Metaverse was a protocol-based interoperable network, he imagined the Metaverse as having a unified and standardized experiential layer, whereas modern interpretations tend to assume it would not. In Snow Crash, the entirety of the Metaverse is contained on a single, geographically organized planet with a literal main street (and related benefits and real estate costs to the locations of various businesses), commutes to and from a user’s home, and programmatic regulations on the dimensions of avatars, buildings, and so on.

Individual platforms and experiences inside the Metaverse may resemble standardized “hub worlds,” such as Tesla’s San Francisco simulations, Apple’s AR mapping solutions, or a future version of Grand Theft Auto. But the overall Metaverse is likely to lack such a uniform expression, directory, or gateway—just like the internet. The World Wide Web, for example, is exhaustively organized and indexed, with sites claiming “namespaces” that are reached at assigned server addresses that are located at assigned network addresses, yet there is no “starting point” for the web other than an empty browser, users do not need a website to surf to one, and there is no required pathway between one page and another. If a user wants to go directly to a given page, they simply type in the address or click a hyperlink that takes them there directly. Smartphones offer a unified view of a user’s apps and a directory of all apps, but there’s rarely any experiential link among them, only minimal standardization across them. And while both Roblox and Fortnite enable users to jump between worlds through portals and doors, most users access various worlds through 2D interfaces that more closely resemble a streaming video service than the Street.

Not only would a planet-based organizational model for the Metaverse be frustrating, but it’s also probably impossible. Many simulations, such as those of Tesla, Apple, and a city’s own digital twin, will cover the same user and real-world location and often interconnect, but will otherwise run in parallel. Fortunately, this model has many technical benefits as well. By splitting users or data across platforms, rather than building a virtual planet with billions of concurrent users and quadrillions of objects, many of the technical challenges discussed throughout this chapter, such as rendering, synchronization, and persistence, are greatly simplified.

With Continuity of Data, Such as Identity, History, Entitlements, Objects, Communications, and Payments

Although establishing an interoperable network requires participants to exchange some data (e.g., identifier, address, location, etc.), it does not specify what data is then exchanged, let alone supported across its vast network. In general, visions of the full-spec Metaverse involve interoperable identities, histories (or records), entitlements (i.e., things a user owns or has the right to access), objects (e.g., virtual goods, avatars, or asset models), communications (just as emails work across all networks, domains, devices, etc.), and payment systems (required for virtual “trade”). Without such a suite, it’s argued there would be no “Metaverse,” just an internet with a growing number of 3D applications. A more 3D-capable internet has value, but it’s less likely to produce a true “parallel plane of existence” or produce an economy that might rival that of the “physical world” (while also underpinning much of it).

Interoperability is also essential to user rights and, in turn, the health of the Metaverse overall. If a user’s virtual entitlements or creations are locked to a given platform, then that platform’s de facto control over the user will grow as time passes and the user’s investment increases. For similar reasons, it will become increasingly difficult for any other platform, new or emergent, to compete with that platform. Interoperability is also needed to ensure that investments (time, money, energy, memories) in the Metaverse endure should a single virtual world or server within it be shut down. In the “real world,” consumers do not contend with these sorts of problems. Many underlying interoperable services and registries are government owned and non-excludable (e.g., passports, national identity numbers, currencies), individuals take physical possession of goods (unlike most digital goods) and these goods don’t disappear if their manufacturer closes, interoperability is physics based (a J.Crew belt works with Gap pants irrespective of any coordination between the two companies or permission from one), intermediaries are not required for most exchange (e.g., USD to Euro, a hat for a T-shirt), and so on.

There are many obstacles to establishing these standards. One is the current state of fragmentation. Almost all the most popular virtual worlds today use their own different rendering engines (many publishers operate several across their titles), with individualized scripting languages, tools, frameworks, and related services. The practical consequences of these engine-by-engine variations can be hard for non-developers to appreciate, but the depth of these differences is demonstrated by how the two most popular engines “disagree” on coordinate axes. In Unity, the y-axis in an X/Y/Z-based 3D model refers to up/down, while Unreal uses the z-axis for up/down and maps the y-axis to left/right. It’s easy for middleware to convert such practices, but the technical variations extend into how code is structured, inputs processed, particles simulated, and so on, rather than just the order of information.

Beyond the underlying logic and rules of these worlds is how the information that runs inside them is structured. There are no “JPEGs,” “MP4s,” “.XLS,” or “PDFs” for 3D objects, let alone environments or player data. As such, parties save their objects, textures, and player data into entirely different file formats and with only the information that they expect to need. Solving this requires not just a format but the philosophy around it. Take the idea of an “interoperable avatar.” It’s relatively easy for developers to agree on the definition of an image and how to present it, and as a static 2D unit of content made up of individually colored pixels, the process of converting one image file type (say, PNG) to another (JPEG) is straightforward. However, 3D avatars are a more complex question. Is an avatar a complete 3D person with an outfit, or is it made up of a body avatar plus an outfit? If the latter, how many articles of clothing are they wearing and what defines a shirt versus a jacket that goes over shirts? Which parts of an avatar can be recolored? Which parts must be recolored together (is a sleeve separated from a shirt)?
