Is an avatar’s head a complete object, or is it a description of dozens of sub-elements like individual eyes (with their own retinas), eyelashes, noses, freckles, and so on? In addition, users expect an anthropomorphic jellyfish avatar and a box-like android to move in different ways. The same applies to objects. If a tattoo is placed on the avatar’s neck, it should stay fixed to their skin irrespective of any movement they make—but a tie hung around that neck should move with (and also be affected by) the avatar. And it should move differently than a seashell necklace, which should also move differently than a feather necklace. Just sharing the dimensions and visual detail of an avatar is not sufficient. Developers need to understand, and agree on, how they work—then build code to support it.

Other areas are less ontological, but just as tricky. Interoperable economies—that is, virtual currency exchanges, goods trading, and so on—have complex tax implications, as well as regulatory burdens relating to money-transfer licenses, customer identification, securities licenses, capital reserves, and so on. For a virtual object on one platform to interoperate on another, systems are required to manage permissions and policies required to manage related liabilities. Harder still, architectures are required to sort exactly what happens (and doesn’t happen) to the relevant data and how. If a player buys an outfit on Platform A and wants to use it in Platform B, does Platform A send the outfit’s ownership record and files to Platform B, which manages it until it’s needed elsewhere, or does Platform A indefinitely manage the outfit and provide Platform B temporary rights to use it? If so, how does Platform A compensate? If the player sells the outfit to a Platform B user who doesn’t have a Platform A account, which company even processes the transaction? If the user alters the item from within Platform B, or adds an item to it from Platform B, how is the record on Platform A altered? If users have virtual items scattered across multiple titles, how do they ever know what, altogether, they own and where what they own can or cannot be used? Solutions are needed that not only establish and maintain an authoritative record but can transfer it to outside parties and provide authenticated access to that record and allow permitted parties to alter it, too.

Standards development is often considered the toughest hurdle faced by Metaverse builders because it is primarily a human process, not a technical one. Moore’s Law, which observes that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles every two years, charts predictable improvements in computing power and cost, while 6G mobile network specifications are already in early development and will doubtless be widely deployed, and the global internet backbone is constantly being expanded and upgraded.11 Standards have no set timeline, inevitabilities, or obvious answers. They are agreed upon, not discovered, and therefore rely on debates and concessions, which are shaped by competitive leverage and deployment, produce unintended side effects, and sometimes result in rival standards that worsen fragmentation rather than reverse it.

Take the widely popular GIF format, first introduced in 1987. Although GIFs often compress their source video file to the point that many individual frames are discarded and the remaining frames have lost much of their visual detail, file sizes remain quite large. There are many alternatives to the GIF—from MP4 to APNG (animated PNG) and WebM—which are typically five to ten times lighter and provide far greater video clarity and detail, in addition to other benefits, such as the ability to be streamed. Despite this, GIF remains the more popular and most widely deployed form of moving image file, which makes it tough for any site or application to reject, thereby ensuring it endures. Yet this endurance has led to extra bandwidth use, more time waiting for files to load, and worse experiences overall. Given the intensity of the Metaverse’s computational and networking-related needs, such suboptimizations add up quickly.

On occasion, it’s clear which prospective standard is “best” before any one alternative sees wide adoption. Even so, the companies that steer or own a lesser alternative will typically resist embracing this rival for strategic reasons—and some of those who have already adopted the lesser alternative will continue to use it simply to avoid the burden of making a shift.

As one reviews the past four decades of the internet, it’s easy to imagine better structures or declare better formats. But the internet’s extensive interoperability was fostered by an irreplicable advantage: its foundational protocols, conventions, and formats were set long before it was commercialized. Accordingly, the internet of today did not need for-profit rivals to agree, let alone concede to, a rival’s proposal. And while many for-profit products on the internet are largely closed or use proprietary protocols, such maneuvers required the development of a product with benefits that far exceeded network effects. While many internet businesses opt out of data sharing or use proprietary protocols and services, the cost is a reduction in network effects and thus success largely depends on producing a product worthy of this trade-off. Instant Messaging services have routinely met this burden by offering greater security, functionality, speed, and reliability over SMS, but no closed alternatives to email have been able to do the same (even though companies such as Google and Microsoft might aspire for a world where all such messages ran through their systems). Conversely, today’s virtual worlds were all built without the intent, let alone ability, to interoperate. As such, opting in to such a model requires substantial technical shifts (or concessions) that provide, at least to start, only marginally greater network effects.

Massively Scaled

For the internet to be “the internet,” it’s generally accepted that it must have a seemingly infinite number of websites and applications, and there must be myriad individual developers behind these pages, too. The Metaverse is similar. It must have a massively scaled number of virtual worlds if it is to be “the Metaverse.” Otherwise, it is more like a digital theme park—a destination with a handful of carefully curated attractions and experiences that can never be as diverse as, or contend with, the outside (real) world.

To most advocates, the size of the Metaverse will far exceed the overall size of the internet today—and the physical world, too. In 2021, Tim Sweeney told the LA Times, “Just as every company a few decades ago created a webpage, and then at some point every company created a Facebook page, I think we’re approaching the point where every company will have a real-time live 3D presence.… That’s starting to happen now. [And] it’s going to be a much bigger thing than these previous generational shifts.”12 Jensen Huang imagines the Metaverse having countless compounding simulations; the US government might have a national simulation, with cities, building operators, and stores within the United States running their own partly overlapping and partly interconnected simulations. The larger the Metaverse, the more used and useful, but also the more difficult the problems of rendering, synchronization, standardization, persistence, and more.

Persistence

In virtual worlds, “persistence” refers to the permanence of events, activities, or data. Most video games today are only selectively persistent. Throughout a match of Fortnite, players build or destroy various structures, set fire to forests, or kill wildlife, and so on, but after the roughly 20-to-25-minute match concludes, all of these changes are effectively deleted by Epic Games. The map once enjoyed and affected by 100 players will never be re-experienced, or even accessible, again. In fact, even within a given match, Fortnite’s virtual world is only partially persistent. A bullet mark on an indestructible rock might appear for only 30 seconds before it, too, is deleted, and thus also any evidence that combat had even taken place at that location. Although the world of World of Warcraft is “continuous,” in contrast to the match-based model of Fortnite, it operates similarly. If a player enters a specific part of the World of Warcraft map, defeats their enemies, leaves, and returns, they’ll typically find that those enemies have respawned. An in-game tradesman who sold a player a rare item only a day earlier might offer them a second as though it would be their first. The worlds of Fortnite and World of Warcraft can have lasting changes only when their developers deploy an update—and the players have little to no control over whether a given choice or event endures indefinitely.

Persistence is partly a creative challenge. The goal of most virtual worlds is entertainment, and most large-scale entertainment products are tightly produced and managed. By limiting persistence, a game’s developer can better predict what might happen and ensure it’s “fun,” as well as plan future updates that will keep the title both fun and fresh. However, persistence is a technical challenge, too. When a tree is cut down in the physical world, there is no concern for whether or not the systems of Mother Earth can handle such an event or remember it, or whether anyone else might be able to see the felled tree at a later date or interact with it. Physics adhere to their own laws, but they never run out of “processing power.” The production, operation, and memory of a virtual world are all confined by what the relevant computers can store, render, compute, and synchronize. Moreover, the effects of persistence compound. In a simple case, a tree being felled means that it is no longer there. But what of its stump? Does it remain? And does the trunk of the tree now lie on the ground? If still visible, do other users see which side it was chopped from, or just that it was generically cut? And does it “biodegrade”? If so, how—generically, or in response to its local environment? How should the tree affect other items which occupy its same space?

These questions of what should persist and how are not philosophical. A programmer (or AI) must make a decision and build the technology to support it. The answer also determines what a user can and cannot do, as well as the computing resources available for other tasks in the simulation, which affects what the world can and cannot do. In games, the answers might seem trivial, but many of the most popular social platforms, such as Roblox, thrive in part due to their comparatively high levels of persistence, which effectively add a fourth dimension (time) to play, and enrich the contributions of any additional user. Digital twins, such as those for a city or factory floor, have particularly high persistence and detail requirements (recall that such models might precisely simulate light, heat, sound, etc.). Networked simulations are also limited by the lowest common denominator of persistence across their network—a good reason for every participant to store as much data as possible, but that also means they must process, render, and synchronize it, too.

Synchronous

For the Metaverse and its individual experiences to be shared, every relevant participant, network, and device must be synchronized in real time. This requires the user to maintain a continuous‡ (i.e., sustained and uninterrupted) connection to a virtual world’s server (both to and from) and that can deliver vast volumes of data (“high bandwidth”) in near real time (“low latency”).

These may not seem like outlandish requirements. After all, there are a hundred million people streaming high-definition video at any given moment, while much of the global economy ran via live and synchronous videoconference software throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. And broadband providers improve the availability, bandwidth, and latency of their networks each year, with internet outages becoming less common each day. However, the internet works so well today because of the many tricks deployed to cover up moments of low bandwidth, high latency, and dropped connections. Spotify, for example, used to start a track’s progress bar immediately after a user selected the track, leading them to believe it was playing even though it had yet to even load.

Although the playback of a Netflix stream is continuous, the company is sending users distinct batches of data, many of which travel through different network paths from the server to that user. By using excess bandwidth to send the user data before it’s needed—such as minutes 45 and 46 when the user is only on minute 44—Netflix can ensure playback continues in the event the user’s device loses its connection to a local Wi-Fi router or cell tower, or if there’s congestion somewhere along the route between Netflix’s server and the user. Because Netflix receives video files anywhere from months to hours before they’re made available to audiences, it is also able to analyze these titles to determine what information can be discarded in the event a user’s bandwidth suddenly drops. Specifically, Netflix’s machine learning systems will scan each frame to simplify its elements—a background sky might be composed of 500 shades of blue which, though beautiful, could be simplified to 200, 50, or 25 without significantly harming the viewer experience. The streamer’s analytics even do this on a contextual basis—recognizing that scenes of dialogue can tolerate more compression than those of faster-paced action, and that the size and resolution of the viewer’s screen matter too. In addition, Netflix will preload content at local nodes. When a user asks for the newest episode of Stranger Things, it might be just a few blocks away and therefore arrives immediately.

These approaches work only because most Netflix content is prerecorded; it’s not possible to “pre-do” anything that has yet to occur. It’s for this reason that live video is substantially less reliable than on-demand streams. And even streaming services that deliver live video have tricks. In most cases, transmissions are delayed by 2 to 30 seconds, which means there’s still the opportunity to pre-send content in case of temporary congestion. Commercial breaks can also be used by both the content provider’s server, or the user, to reset the connection in case the prior one proved unreliable. Most live videos require only a one-way continuous connection—for instance, from CNN’s server to the user. Sometimes there is a two-way connection, as in the case of a Twitch chat, but only a sparse amount of data is being shared (the chat itself) and it’s not of critical importance, as it does not directly affect what’s happening in the video (remember, it probably happened 2 to 30 seconds earlier).

Overall, very few online experiences require high bandwidth, low latency, and continuous connectivity other than real-time-rendered, multiuser virtual worlds. Most experiences just need one or, at most, two of these elements. High-frequency stock traders (and especially high-frequency trading algorithms) want the lowest possible delivery times, as this can be the difference between buying or selling a security at a profit or a loss. However, the orders themselves are straightforward, are data light, and don’t require a server connection to be sustained for seconds, let alone hours.

The major exception is videoconferencing, which involves many people receiving and sending high-resolution video files, all at once, and participating in a shared experience. Yet these experiences, too, can take advantage of software solutions that don’t work for real-time-rendered virtual worlds—and work even when these solutions fall short.

As with all networking activities, the data packets that make up a video call occasionally arrive late due to network congestion or temporary connectivity loss. In the case of videoconferencing, this means that at least one member of the call (if the network error occurred near their device) or many (if it happened near the speaker) might miss a few of the speaker’s words or receive a garbled version of them. This usually doesn’t matter, as humans are adept at deducing the speaker’s overall point (and potentially the exact words they said), but modern videoconferencing software, such as Zoom and Microsoft Teams, now deploys machine learning solutions to help out. If a user loses their connection, the application’s server will send the requisite audio once they regain connectivity, which is then played at roughly 1.5-times speed and with pauses programmatically edited out, so that the user can still hear what they missed and then catch up to being “live.” And because videoconferences have a single active participant and many passive viewers, this disruption typically happens without any other members of the call even knowing. Should the connectivity issues affect the speaker, everyone is affected, but another member of the call can take over or everyone can wait until the speaker reconnects. Everything is fine. If this issue continues, the application will usually stop uploading or downloading video from various members of the call, in order to prioritize what matters most: audio. And in the case of varying latency—that is, members of the call are receiving “live” video and audio a quarter, half, or even full second behind or in front of each other—it’s likely that users are annoyed, but with a little patience, they can figure out how to proceed.

In contrast to a video call, virtual worlds send more complex data, which is needed on a far timelier basis, both to and from a larger set of users, and with greater consequences resulting from network hiccups. Imagine, as an example, a multiplayer shooter game. If Player A lags 75 milliseconds behind Player B, they might shoot in a location where they believe Player B to be, but Player B and the game’s server know Player B has already left. This discrepancy means the virtual world’s server must decide whose experiences are “true” (that is, which should be rendered and persist across all participants) and whose experiences must be rejected. And if the user lags too frequently, or for too long, the server operating the virtual world might kick them out of the match altogether in order to preserve the experience of other players (though as any fan of team sports knows, the expulsion of a player disrupts the rest of the match regardless of why they were ejected).

The Metaverse is not a game, let alone a fast-moving shooter with gameplay that’s decided by as little as a single pixel or hundredth of a second. Yet the Metaverse’s synchronization requirements and obstacles are far greater. Unlike a match of Call of Duty, there might be millions of synchronized devices, users, sensors, and equipment, rather than just a few dozen. Users are more likely to be spread around the world, rather than between 10 and 1,000 miles apart, thereby elongating the travel times. There is also more data to synchronize and it’s of greater consequence and more likely to persist as well. Furthermore, human interaction is incredibly sensitive; a smile that happens a bit too late (or not at all) or misaligned gazes can quickly exhaust, alienate, or creep out users.

The Metaverse can’t really function as a parallel plane for human existence if many of those within it experience conflicting (and then invalidated) versions of it. But at present, only three-quarters of American broadband households can reliably participate in high-fidelity real-time-rendered virtual worlds. Fewer than one-quarter of broadband households in the Middle East can, and fewer than one in ten in India.13 To improve these figures, many solutions are needed. As discussed in Chapter 2, the Internet Protocol Suite does not currently acknowledge, let alone prioritize, real-time transmission across the internet. Another obstacle is the physical internet backbone, which is shaped not to minimize delivery time, but by geographic, environmental, political, and economic realities. Indeed, even the speed of light is limiting.

Unlimited Users and Individual Presence

“Concurrency,” or the number of active users at a given moment, is one of the foundational problems for the Metaverse, and for a fundamental reason: it leads to exponential technical burdens. Take synchronization as an example. It’s obvious that as more users join a simulation, there is more “work” to be done and more potential points of network failure. Yet adding a third user to a two-user simulation does not increase synchronization requirements by 50%, but by over 100%. In the first case, User A’s actions must be synchronized with User B’s, and User B’s inputs with those of User A, but in the latter case, User C must be synced with Users A and B, and each must be synchronized with C. Synchronization points grow from two to six. Adding a fourth user doesn’t increase synchronization work by a third but by more than double, as each of Users A, B, and C must sync with a third user and User D must sync with each of them, too. And as users increase, the number of events/actions to simulate per second tends to increase and their predictability decreases. This reduces computing resources available for logic processing, rendering, and persistence management.

Today, even virtual worlds that have no persistence, span fewer than ten square kilometers in surface area, tightly control user activities, and are operated by some of the most technically capable companies in the world can struggle to sustain more than 50 to 150 users at the same time. What’s more, 150 concurrent users is possible only because of how these titles are creatively designed.

In Fortnite, up to 100 players can participate in a richly animated virtual world, and each player controls a detailed avatar that can use more than a dozen different items, perform dozens of dances and maneuvers, and build complex structures tens of stories tall. However, Fortnite’s roughly five-square-kilometer map means that only one dozen to two dozen players will encounter one another at once—and by the time players are forced into a smaller portion of the map, most players have been eliminated and turned into data on a scoreboard. During Fortnite’s social events, such as its famous 2020 concert with Travis Scott, players converge on a much smaller portion of the map and cannot be eliminated. Accordingly, the title’s standard cap of 100 players per instance was halved, while many items and actions, such as building, were disabled, thereby further reducing the workload.

While Epic Games can rightly say that more than 12.5 million people attended this live concert, these attendees were split across 250,000 separate copies of the event (meaning, they watched 250,000 versions of Scott) that didn’t even start at the same time.

Another good example comes from World of Warcraft. To play, users must first pick a “realm”—a discrete server that manages a complete copy of the roughly 1,500-square-kilometer virtual world, and from which they cannot see or interact with any other. In this sense, it may be more accurate to call the game “Worlds” of Warcraft. Users can move between realms, thereby philosophically uniting these many worlds into a single “massively multiplayer online game,” but each realm is capped at several hundred participants, and if there are too many users in a specific area, the game creates several distinct and temporary copies of this area, while splitting groups of users among them.

The best example, though, is CCP Games’ EVE Online, a technical marvel that debuted months before Second Life or MySpace. Save for occasional downtime for maintenance or updates, EVE Online has run continually since its debut on May 6, 2003, and its virtual world has never reset. This virtual world is also enormous, spanning nearly 8,000 star systems and nearly 70,000 planets. And unlike Fortnite or World of Warcraft, all of its users are in the same game and at the same time, with no distinct matches or realms.

The scale of EVE Online is possible due to its innovative systems architecture, as well as its brilliantly flexible creative design. The virtual world of EVE Online is essentially just empty three-dimensional space with wallpaper backgrounds that look like a galaxy. Users cannot truly visit a planet and activities such as mining are more akin to setting up a Gmail account than constructing a virtual rig. As such, the persistence of EVE Online primarily concerns a relatively modest set of “entitlements” (an industry term), such as a player’s ships and resources. The result is less computational work for CCP Games’ servers, and for its users’ devices, which need not render a virtual world that is constantly changing form, just the few objects changing inside of it.

Furthermore, very little happens in EVE Online on a daily, quarterly, or even yearly basis. This is because the goal in EVE Online, to the extent one exists, is for various factions of players to conquer planets, systems, and galaxies. This is achieved primarily through the establishment of corporations, formation of alliances, and strategic positioning of fleets. Indeed, much of EVE Online actually takes place in the “real world,” via third-party messaging applications and emails, and not even on CCP’s servers. Users have spent years planning attacks, going undercover with enemy guilds in order to later betray them, and creating enormous personal networks that trade resources and construct new ships. While large-scale battles do happen, they’re remarkably rare—and involve the destruction of assets in the virtual world (e.g., ships) rather than of the virtual world itself. The former is far easier for a processor to manage than the latter because it is about removing objects in the world, not altering the world. The nature of space-based combat also means that action is limited in variety and relatively simple in mechanics. Ordering a ship to mine resources from a planet, or send a succession of blasts from and to a fixed position, is far less complex than a pair of individually animated avatars dancing, jumping, and shooting each other.

Because EVE Online is set in the vastness of space, most users are far away from one another—enabling CCP Games’ servers to effectively treat them as being in separate virtual worlds until necessary, just like Warcraft. And while players do sometimes want to converge on the same location—such as a battle site—the mechanics of EVE Online spread out this behavior and dissuade it, too. Depending on the ship and intended travel distance, it can take tens of seconds to several minutes for a given ship to warp to another system—and getting to its final destination might require several systems warps. The time involved in such flights has a direct and indirect benefit for CCP Games. First, it reduces the risk of too many ships arriving at any given moment and instead distributes these arrivals over a few minutes or more. Second, it discourages users from relocating a large number of their ships—or moving in the first place—as the user might not be able to return fast enough should an attack occur after they leave. “Warps” also deplete a ship’s capacitor, thereby producing a resource-related cost to relocation. To aid instances in which there are too many user activities (e.g., ship relocations) or instructions (e.g., to continue to fire on an opponent’s ship), EVE Online’s engine will deploy “time-dilation,” slowing the game’s passage of time from one in-game second being equivalent to one real-world second to as little as one-to-ten, which enables the game’s server to catch up and properly synchronize all inputs and outputs. While EVE’s time-dilation math is fictional, the concept broadly reflects the theory that spacetime dilates in response to the density of heavy and/or high-velocity objects.

EVE’s scale, reliance on real-world decisions, and focus on infrastructure, inventories, and locations, rather than virtual outfits or gunfights, makes it a better representation of what the “real world” Metaverse is likely to be like than games such as Fortnite or Roblox—and easier to operate than these titles, too. Even so, EVE Online inevitably encounters problems. At one point in the 2000s, a group of players realized that a specific star system, Yulai, sat near many high-traffic planets inside a major star cluster, making it an enticing spot to establish a new trading hub.14 They were right. Not long after setting up shop, many buyers began to flock to the area, which attracted additional sellers, then more buyers, and so on. Ultimately, the number of transactions that were occurring inside this hub caused the CCP Games’ servers to start to buckle, leading the publisher to alter the EVE Online universe so that the destination would be less convenient to visit.

The lessons from “the Yulai Problem” helped CCP Games design, expand, and overhaul its maps in the years that followed. But in the real world, trade hubs can’t be moved, nor can travel distances be altered. And no matter how the universe of EVE Online is distributed, CCP cannot prevent another inevitable computing challenge: the sudden outbreak of battles so strategically important that thousands of users suddenly converge to save their faction or defeat another. In January 2021, the largest battle in EVE’s history occurred. It was more than twice the size of the prior record and the culmination of a nearly seven-month escalation between the Imperium Faction and a coalition of enemies called PAPI. Or at least, it should have been. The only real losers were CCP Games’ servers, which could not keep up with 12,000 players appearing in a single system, and any of those players who were hoping for a decisive victory.15 Roughly half of the players were unable to ever enter the system, while many of those who did were placed in a sort of purgatory—if they logged in to the game, they’d likely be destroyed before having a chance to enter any coherent commands, while leaving meant that their server spot might be taken up by an enemy that would destroy their allies. There was an eventual winner—Imperium—but this was mostly by default, as the defender naturally wins in a battle that never actually takes place.

For the Metaverse to serve as a platform for human socializing, as well as a computing layer for the real world, it must be able to support large numbers of users and IoT devices without compromising essential technical functions. Furthermore, participants must be individually represented within the Metaverse’s many simulations and able to affect it, too. If these requirements were rendered merely optional, the Metaverse would be technically easier—there would be fewer users to synchronize, fewer simultaneous events and inputs to process, and a reduced need for real-time bandwidth and delivery, and users would be able to share a rendered image instead of needing to generate their own custom view. However, such a limitation would make the Metaverse just a virtual diorama or a larger-scale version of the reality series Big Brother.

Getting to the Full-Spec Metaverse

In “Pygmalion’s Spectacles,” Professor Ludwig’s sales pitch invokes the teachings of George Berkeley, an 18th-century subjective idealist who is best known for the saying “To be is to be perceived.” Today, Berkeley’s ideas are more commonly expressed through a thought experiment: “If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound?” The question is commonly attributed to the philosopher but is at best a liberal reinterpretation of his writings. Regardless, Berkeley’s arguments and thought exercises have endured in pop culture for centuries because they are fun and hinge on important and ever-evolving technicalities and concepts.

According to an immaterialist such as Berkeley, the tree—standing, falling, or fallen—exists if someone (or God) perceives it. Others claim that what’s meant by “sound” is just vibrations that propagate through matter. As these vibrations exist irrespective of an observer, the tree does, in fact, make a sound whether or not someone is around to hear it. Another perspective alleges that “sound,” specifically, is a sensation experienced by a brain when these vibrations interact with nerve endings. If there are no nerves to interact with vibrating particles, there can be no sound.

One hundred four years after Berkeley’s death, the Frenchman Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville devised the phonautograph, the first device capable of recording sound waves as they propagated through a medium such as air or wood. From this point on, one could argue that many sounds were now heard by artificial observers, making the distinction between vibrations and sound sensations irrelevant. Nevertheless, 21st-century quantum mechanics largely agrees that without an observer, existence is at best a conjecture that cannot be proved or disproved—thus all that can be said is that the tree might exist—though Albert Einstein, who was instrumental in founding the field of quantum mechanics, took issue with this view.

Although 21st-century examples of Fortnite concerts and EVE Online battles are helpful to explain the technological requirements of the Metaverse, it’s Berkeley’s 18th-century tree that best reveals the difficulty of creating a virtual plane of existence for all of humanity. As William Gibson explained in Neuromancer, the Metaverse (or as he called it, the cyberspace matrix) does not really exist. Instead, it is a “consensual hallucination” that’s “experienced daily by billions.… A graphic representation of data abstracted from the banks of every computer in the human system.”16

Accordingly, every aspect of the Metaverse, from its many trees to their individual leaves, and the forests in which they are situated, must be created by a human agent or a subagent thereof (such as a generative AI program). Every aspect of this data, too, must be set—from the specific coloring of the tree to its texture, the way it moves in the wind, what is required to chop it down, the sound it makes when falling, and so on. And for a user to experience this data, they must have systems capable of understanding and representing it. For the data to be part of a shared human experience, it must also be shared with billions of other people, each of whom can correctly interpret and affect it, while sharing their own data back.

Circa 1880 Engraving of Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville’s Phonautograph

In 2024, billions of people can observe a hyperrealistic virtual tree fall in a hyperrealistic forest. But if many users want to observe such an event, they must be separated into individual groups that each watches a different copy of that tree fall and hears the sound of that tree falling. Alternatively, the complexity of that tree may need to be reduced—its rough bark smoothed out into a textureless and uniform brown and its fall reduced to a generic thud. And those who do observe the same tree might see and hear it at slightly different times, thereby determining who responds to it first and last, and requiring some system to decide whose responses should be considered “true” or “false.” Some users might be able to hear the tree fall in spatial sound and see it in a high-resolution, high-frame-rate immersive headset, while another cohort might be treated to flattened sound and a lower-frame-rate, 2D display. And no matter how many see the tree fall, the Metaverse might forget this same fact and reestablish the tree minutes later as though it had never been felled. Or it might remember the tree as having fallen, but differently than its observers. And some systems within the Metaverse might not even recognize the tree as being a tree, let alone be able to use it, or understand who does and doesn’t own it.

The Metaverse will become “the Metaverse” only if it can support a large number of users experiencing the same event, at the same time, and in the same place, without making substantial concessions in user functionality, world interactivity, persistence, and rendering quality, and without fragmenting participants into different and occasionally conflicting instances. This does not require billions of people to share in any single experience at the same time, nor the ability to infinitely affect every particle of it—just as all real-world locations can have capacity limits, dress codes, and prohibited behavior. Yet it’s clear that the shortfalls of current technology are significant.

To close the gap between the present day and the long-awaited Metaverse-shaped future, numerous technologies are required. Some of these technologies exist today, but require substantial enhancements or investments. Some must be created. In other cases, new business models and coding practices are required.

The rest of this book is dedicated to these requirements, the potential solutions to them, and the ways they affect one another.

  1. * How much, if any, of this improvement can be attributed to technology versus pedagogy (or other drivers, such as reductions in childhood poverty) is unknown.

  2. † It is possible to have much lower frame rates, but this usually involves enormous mechanical concessions. For example, a basic game of checkers could have as few as one frame per second without any experiential consequences. Titles played on small screens with limited visual detail, such as those of the Nintendo Switch, often run at 20 fps, but increase to 30 fps when connected to a TV and electrical outlet, thereby providing a larger display and infinite access to power versus an onboard and portable battery.

  3. ‡ This is often referred to as a “persistent” connection, but in the interests of differentiating it from the persistence of a virtual world, the term “continuous” will be used instead.

Chapter 5 NETWORKING VERSUS THE SPEED OF LIGHT

Discourse on the Metaverse typically focuses on the video games that are the most popular, yet the most technically impressive exemplar is a title that, over its lifetime, will likely count fewer players than Roblox, Minecraft, and Fortnite reach in an average day. In fact, the title’s aim is not socializing or the ability to traverse fictional realms or build virtual wonders. Instead, it’s designed to precisely reproduce an experience many deem unpleasant, dull, or terrifying: airplane travel.

Bandwidth

The first Flight Simulator was released by Sublogic in 1979 for the Apple II computer, and though renders were limited to fewer than 200 colored lines atop a uniform black background, the title nevertheless amassed a cult following. In 1981—two decades before the debut of Microsoft’s Xbox video game console—Alan Boyd, the 32nd-ever employee at Microsoft and its head of acquisitions, approached Sublogic hoping to license the franchise and produce a new entry that would enable Microsoft to differentiate the still-to-come 16-bit Windows PCs from 8-bit computers such as the Apple II.1

By 2006, Microsoft had released ten total entries in the rechristened Microsoft Flight Simulator (MSFS) line, and in 2012 The Guinness Book of World Records dubbed MSFS the longest-running video game franchise in history, beating Space Invaders and Oregon Trail, which were a year and a half older but had become dormant, and Pac-Man and Donkey Kong/Super Mario, which launched in 1980 and 1981.2 Despite this heritage, it took until the 12th entry, which was released in August 2020, for MSFS to soar into the public consciousness. The New York Times wrote that the 2020 MSFS provided “a new way of understanding the digital world,” offering a view “that is more real than the one we can see outside [and] a picture that illuminates our understanding of reality.”3 A number of publications, including Time magazine and Polygon, named MSFS one of the best games of 2020.

In theory, MSFS is what many people see it as: a game. Within seconds of opening the application, they’ll be reminded that Microsoft’s Xbox Game Studios developed and published it. However, the goal of MSFS is not to win, kill, shoot, defeat, beat, or score on another player or an AI-based competitor. The goal is to fly a virtual plane—a process that involves much of the same work as flying a real one. Players will communicate with air traffic control and their copilots, wait to be cleared for takeoff, set their altimeter and flaps, check for fuel reserves and mixtures, release their brake, slowly push the throttle, and so on, all before following their selected or designated flight path while managing conflicting routes and accommodating the flight paths of other virtual planes.

Every entry in the MSFS series has offered that sort of functionality, but the 2020 edition is extraordinary—the most realistic and expansive consumer-grade simulation in history. Its map is over 500 million square kilometers—just like the “real” planet earth—and includes two trillion uniquely rendered trees (not two trillion copy-and-pasted trees, or two trillion trees made up of a few dozen varieties), 1.5 billion buildings, and reproductions of nearly every road, mountain, city, and airport across the world.4 Everything looks like “the real thing” because MSFS’s virtual world is based on high-quality scans and images of the “real thing” that are then transformed into 3D models using Microsoft’s Azure Stack.

MSFS’s reproductions and renders aren’t perfect, but they are still stunning. “Players” can fly past their own house and spot their mailbox or the tire swing in the front yard. When the “game” conjures a sunset that’s reflected across a bay and then refracted yet again by the plane’s wings, it can be difficult to distinguish between a screenshot from MSFS and a real-world photograph.

MSFS’s life-size and lifelike “virtual world” is made up of nearly 2.5 petabytes of data—roughly a thousand times larger than Fortnite and equivalent to more than 2.6 million gigabytes.5 There is no way for a consumer device (or most enterprise devices) to store this amount of data. Most consoles and PCs top out at 1,000 gigabytes, while the largest consumer-grade Network Attached Storage (NAS) drive is 20,000 gigabytes and retails for close to $750. Even the physical space required to store 2.5 petabytes is impractical.

But even if a consumer could afford such a hard drive and enough space to house it, MSFS is a live service. It updates to reflect real-world weather (including accurate wind speed and direction, temperature, humidity, rain, and light), air traffic, and other geographic changes. This allows a player to fly into real-world hurricanes or to trail real-life commercial airliners on their exact flight path while they’re in the air in the real world. This means that users cannot “prebuy” or “pre-download” all of MSFS—much of it doesn’t yet exist!

MSFS works by storing a relatively small portion of the game on a consumer’s device—roughly 150 GB. This portion is enough to run the game offline, as it contains the game’s core code, visual information for numerous planes and cities, and generic textures and assets to populate a map the size of the earth. The trade-off of offline play is that users see mostly procedurally generated environments and objects, with landmarks such as Manhattan broadly familiar but populated with generic, mostly duplicated buildings that bear only an occasional and sometimes accidental resemblance to their real-world counterparts. Some preprogrammed flight paths exist, but they cannot mimic actual live routes, nor can one player see another player’s plane.

It’s when players go online that MSFS becomes a true wonder, with Microsoft’s servers streaming new maps, textures, weather data, flight paths, and whatever other information a user might need. In a sense, players experience the MSFS world exactly as a real-world pilot might. When they fly over or around a mountain, new information streams into their retinas via light particles, revealing and then clarifying what’s there for the first time. Before then, a pilot knows only that, logically, something must be around the corner.

Many gamers assume this is what happens in all online multiplayer video games. But the truth is that most online games try to send as much information as possible to the user in advance of them playing, and as little as possible when they’re actively playing. This explains why playing a game, even a relatively small one such as Super Mario Bros., requires purchasing cartridges or discs that contain multi-gigabyte game files, or waiting tens of minutes or even a couple of hours downloading and installing these game files. From time to time, a player might be told to download and install a multi-gigabyte update before they can play again. These files are so large because they contain nearly the entire game—namely, its code, game logic, and all the assets and textures required for the in-game environment (every type of tree, every avatar, every boss battle, every weapon, and so on).

For the typical online game, what actually comes from online multiplayer servers? Not much. Fortnite’s PC and console game files are roughly 30 GB in size, but online play involves only 20–50 MB (or 0.02–0.05 GB) in downloaded data per hour. This information tells the player’s device what to do with the data it already has. If a user is playing an online game of Mario Kart, Nintendo’s servers will tell the user’s Nintendo Switch which avatars their opponents are using and therefore must be loaded by the device. During the match, the user’s continuous connection to the server then enables a near constant stream of data on exactly where these opponents are (“positional data”), what they’re doing (sending a red shell), communications (e.g., a teammate’s audio), and various other information, including how many players are still in the contest.

That online games remain “mostly offline” comes as a surprise even to avid gamers. After all, most music and video is now streamed—people don’t pre-download songs or TV shows anymore, let alone buy physical CDs to store them—and video gaming is supposedly a more technically sophisticated and forward-looking media category. Yet it is precisely because games are so complicated that those who make them choose to marginalize the internet. Connections are not reliable, bandwidth is not reliable, latency is not reliable. As discussed in Chapter 4, most online experiences can survive this unreliability, but games cannot. As a result, developers chose to rely as little on the internet as possible.

A mostly offline approach to online games works well, but it imposes limitations. The fact that a player’s device can tell individual users which assets, textures, and models should be rendered means that every asset, texture, and model must be known and stored in advance by the same device. By sending rendering data on an as-needed basis, games can have a much greater diversity of virtual objects because they need not be preloaded to a consumer-grade hard drive. MSFS aspires for every town not just to differ from every other but to exist as it does in real life. And it doesn’t want to store 100 types of clouds and then tell a device which cloud to render and with what coloring; rather, it wants to dictate exactly what that cloud should look like.

When a player sees their friend in Fortnite today, they can interact using only a limited set of preloaded animations (or “emotes”), such as a wave or a moonwalk. Many users imagine a future where their live facial and body movements are re-created in a virtual world. To greet a friend, they won’t pick Wave 17 of the 20 waves preloaded onto their device but will wave uniquely articulated fingers in a unique way that has never happened precisely that way before. Users also hope to bring their myriad virtual items and avatars across the myriad virtual worlds connected to the Metaverse. As MSFS’s file size suggests, it’s simply not possible to send so much data to the user in advance. Doing so requires not only impractically large hard drives but also a virtual world that knows in advance anything that might be created or performed.

The need to “pre-send” an otherwise living virtual world has other implications. Every time Epic Games alters Fortnite’s virtual world—say, to add new destinations, vehicles, or non-playable characters—users have to download and install an update. The more Epic adds, the longer this takes and the longer a user must wait. The more frequently a world is updated, the more delays a user will experience.

The batch-based update process also means that virtual worlds cannot truly be “alive.” Instead, a central server is choosing to send a specific version of a virtual world out to all users, a world that will endure until the next update replaces it. Each edition is not necessarily fixed—an update might have programmed changes, such as a New Year’s Eve event or snowfall which increases daily—but it is pre-scripted. Finally, there are limitations to where users can go. During Travis Scott’s ten-minute event on Fortnite, some 30 million players were instantly transported from the game’s core map to the depths of a never-before-seen ocean, then to a never-before-seen planet, and then deep into outer space. Many people may imagine that the Metaverse operates in similar fashion—that users can easily jump from virtual world to virtual world without first enduring long loading times. But to put on the concert, Epic had to send users each of these mini-worlds in full, days to hours before the event, via a standard Fortnite patch (users who had not installed the update were denied entry to the event). Then, during each set piece, every player’s device was loading the next set piece in the background. It was notable that each of Scott’s concert destinations was smaller and more limited than the one before it, with the last being a largely “on rails” experience in which users simply flew forward in largely nondescript space. Think of this as the difference between freely exploring a mall versus traversing one via a moving walkway.

The Travis Scott concert worked so well because Epic Games, in addition to being one of the most creative game developers in the world, designed the experience in a manner that hid its technical limitations. Concerts are also inherently structured events—participants don’t expect to be able to do anything they can imagine but, instead, expect to be mostly guided through a predetermined set list that begins and ends at a fixed time. The decentralized and boundless Metaverse doesn’t have such conveniences.

Some might conclude from the popularity of Roblox and the immensity of MSFS that modern internet infrastructure can now handle Metaverse-style live data streaming. In truth, the model, too, is possible only in a highly constrained fashion and for specific use cases. Roblox, for example, doesn’t need to cloud-stream much data because most of its in-game items are based on “prefabs.” The game is mostly just telling a user’s device how to tweak, recolor, or rearrange previously downloaded items—just as all Lego builds are composed of fewer than 3,800 unique pieces (and 10 of these pieces constitute 20% of all pieces shipped to customers).6 Roblox’s graphical fidelity is also relatively modest and therefore its texture and environmental file sizes are relatively small, too. Overall, Roblox’s data usage is much greater than that of Fortnite—roughly 100–300 MB per hour, rather than 30–50 MB—but still manageable. At its target settings, MSFS demands nearly 25 times as much hourly bandwidth as Fortnite and 5 times as much as Roblox. This is because it’s not sending data on how to reconfigure or recolor a preloaded house but instead sending a user’s device the exact dimensions, density, and coloration of a multi-kilometer cloud or a nearly exact replica of the Gulf of Mexico’s shoreline. Yet even this need is simplified in ways that won’t work for the Metaverse.

While MSFS requires lots of data, it need not arrive particularly quickly. As with real-world pilots, MSFS pilots cannot suddenly teleport from New York State to New Zealand, nor see downtown Albany from 30,000 feet above Manhattan, nor descend from the firmament to the tarmac in seconds. This provides the player’s device with lots of time to download the necessary data. In fact, the MSFS client can easily predict where the player is headed and preemptively download the related data. And even if MSFS doesn’t receive all of the data it requested on time, the consequences are modest: some of Manhattan’s buildings will temporarily be procedurally generated, rather than resemble the real thing, with the realistic details filled in as the user gets closer to the city.

MSFS is a remarkable creative experience, technical achievement, and case study on why so many came to view the Metaverse as a practical opportunity in 2020 and 2021—not just an inevitable part of some distant future. Nevertheless, the 2020 MSFS is still far from “the Metaverse.” Overall, the title has more in common with a diorama than Neal Stephenson’s bustling Street. Only a handful of MSFS’s 1.5 billion buildings can be entered, and none appear operational (let alone do anything). And though AI-operated vehicles can be seen on its countless roads, no traffic jams ever occur, nor does the AI adhere to any realistic patterns, such as rush-hour traffic or 3:30 pickups at the local school. Indeed, if a user lands their plane on the local freeway, nearby cars will not only drive as though there was no such emergency landing, they pass through the plane altogether. There are no baseball or football matches playing on the millions of fields a virtual pilot might see while flying (least of all ones the pilot could join). Altogether, a user can engage with no more than 49 other players—and no one can modify MSFS’s virtual world (creating a new map is out of the question).

There is nothing wrong or inherently disappointing about MSFS’s limitations. The title’s goal is to let users traverse a surface-level model of the earth, not engage in an earth-like ecosystem. But if users want to use a platform capable of the latter functionality, they will need to be able to download far more data per hour than even the fullest version of MSFS demands today—and they will need it on a timelier basis, too. A computer might be able to guess what a Manhattan skyscraper’s windows look like—and a user might be able to wait for the real thing—but the Metaverse is more than just an empty model of the known world. And this means tackling the least understood element of internet connectivity today: latency.

Latency

Bandwidth and latency are often conflated, and the mistake is understandable: both impact how much data can be sent or received per unit of time. The classic way to differentiate the two concepts is by likening an internet connection to a highway. “Bandwidth” is the number of lanes on the highway, and “latency” is the speed limit. If a highway has more lanes, it can carry more cars and trucks without congestion. But if the highway’s speed limit is low—perhaps due to too many curves or because it’s laid in gravel rather than pavement—then the flow of traffic is slow even if there’s spare capacity. Similarly, a high speed limit with only one lane results in constant congestion—the speed limit becomes an aspiration, not a reality.

The challenge with real-time-rendered virtual worlds is that users aren’t sending a single car from one destination to another. Instead, they’re sending a never-ending fleet of cars tethered together both to and from that destination (as Chapter 4 detailed, a “continuous connection” is needed). It’s also not possible to send these cars in advance because their contents (i.e., data) are created only milliseconds before they hit the road. Furthermore, these cars must drive at their fastest possible speed because if they arrive late, the rest of the fleet behind them will carry the wrong packages, too, as will many of the other cars on the road. And should any portion of the fleet ever be diverted to a relief highway or road, it might be necessary to restart the entire fleet’s trip—even if this new route is equally fast.

As “speed” is an abstract concept, it’s helpful to specify how the latency requirements of the Metaverse differ from those of the internet today. In 2024, most internet usage involves a single device pulling static copies of information from a single server, such as a consumer’s iPhone downloading an email or loading a webpage. As the user is not engaged in a simulation or any live experience, a 500-millisecond (or half-second) or longer delay has no consequence other than mild frustration—and tolerance is surprisingly pretty high. Most users don’t notice a 150–200 ms delay between a single button press, such as that of a Netflix pause-or-play button, and the relevant application’s response to that input. Moreover, latency is typically the least valued networking attribute; when watching Netflix, a user would likely prefer higher-resolution video (“bandwidth”) and uninterrupted playback (“reliability”) to an 80 ms–faster start (“latency”). Even when users are participating in a shared experience, latency requirements are typically low. It rarely matters whether an iMessage or WhatsApp message arrives within 50 ms rather than 500 ms—and such a margin is inconsequential in contrast to the speed in which the recipient reads it. Latency in a video call is unquestionably annoying but also straightforward to manage; participants just learn to wait a bit after the speaker stops speaking. Even a second (1,000 ms) is workable.

But the human tolerance for latency in interactive experiences is incredibly low. When controlling a virtual character, a user’s brain must feel as though this avatar is a direct extension of the user’s inputs, rather than merely the accurate execution of them. This is the difference between waving a flag and pressing a button that waves a flag. As these inputs are happening in a continuous fashion, unlike a one-off press of a play-or-pause button, delays are even more noticeable to users, as is variability in response times.

Recall that many modern 3D simulations aspire for at least 60 rendered frames per second, equivalent to at least one frame every 16 ms. The inevitable outcome is that even a seemingly modest 100 ms delay can lead to a dozen consecutive frames that do not reflect what a user has already done and what their brain expects to see. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that more real-time-rendered virtual worlds are multiuser. As such, variations in latency among users mean that certain users (or devices, or networks) are effectively ahead of or behind one another, which results in some users being able to respond to information that others haven’t even received. To put what is still an abstract conversation about speeds and milliseconds into perspective, avid gamers typically notice that latency affects their play at 48 ms, while some can correctly note delays after only 5 ms.7 Crucially, these determinations do not correlate with skill, just total playtime (i.e., experience). And on average, even novice players will realize that latency, rather than their video game skills, are to blame for their poor play by 100–110 ms.8 At 150 ms, games that involve quick responses are simply unplayable. In contrast, the average person does not even notice when the audio and video of a movie or TV show are out of sync unless the audio is 45 ms early or 125 ms late (170 ms total variance). Acceptability thresholds, as they’re generally called, are even wider, at 90 ms early and 185 ms late (275 ms).

The Metaverse isn’t a fast-moving pixel-precise game like Fortnite or Call of Duty, but its requirements are nevertheless quite high. The more realistic an avatar—such as the hyperreal “personas” created by the Apple Vision Pro’s face scan—the more sensitive humans are to the movement, detail, and timing of a smile or eye movement. To this end, few movie watchers are put off by the mouth movements of a cartoonish Pixar character, but many are creeped out by a photoreal CGI human whose lips don’t move exactly right (animators famously call this the “uncanny valley”).

As a category, VR and AR devices are particularly intolerant of latency. In contrast to “2D” displays, such as those of a PC, television, or smartphone, which use keystrokes, touchscreen taps, and mouse movements for inputs, HMDs often rely on a user’s head, eye, and body movements. These latter methods often activate a user’s inner ear, which in turn makes them more susceptible to disconnects between what they are doing (turning left or right, squatting, waving, and so on) and what their eyes can see. The result can be nauseating in a literal sense—less so for experiences where both the user and their virtual avatar remain in a fixed position, as in the case of a meeting, watching streaming video, and some stand-in-place fitness experiences, but brutally so when the user is making steps forward, backward, and side to side and/or their avatar is leaping, climbing, running, and so on. For similar reasons, VR and AR headsets aim not for 30 to 60 or even 90 frames per second but 120–240 fps, which aids visual clarity but also increases the number of “old frames” seen by a user if latency increases.9 AR device experiences, even those on a smartphone, face another challenge—their renders sit atop the “real world,” which “renders” at the speed of light (an object 100 meters away therefore arrives in 0.0003 ms, or 0.0000003 seconds). A device that is constantly loading information after a viewer has looked elsewhere is useless, and one that is partly lagging is likely to be more frustrating than helpful.

Separate from the issue of what’s tolerable is how latency affects usage. Subspace—a real-time bandwidth start-up whose executive team consists of the former senior vice president of infrastructure and security at League of Legends maker Riot Games, the former head of software at SpaceX, and the former head of video infrastructure at Google—says that video game players typically increase or decrease their weekly play time by 6% for every 10 ms decrease or increase in latency. This correlation holds beyond the point at which even “expert” gamers consciously notice latency levels, too.

Fortunately, not all Metaverse applications need ultra-low latency. Digital twins, such as those that oversee an airport terminal or factory floor, have higher acceptability thresholds because they simulate slower-moving and more predictable agents and objects. A relatively tiny portion of their simulations involves synchronization with distant users, devices, or networks. And while industrial AR devices still face high frame-rate requirements, their usage is typically concentrated to a few areas and they can therefore preload more of the data that might be needed, rather than query a distant server for real-time support. That said, the role of latency should not be underestimated. The more powerful a digital twin, the more powerful the computational power that’s required (as discussed in the following chapter). Most companies outsource their compute needs to cloud computing companies such as Amazon’s AWS, whose data centers might be thousands of kilometers away, and charge heavily for real-time bandwidth delivery due to its scarcity. And while industrial simulations often move slower than their fictional counterparts, latency-related inaccuracies compound over a higher volume of interactions, decisions, and AI recommendations.

With a greater understanding of latency requirements, it’s possible to reassess the current state of delivery time. The median time for data to be sent between the 25 largest cities in the United States is roughly 18 ms,10 which meets nearly all requirements for ultra-low latency experiences but doesn’t tell the full story of delivery times. For example, the specific city pairing matters greatly. Dallas to Houston averages only 2.5 ms one way, while New York City to Los Angeles takes 30 ms, and Orlando to Seattle typically exceeds 35. In addition, these sums reflect only city-to-city or data-center-to-data-center transit time, and therefore excludes the time required for a device outside these locations to send in their data or to receive it. This “last mile” is typically the slowest and least reliable part of delivery. Unfortunately, many buildings or neighborhoods still rely on low-capacity (i.e., low-bandwidth) coaxial copper cable and can easily congest. Households and devices that rely on cellular networks for data face 20 or even 40 ms in added latency compared to wired fiber optics. And while Wi-Fi typically covers only the last few feet of delivery, Wi-Fi routers add 1–2 ms—a small margin, but one that not all users can afford.

Moreover, all connections suffer from “jitter,” variances in delivery time relative to the median. While most jitter is tightly distributed around the connection’s median latency, it can spike latency severalfold due to a congestion at a local internet node, or an event as trivial as a neighbor or family member turning on Netflix or receiving a FaceTime call. Though temporary, such a jump can sever a network connection or otherwise ruin a shared experience.

International delivery is even more difficult. Median delivery times from data centers in the US Northeast to those in Northeast Asia are as long as 170 to 200 ms, and it takes up to 350 or 700 ms for a packet to go from a user in one locale to a user in the other, with jitter also more common, long-lasting, and severe.

Given the many latency-related obstacles faced by internet users some 40 years after the formalization of TCP/IP, it might come as a surprise that there are hundreds of millions of people who frequent online virtual worlds. Yet this is possible only due to numerous tricks and solutions that, unfortunately, don’t work well in the Metaverse. Case in point: Most high-fidelity multiplayer gaming is “match made” around server regions. By limiting the player roster to those who live in the northeastern United States, or Western Europe, or Southeast Asia, game publishers can minimize latency within each region. And because gaming is a leisure activity and typically played with one to three friends, this clustering works well enough. Multiplayer games also use “netcode” solutions that correct for synchronization issues and conflicts. Delay-based netcode will tell a player’s device to artificially delay its rendering of its owner’s inputs until the most latent player’s inputs arrive. This will irk players with muscle memory attuned to low latency, but it works. Rollback netcode is more sophisticated. If an opponent’s inputs are delayed, a player’s device will proceed based on what it expects to happen. If it turns out the opponent did something different, the device will try to unwind in-process animations and then replay them “correctly.”

Although the above tools are effective, they scale poorly. Netcode works well for titles in which player inputs are fairly predictable, such as driving simulations, or those with relatively few players to synchronize, as is the case in most fighting games. It is exponentially harder to correctly predict and coherently synchronize the behaviors of dozens of players, especially when they are participating in a sandbox-style virtual world with cloud-streamed environmental and asset data. And large though the gaming industry might seem on a revenue basis, it remains highly constrained in reach. Even in the United States, which has only 4% of the world’s population and 6% of its land by surface area, yet 26% of its internet networks, Subspace estimates that barely three-quarters of broadband homes can reliably play high-fidelity games such as Fortnite or Call of Duty.11 In contrast, the Middle East has 5% of the world’s population, 5% of its land, but only 3% of its networks, and fewer than one in four homes can reliably play the aforementioned titles.12 It’s even harder to play in India, which has 18% of the world’s population, 2% of its land, and 3.5% of its networks, with only one in ten broadband homes meeting high-fidelity gaming requirements.13

The Battle between H. sapiens and c

Outlandish though it may seem, the fight to minimize network latency is, at its core, a fight against the speed of light. Consider, as an example, the quest to send just a single byte from a data center in downtown New York City to one in downtown Tokyo or Mumbai as rapidly as possible. At a distance of 11,000–12,500 kilometers, a light photon could hypothetically complete such a trip in between 36 and 42 ms. The physics of the universe, in other words, has only a roughly 6–12 ms margin over the physics of the human brain. In practice, this millisecond benchmark is impossible to attain.

One impediment is silica glass. Many assume that data sent via fiber-optic cables travels at the speed of light. This is technically true, but all glass fibers, unlike the vacuum of space, reflect light. For one thing, the path of a given beam of light is not straight even if the cable itself is perfectly straight. Instead, a beam of light travels in more of a tight zigzag as it bounces between the inside edges of a fiber-optic cable core. The result is a more than 45% elongation of a route, which produces a minimum possible latency of 52–61 ms. Although such a delay already tests the patience of avid gamers, this figure is hypothetical. In 2021, Amazon’s AWS, Microsoft’s Azure, and Google’s Cloud Platform averaged more than 110 ms when sending a packet one way from their northeastern American data centers to their Asia-Pacific data centers, which route to Mumbai and Tokyo. Travel inside the United States faces a comparable increase. Although beams of light could travel from New York City to San Francisco in 14 ms and through fiber optics in 20 ms, average transit times are over 30 ms. There are several causes for these increases.

While the phrase “internet backbone” brings to mind a largely planned-out and partly federated network of cables, the internet is really a loose federation of private networks with individual aims and little concern for collective efficiency. Furthermore, internet cables are rarely laid out as the crow flies. Instead, they must navigate environmental concerns, existing public and private infrastructure (cities, parks, freeways), governmental permits and ordinances, and the costs of given routes (a longer route may require only earthen trenches or may piggyback on an in-construction highway, while the shortest might require blasting rock). In general, the more direct the intended path of a cable, the more likely it is to be politically, socially, financially, or environmentally challenged. And in most cases, there’s not much of a business case for a specific network to be laid so that it is a few milliseconds faster. As a hypothetical, imagine a private broadband operator seeking to connect two cities or regions that are roughly 300 kilometers apart. The most direct path would allow data packets to arrive in 1.3 ms, but laying this cable might require digging through a river or under a school. An alternative route might follow local roads and be laid during an existing roadway repair process. This latter option might save effort and money, but add 100 kilometers and, with it, another 0.4 ms. These milliseconds add up when a user needs to reach a person or server many thousands of miles and many dozens of networks away, but the internet users directly connected by this hypothetical cable won’t pay for the 0.4 ms in savings, and most of the latency challenge comes from the aggregation of the networks in use, not that one segment.

Many countries and even major international cities lack a direct connection. New York City has a direct undersea cable to France but not to Portugal. Traffic from the United States can go directly to Tokyo, but reaching India requires jumping from one undersea cable to another on the Asian or Australian continent, a process that adds thousands of kilometers to the trip. To shorten this path, a dedicated line would need to be dug across at least Thailand, if not also Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar. And again, such a connection would solve only for shore-to-shore transmission. In 2020, the US government effectively outlawed the construction of cables that directly connected the United States to Hong Kong or mainland China, prompting a still-under-construction cable funded by Facebook and Google to redirect to the Philippines and Taiwan.14 The following year, the World Bank abandoned a cable project that would have connected three Pacific Island nations, after the United States protested its construction by a Chinese supplier.15

US Internet Backbone

The layout of the internet’s many networks is exacerbated by the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), one of the core application layer protocols of TCP/IP. When a given device wants to send data to another unaffiliated device or server, at least one intermediary network is required, but within a large country, it’s common for data to travel across five to seven networks. International delivery might span one to two dozen network “hops” or more, depending on how remote and far away the two devices or servers are. These pathways are not fixed, either. Two emails sent from the same device in New York to the same device in Los Angeles might start on the same Wi-Fi network and Verizon FiOS wireline network and terminate on the same AT&T wireless network, but in the meantime, one email might travel through the midwestern United States and head south along the Pacific Coast, while the other might first head south to the Carolinas before traveling across the Southwest. The BGP dictates these pathways by helping every single network leg choose which network will pass a given packet of data. Accordingly, an American’s daily internet usage might involve hundreds or even thousands of the country’s more than 30,000 networks.16

Global Submarine Internet Cable Backbone

Although BGP successfully routes traffic across more than 110,000 networks globally, it does not know what data is being sent (e.g., an email versus video call), whether it’s an initiation or response (e.g., a user sending a request for the New York Times homepage, or the New York Times website sending that data back), its urgency (the relevance of 10, 50, or 200 ms), the impact of congestion (whether a key connection might be severed), and so on. Instead, the internet’s “air traffic controller” applies a standardized methodology for routing data, which essentially weighs the shortest path, the fastest path, and the cheapest path, with a general preference for cost.

BGP’s ruleset reflects the internet’s original asynchronous network design. Its goal is to ensure that all data is transmitted successfully and inexpensively. But as a result, many routes are far longer than necessary—and inconsistently so. Although a Fortnite player might be located only 500 kilometers from a local server and have a shortest possible network path of 650 kilometers, their data might take an 800-kilometer path while their neighbor ends up traveling 50% farther. Moreover, one of these connections might end up severed, or suffer from recurring bouts of 150 ms latency, all to prioritize traffic that doesn’t need to be delivered in real time, such as an email.

Not FTL, but Hopefully Fast Enough

The many factors listed above explain why a data packet that could travel from New York City to San Francisco, Tokyo, or Mumbai in 14, 36, or 42 ms is instead limited to a minimum of 20, 52, or 61 ms and actually averages 30, 110, or 130 ms. Improving these times will be expensive, difficult, and slow. But there is reason for optimism.

Internet access continues to improve on an annual basis, with average bandwidth increasing, latency falling, and prices (in real terms) declining. The emergence of what many accountancies, consultancies, and investment banks expect will be a multitrillion-dollar Metaverse economy, alongside additional growth in the digital economy, will lead to even greater investments.

In the average year, close to $3 billion is spent laying new submarine cables, many of which reach populations that had previously lacked high-speed internet.17 The average fiber pairing per cable has grown from 4 to 14 over that time, too, substantially increasing capacity.18

Compared to wireline infrastructure, it’s comparatively easy to upgrade wireless towers and stations. 5G networks are primarily billed as offering wireless users “ultra-low latency,” with the potential of 1 ms and a more realistic 10 ms expected compared to the 10–20 ms average of today’s 4G networks. This is not a complete solution, as it reflects only the latency from a user’s device to a tower, after which the fixed-line internet backbone takes over. However, it is a substantial leap for mobile devices as well as rural homes without access to in-the-ground broadband.

Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet company, promises to provide high-bandwidth, low-latency internet service across the United States and eventually the rest of the world. In contrast to prior satellite internet companies, such as Viasat or EchoStar/Hughes Network Systems, Starlink satellites are an average of 550 kilometers above the earth, rather than 35,700 kilometers,19 which reduces the theoretical transit time required for a customer to send their data to a satellite and for that satellite to send the data back to earth from roughly 250 ms to 4 ms. As Starlink’s lower-earth-orbit satellites are less than a tenth of the weight of their geosynchronous competitors, the company’s launch costs are substantially lower, which enables more of these satellites to be sent into orbit, which then reduces the distances between a customer and the nearest available satellite.

Though an unprecedented technical achievement, satellite internet doesn’t achieve ultra-low latency, especially at great distances. Though Starlink aspires to 10–20 ms one-way latency (20–40 ms round trip), at the start of 2023, it averages more than 30 ms (60 ms+) when sending data to and from a US server or device—more than double the industry average.20 In Puerto Rico, latency averaged about 60 ms (120 ms) when sending to and from local computers, four and a half times the local average, while the Philippines was 80 ms (160 ms), seven times the average.21 Starlink’s actual latency far exceeds its theoretical minimum for several reasons. For example, a given packet of data might need to daisy-chain across several Starlink satellites before being sent down to earth, after which it must still travel through terrestrial networks to reach its destination—and then repeat the process coming back. In some cases, Starlink even exacerbates the speed-of-light problem compared to purely terrestrial alternatives. New York to Philadelphia is around 150 kilometers in a straight line and potentially 200 kilometers by cable, but over 1,200 kilometers when traveling to a low-orbit satellite and back down.* Compared to fiber-optic cables, Starlink also faces severe capacity constraints. Residential fiber-optic cables can support up to 100 gigabytes per second in bandwidth, while submarine cables can reach into the single-digit terabytes per second. Starlink satellites max out at 20 Gbps, which allows them to support a maximum of 2,000 simultaneous users and experience speed degradation as usage grows.
