Between Q1 2021 and Q3 2023, average download speeds for US Starlink customers fell from roughly 90 Mbps to 65 Mbps, due to increases in users and usage, with one-way latency growing from 20 ms to 30.22 Due to lower average population density, Canadian customers experienced no material decline over that period.

As SpaceX founder Elon Musk acknowledges, Starlink is focused on “the hardest-to-serve customers,” people whom telecommunications companies “otherwise have trouble reaching.”23 With this in mind, satellite delivery should be seen as enabling more people to meet the minimum latency specifications for the Metaverse, rather than offering improvements for those who already meet it. Still, the impact of the technology continues to grow, as do its minimum service levels. In 2018 Musk estimated that Starlink would require $10 billion in investment until achieving sustainable profitability.24 By mid-2021, Musk’s estimate had grown to more than $30 billion25 as the company ratcheted up its global ambitions. At the end of 2023, Starlink’s network spanned an estimated 5,600 satellites—over 60% of all active satellites26—and planned to launch another 6,500 by 2025, with the hopes of eventually operating more than 42,000.27 In 2019, Amazon announced Kuiper Systems, which has similar aims to Starlink and leverages Amazon founder Jeff Bezos’s aerospace company, Blue Origin. Amazon expects to launch over 3,000 satellites by 2030,28 with an investment budget of more than $10 billion.29 SpaceX’s and Amazon’s satellites may relay traffic to each other, just as independent fiber networks do today. But even if these rival constellations remain fully separate, growth in their fleets will increase the number of customers that can be supported and the average bandwidth they’re afforded, while also reducing latency by shortening the average distance between satellites, and from satellites to industrial receiver stations on earth.

Prior to Starlink’s commercial launch in 2020, Facebook, Google, and various start-ups aspired to build internet networks using solar-powered drones or high-altitude balloons in the stratosphere. The benefits of such equipment would include significantly shorter distances to customers compared to lower-earth-orbit satellites and far lower launch costs. Beginning in 2016, Facebook’s Aquila project deployed a series of drones roughly 140 feet wide and weighing 900 pounds that flew at altitudes between 18,000 and 27,000 kilometers (93% closer to the ground than Starlink’s satellites) and were intended to operate continuously for 90 days. Facebook hoped that drones might one day provide internet to four billion people, most of whom lacked acceptable alternatives. Beginning in 2011, Google’s Project Loon launched 50-foot-wide and 40-foot-tall superpressure helium balloons to altitudes between 18 and 25 kilometers, which operated for an average of 100 days before needing to return to earth. In 2018, Facebook halted development on Aquila, while Google shut Loon down in 2021, citing various technical obstacles, rival priorities, and the deployment of 4G networks across the developing world. Despite the failure of these projects, there is still hope that stratospheric internet will prove viable in the decades to come. To this point, Starlink’s satellites not only boasted considerable advances over the satellite models of the 2000s and early 2010s, but the company also realized the very vision once touted by the Bill Gates–backed Teledesic. Between 1994 and 2002, Teledesic had raised over $1 billion as part of its $9 billion plan (equivalent to $19 billion in 2024 dollars) to launch 850 satellites into orbit roughly 700 kilometers above the earth.30 By 1997, the company’s plans were shrunk to 288 satellites at 1,400 kilometers, and in 2002, Teledesic suspended operations.31

In theory, improving the Border Gateway Protocol is the cheapest and fastest way to improve delivery times. The Internet Engineering Task Force does not dictate standards development or mandate the adoption of any updates. Instead, it helps organize working groups who put forward various proposals. And while these proposals sometimes receive tacit or explicit approval from IETF leaders or sponsors, their adoption—and thus ability to become standards—requires the voluntary embrace of the many companies that constitute “the internet.” In the case of BGP, this would involve hundreds of computing-device and modem/router manufacturers, over 110,000 network operators, millions of application developers, and so on. Not all of these groups would need to adopt a change for there to be benefits—better routing on two of seven network hops between a user and a server would nevertheless save precious milliseconds—but a critical mass of adoptees is required to have any meaningful effect. And although the benefits of a real-time protocol or packet classification is obvious, the specific solution is less clear. Remember, BGP has multiple criteria in its rank-order preference. Should BGP prioritize real-time traffic that has the greatest distance to travel or the lowest plausible tolerance? Should real-time traffic be moved to the “front of the line” or be boosted by some fixed percentage (and if so, how much)? Should real-time traffic be boosted irrespective of network congestion, thereby significantly worsening the experience for non-real-time traffic? And because the internet is decentralized and largely ungoverned, what system might avoid applications and/or networks coding their traffic as real-time irrespective of its latency needs? Such coding would aid delivery reliability and speed, which benefits most developers and users, even if it’s not required—but it would also take up scarce capacity needed by traffic that did need real-time delivery.

A potential solution for real-time bandwidth standards and protocols may stem from the growing ownership of key backbone infrastructure by big-tech companies. In 2012, data sent to and from Amazon, Facebook, Google, and Microsoft constituted less than 10% of traffic transmitted on submarine cables. A decade later, these four companies were more than two-thirds of total traffic, with companies such as Nvidia, Netflix, and Apple taking up much of the rest. In response to bandwidth fees as well as the desire to improve connectivity across the developing world through non-stratospheric means, these companies began to acquire and purchase the future capacity of existing submarine cables, and co-finance or fully fund the laying of new ones. By the end of 2024, Facebook is expected to have the greatest share of global submarine infrastructure among tech giants, having increased from 0% in 2015 to partial, complete, or de facto (i.e., capacity-based) ownership of 13%—a portion representing more than 170,000 kilometers of cables and connecting nearly 33 countries across 47 connections, while reaching 36% of the global population, mostly in Africa and Southeast Asia.32

Facebook’s Submarine Cable Infrastructure

The most immediate impact of infrastructure investments by Facebook and its peers will be a reduction in global latency to connected countries, and improved bandwidth should be another benefit. On the other hand, the reach of these companies—especially when combined, and in the context of their broader share of internet traffic—gives them an outsized ability to promote, steer, or deploy potential supplementations to BGP, or to private alternatives.

  1. * As light beams zigzag through silica glass but travel straight through the atmosphere and space, the effective ratio between the two options is closer to 1:4, not 1:6.

Chapter 6 COMPUTING ENTIRE UNIVERSES

Sending enough data in a timely fashion is just one part of the process of operating a synchronized virtual world. The data must also be understood, code must be run, inputs assessed, logic performed, environments rendered, and so on. This is the job of central processing units (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs), each and together broadly described as “compute.”

Compute is the resource that performs all digital “work.” For decades, there have been increases in the number of computing resources available and manufactured per year. Despite this, computing resources have always been and will likely remain scarce—because when more computing capability is available, more calculations and more complicated calculations tend to be made.

Think back to the example of the blockbuster film Monsters University from Chapter 4. To render the 2013 production, Pixar built a supercomputer comprising 2,000 conjoined industrial-grade computers with a combined 24,000 cores.1 As each of the film’s 120,000 frames took roughly 30 core hours to render, Pixar’s supercomputer, which cost tens of millions of dollars to assemble, could squeeze rendering time down to about five seconds per frame—if the entire computer was assigned to that single frame.* Despite the enormous investment in Monsters University’s data center, Pixar replaced many of these computers and cores with newer and more capable processors over the following years. But rather than use this power to render frames more quickly, Pixar opted for more sophisticated renders. Consider that one scene in the studio’s 2017 film Coco had nearly eight million individual lights in the background, which required more than 1,000 core hours per frame to render. Eventually, Pixar opted to simplify the rendering process by “baking” a number of lights in 20-degree longitudinal and latitudinal increments—that is, reducing their responsiveness to the camera2—which helped reduce rendering times to 55 hours per frame.

Another example is offered by the swelling physical size of video game consoles. The first Sony PlayStation, released in 1994, weighed 3.2 pounds (1,450 grams) and measured 10.75 inches by 7.5 inches by 2.5 inches (resulting in a volume of 202 cubic inches). In 2020, it was possible to manufacture a device as powerful as the original PlayStation for less than 5% of the inflation-adjusted cost and 3% of the size.3 Instead, Sony’s fifth-generation PlayStation weighed 210% more than the first (i.e., 9.9 pounds, or 4,500 grams) and was 220% larger (though it was also 15% cheaper on an inflation-adjusted basis). Most of this increase related to the decision to place more computing power in the device—and larger fans for its high-end CPUs and GPUs as they performed their calculations. These investments enabled substantial improvements in graphical realism (e.g., light scattering and reflections) coupled with a doubling in frame rates and a nearly 30-fold increase in maximum resolutions. Excitingly, the most important improvements were gameplay related.

By the start of the 2020s, many of the most popular games in the world were those that supported unstructured, sandbox-style play such as Roblox and Minecraft and/or high levels of concurrent users, such as Roblox, Fortnite, and Call of Duty: Warzone. While these titles are incredible creative achievements, their underlying ideas are far from new. For decades, developers have imagined experiences with dozens of live players (if not hundreds or thousands) in a single, shared simulation and heretofore-unexplored virtual environments limited only by the imagination of the individual user. The issue was that these capabilities were not possible without enormous constraints, many of which were too great for the average consumer.

While virtual worlds such as EVE Online had included hundreds or even thousands of concurrent users (CCUs) since the late 1990s, individual players could not congregate via avatars. Instead, users directed large and mostly static ships that would relocate in space or exchange artillery fire. Dozens of World of Warcraft avatars can be rendered in the same place, but model detail is limited, the perspective is relatively zoomed out, and players have limited control over what each avatar can do. And if too many players have converged on a single area, the game’s server would temporarily “shard” it into concurrently operating but independent copies of that space. Some games even chose to limit real-time rendering to individual players and select in-game AI, with the entire background pre-rendered and thus impossible for players to affect. Engaging in any of these experiences also required a player to buy a dedicated gaming PC, which could run into the thousands of dollars. Even if such a device wasn’t strictly necessary, a user likely had to “turn off” or “turn down” the game’s rendering capability or halve the frame rate.

It was only by the mid-2010s that millions of consumer-grade devices could manage a game like Fortnite—one with dozens of richly animated avatars in a single match, each one capable of a wide range of actions, and interacting in a vivid and tangible world, rather than the cold vastness of space. It was around this same time that enough affordable servers were available that could manage and synchronize the inputs coming from so many devices.

Not only did these computational advancements lead to new or newly popular game genres, but the video gaming industry quickly expanded into the sorts of media experiences that were previously “IRL only,” such as concerts, and appealed to those who had historically shown little interest in games. By the end of 2023, Roblox had an estimated 355 million monthly active users4—more than the entirety of PlayStation, Xbox, and Nintendo combined, and half as many as Snap.

But as mentioned in Chapter 4, these games feel so ahead of their time in part because of specific design decisions that allow them to work around current computational constraints. Most battle royales support 100 players, but they also use enormous maps with numerous “points of interest” to scatter players far from one another. This means that while the server needs to track what all the players are doing, each player’s device doesn’t need to render them or track or process their actions. And while players must ultimately converge on a small space—sometimes the size of a dorm room—the very premise of a battle royale means that almost all players have been defeated at that point. And as the map shrinks, it becomes harder to survive. A battle royale player might need to worry about 99 competitors, but their device faces far fewer opponents.

These tricks only go so far. The mobile-only battle royale Free Fire, which had as many as 100 and 150 million daily active users during parts of 2020 and 2021,5 focused on players in Southeast Asia and South America, most of whom owned low-to-mid-range Android devices, rather than more powerful iPhones and high-end Androids. As such, Free Fire’s battle royale is limited to 50 players, not 100. When titles such as Fortnite and Roblox operate social events in a more confined space, such as a virtual concert venue, CCUs are typically capped at 50 or fewer. They also limit what users can do compared to the standard game modes. The ability to build might be turned off, or the number of dance moves reduced from the normal dozen or two to only a single preset option. And players who have CPUs and GPUs that are less powerful than average will face even more compromises; their game might not load the custom avatars of other players, as they have no gameplay consequence, and instead render each one as a stock character. For all the marvels of Microsoft Flight Simulator, fewer than 1% of desktop or laptop Macs and PCs can even run the title on its lowest graphical settings (and fewer still would be able to do so if its map was truly “alive,” rather than just its weather and airplane traffic).

Computing capabilities improve every year. Roblox supports up to 200 players in its relatively lower-fidelity worlds, with up to 700 players possible in beta testing since August 2020.6 Still, these platforms remain quite far from the point at which the only constraint is creative. The Metaverse will involve hundreds of thousands participating in a shared simulation and with as many custom virtual items as they like; full motion capture; the ability to richly modify a virtual world (rather than pick from a dozen or so options) with full persistence; and rendering that world not just in 1080p (typically considered “high definition”) but 4K or even 8K. Even the most powerful devices on earth struggle to do this in real time because every single asset, texture, and resolution increase or added frame and player means an additional draw on scarce computing resources.

Nvidia’s founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, imagines the next step for immersive simulations as taking people far beyond more realistic-looking explosions or a more animated avatar. Instead, he envisions the application of the “laws of particle physics, of gravity, of electromagnetism, of electromagnetic waves, [including] light and radio waves … of pressure and sound.”7

Two Sides of the Same Problem

Exactly how much more computing power is required to operate and render the Metaverse is unclear. In October 2021, John Carmack, the id Software founder and former Oculus CTO, said that if he’d been asked 20 years earlier whether “one hundred times the processing power” would be sufficient to meet this duty, he would have said yes.8 Yet even though billions of devices now hold such capability, Carmack insists that the Metaverse remains at least five to ten years away and would still face “serious optimization trade-offs” even at the further edge of that prediction.9 Two months later, Raja Koduri, Intel’s senior vice president and general manager of its Accelerated Computing and Graphics Group, published similar thoughts on Intel’s investor relations site. Koduri said that “indeed, the metaverse may be the next major platform in computing after the world wide web and mobile … [but] truly persistent and immersive computing, at scale and accessible by billions of humans in real time, will require even more: a 1,000-times increase in computational efficiency from today’s state of the art.”10 There are varying perspectives on how best to solve the need for more compute.

One argument is that as much “work” as possible should be performed in remote, industrial-grade data centers rather than in consumer devices. That most of the work involved in a virtual world happens on each user’s device strikes many as wasteful because it means many devices are performing the same work at the same time in support of the same experience. In contrast, the superpowerful server operated by the virtual world’s “owner” is just tracking user inputs, relaying them when necessary, then refereeing process conflicts when they occur. It doesn’t even need to render anything!

An example helps bring this to (virtual) life. When a player shoots a rocket launcher at a tree in Fortnite, this information (the item used, its attributes, and the trajectory of the projectile) is sent from that player’s device to Fortnite’s multiplayer server, which then relays that information to all the players who require it. Their local machines then process and act on that information: they show the explosion, determine whether their players are harmed, remove the tree from the map, allow the players to move through where it once was, and so on.

In practice, players might not even see the same visual explosion, even though the “same” explosive hit the exact “same” tree at the exact “same” angle at the exact “same” time, and the exact same logic was applied to process the cause and effect. This reflects the fact that (due to variable latency) a given device might think the rocket was sent slightly earlier or later, and from a slightly different position. Usually this doesn’t matter, but sometimes it is enormously consequential: Player 1’s console might determine that Player 2 was killed by the explosion that destroyed the tree, while Player 2’s console would say Player 2 took significant, but not fatal, damage. Neither console is “wrong,” but the game obviously can’t proceed with both versions of the “truth.” And so the server must “pick.”

The current reliance on personal devices creates other limitations, too. Consumers can experience only what their own device can manage. A 2019 iPad, 2013-era PlayStation 4, and a 2020 edition PlayStation 5 will all present Fortnite differently. The iPad will be limited to 30 frames per second, while the PlayStation 4 will offer 60 fps, and the PlayStation 5, 120 fps. The iPad will likely load only selective map textures and maybe even skip avatar outfits, while the PlayStation 5 will show refracting light and shadows, something the PlayStation 4 cannot. This, in turn, means that the overall complexity of a virtual world ends up partly limited by the lowest-end device that can access it. Epic Games has decided that the avatars and outfits in Fortnite shouldn’t have an impact on its gameplay, but changing its mind might entail cutting off many players. What’s more, the constraints of tablets and consoles are quaint in comparison to VR and AR headsets, which must be far smaller and more lightweight than typical computing devices, yet have far greater computational demands (more on this topic in Chapter 9).

Shifting as much processing and rendering to industrial-grade data centers seems both more efficient and essential to building the Metaverse. There are already companies and services pointing in this direction. Google Stadia and Amazon Luna process all video gameplay in remote data centers, then push the entire rendered experience to a user’s device as a video stream (this is called “cloud gaming”). In this case, the only thing a client device needs to do is play this video and send inputs (move left, press X, and so on)—similar to watching Netflix.

Proponents of this approach often highlight the logic of powering residential homes using industrial power plants and grids, not private generators. The cloud-based model allows consumers to stop buying consumer-grade, infrequently upgraded, and retailer-marked-up computers and instead rent access to enterprise-grade equipment that is more cost-efficient per unit of processing power and more easily updated. Whether a user has a $1,500 iPhone or an old Wi-Fi-enabled fridge with a video screen, they could play a computationally intensive title such as Cyberpunk 2077 in all its fully rendered glory. Why should a virtual world depend on a small piece of consumer hardware wrapped in plastic-dye covers, rather than on a multimillion-dollar (if not billion-dollar) server stack owned by the company that operates the virtual world?

For all the ostensible logic of this approach, and the success of server-side content services such as Netflix and Spotify, remote rendering is not the consensus solution among game publishers today. Tim Sweeney has argued that “initiatives to place real-time processing on the wrong side of the latency wall have always been doomed to failure because, even though bandwidth and latency are improving, local computing performance is improving faster.”11 Put differently, the argument is not whether remote data centers can offer better experiences than consumer-owned ones. They obviously can. Rather, it’s that networks get in the way and will likely continue to do so.

It’s here the power generator analogy begins to break down. In most of the developed world, households don’t worry about whether they receive the power they need and as quickly as it’s needed. The same cannot be said for data. As Chapter 5 reviewed, modern video games send only 30–300 MB per hour and many users can’t reliably receive this data on a timely basis. A cloud-streamed video game that’s in 2K resolution at 60 frames per second is 10 GB per hour, with many gamers hoping for 4K and 120 frames per second (or 40 GB per hour); and the needs for VR and VR headsets are even higher.12

Furthermore, remote compute has yet to prove itself to be more efficient for rendering and, in many cases, general processing. This is a consequence of several interconnected issues. First, a GPU does not render an entire virtual world, nor even much of it, at any given point. Instead, it renders just what’s necessary for a given user when that user needs it. When a player turns around in a game like The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, the Nintendo Switch’s Nvidia GPU effectively unloads everything that was previously rendered in order to support the player’s new field of view. This process is called “viewing-frustum culling.” Other techniques include “occlusion,” in which objects that are in a player’s field of view are not loaded/rendered if they are obstructed by another object, and “level of detail” (LOD), in which information, such as the nuanced texture of a birch tree’s bark, are rendered only when the player should be able to see it.

Culling, occlusion, and LOD solutions are essential to real-time-rendered experiences because they enable a user’s device to concentrate its processing power on what the user can see. But as a result, other users cannot “piggyback” off the work of one player’s GPU. Some readers might think this is a lie, recalling many hours spent playing Mario Kart on the Nintendo 64, which allowed players to “split” a TV screen into four, one for each driver. Even today, Fortnite allows a single PlayStation or Xbox to cleave a screen in half so that two players might play at once. But in this case, the relevant GPU is supporting simultaneous renders for multiple participants, not users. The distinction here is critical. Every player must enter the same match and level—and cannot leave it early, either. This is because the device’s processors can load and manage only a finite amount of information, and its random-access memory system will temporarily store various renders (e.g., a tree or building) so that it can be continuously reused by each player, rather than rendered from scratch each time. Each player’s resolution and/or frame rate also drops by an amount proportional to the number of users. This means that even if two TVs are used to operate two-player Mario Kart, rather than one TV split in two, each player receives half as many rendered pixels per second.†

It is technically possible for a GPU to render two entirely different games. A top-of-the-line Nvidia GPU can certainly support two distinct emulations of a 2D side-scrolling Super Mario Bros., or one version of Super Mario Bros. and another similarly low-powered title. But this is not done in a compute-efficient manner. An Nvidia GPU that might run high-end Game A at its fullest rendering specifications cannot run two versions of the title at half of the specifications—or even a third. It also cannot trade off its power between two games based on what they need and when, like a parent helping their two kids study or get to bed. Even if Game A can never use all of a given Nvidia GPU’s power, that spare cannot be assigned elsewhere.

GPUs do not generate generic rendering “power” that can be divided across users in the way a power plant splits electricity across multiple homes, or in the way a CPU server can support input, location, and synchronization data for a hundred players in a battle royale. Instead, GPUs typically operate as a “locked instance” supporting a single player’s rendering. Many companies are trying to solve efficient GPU splitting, but until it’s possible, there’s no inherent efficiency in designing “mega-GPUs” akin to large industrial power generators, turbines, or other infrastructure. While power generators are typically more cost-efficient per unit of power as their capacity increases, the reverse is true with GPUs. A GPU that’s twice as powerful as another, in a simplified sense, costs more than twice as much to produce.

The difficulties of “splitting” or “sharing” GPUs explains why Microsoft Xbox’s cloud game streaming server farms are, in fact, made up of racks and racks of de-shelled Xboxes, each one serving a player. Put another way, Microsoft’s electrical power plant is really just a network of single-household power generators, rather than a single, neighborhood-sized one. Microsoft could use bespoke GPU and CPU hardware to support cloud instances, rather than the GPU and CPU hardware in its consumer-centric Xboxes, but this would require that every Xbox game be developed to support an additional “type” of Xbox.

Cloud-rendering servers also face utilization issues. A cloud gaming service might require 75,000 dedicated servers for the Cleveland area at 8 p.m. Sunday, but only 20,000 on average, and 4,000 at 4 a.m. Monday. When consumers own these servers, in the form of consoles or gaming PCs, it doesn’t matter that they’re unused or offline. Data-center economics, conversely, are based on optimizing for demand. As a result, it will always be expensive to rent high-end GPUs with low utilization rates.

This is why Amazon Web Services gives customers a reduced rate if they rent servers from Amazon in advance (“reserved instances”). Customers are guaranteed access for the next year because they’ve paid for the server, and Amazon is pocketing the difference between the cost and the price the customer is charged (in 2021, AWS’s cheapest Linux GPU reserved instance, equivalent to a then-top-of-the-line PlayStation, cost over $2,000 for one year). If a customer wants to access servers when they need them (“spot instances”), they might find they’re not available, or that only lower-end GPUs are. This last point is key: the computing shortage is not solved if the only way to make remote servers affordable is to use older, less capable units, rather than replace them.

There is another way to improve cost models: consolidate servers into fewer locations. Rather than operate separate cloud game streaming centers in the states of Ohio, Washington, Illinois, and New York, a company could just build one or two nationally. As the number and diversity of customers increases, demand tends to stabilize, resulting in greater average utilization rates. But concentrating data centers also means increasing the distance between remote GPUs and the end user, thereby increasing latency. This is the core challenge of so-called “edge compute”—a cloud computing model that uses a larger number of small data centers closer to end users instead of larger data centers that are farther away from the average user—latency and utilization will forever be in competition. Matthew Prince, the founder of the content delivery network and cloud cybersecurity giant Cloudflare, has argued that the primary role for edge data centers is not minimizing delivery time in exchange for higher costs but, instead, regulatory compliance.13 In many countries, especially European nations, governments require consumer data to be stored domestically and prohibit the quotidian transfer of this data into foreign servers. The result is that edge compute is sometimes a requirement of cloud-focused processing and rendering strategies.

Shifting computing resources into the cloud also creates many new costs. One area of importance is temperature. Side-by-side, always-turned-on devices running at data centers create considerable heat—far more than the aggregate heat of those servers sitting in a living room credenza. Servicing, securing, and managing this equipment is costly. The shift from streaming limited bits of data to high-resolution, high-frame-rate content means substantially higher bandwidth costs, too. Yes, Netflix and others make the costs work, but they’re typically sending fewer than 30 frames of video per second (not 60 to 120) with a lower resolution (e.g., 1K or 2K, not 4K or 8K, which Google originally promised for Google Stadia), on a non-real-time basis, and from nearby servers that are storing files rather than performing intensive computing operations.

For the foreseeable future, what might be designated “Sweeney’s Law”—improvements in local compute will continue to outpace improvements in network bandwidth, latency, and reliability—seems likely to hold. Although many believe that Moore’s Law, which was coined in 1965 and states that the number of transistors in a dense integrated circuit doubles about every two years, is now slowing down, CPU and GPU processing power continues to grow at a rapid pace. Difficult though it is to believe, the iPhone 15 Pro has 19 billion transistors—19 times more than the entirety of Pixar’s 1995 industrial render farm.14 These advances are also rapidly adopted by consumers, too, with the average smartphone worldwide replaced every 24–40 months.15

Outside the Law

Sweeney’s Law does not mean that all Metaverse-related compute will occur locally and/or on the relevant user’s device. As discussed in Chapter 5, industrial simulations tend to require more remote processing, and are more predictable in demand, less price sensitive than leisure-based simulations such as those used for video games or to create movies, and more tolerant of latency. As consumer usage of the Metaverse grows, especially in major cities and for non-leisure use cases such as AR shopping or travel, consumer demand for remote processing and rendering will vary less throughout the day, which improves utilization rates. Many generative AI models require too much hard drive space to be stored on a local device and cannot be processed on said device, either. In many cases, their outputs—a 3D model, or chatbot response—also do not require ultra-low latency.

The insatiable need for more processing power—ideally, located as close as possible to the user but, at the very least, in nearby industrial server farms—invariably brings to mind a third option: decentralized computing. With so many powerful and often inactive devices in the homes and hands of consumers, near other homes and hands, it feels inevitable that systems will emerge that share idle processing power.

Culturally, at least, the idea of collectively shared but privately owned infrastructure is already well understood. Anyone who installs solar panels at their home can sell excess power to their local grid (and, indirectly, to their neighbor). Elon Musk touts a future in which a Tesla earns its owner’s rent as a self-driving car when it’s sitting unused in their garage, expensive parking lot, or city street.

As early as the 1990s, programs emerged for distributed computing using everyday consumer hardware. One of the most famous examples is the University of California, Berkeley’s SETI@home, wherein consumers would volunteer use of their home computers to power the search for alien life. Sweeney has highlighted that one of the items on his “to-do list” for the first-person shooter Unreal, which shipped in 1998, was “to enable game servers to talk to each other so we can just have an unbounded number of players in a single game session.” Nearly 20 years later, Sweeney admitted that goal “seems to still be on our wish list.”16

A SETI@Home Version 1.0 Screensaver

Although the technology to split GPUs and share non-data-center CPUs is still nascent, some believe that blockchains provide both the technological mechanism for decentralized computing and its economic model. The idea is that owners of underutilized CPUs and GPUs would be “paid” in some cryptocurrency for the use of their processing capabilities. There might even be a live auction for access to these resources, either those with “jobs” bidding for access or those with capacity bidding on jobs.‡

Could such a marketplace provide some of the massive amounts of processing capacity that will be required by the Metaverse? Imagine, as users navigate immersive spaces, their account is continuously bidding out the necessary computing tasks to mobile devices held but unused by people nearby, perhaps even those they are walking by, all to animate the synthetic experiences that surround them. And later, when this user is no longer using their device, they would be earning tokens as they return the favor (more on this in Chapter 11). Proponents of this crypto-exchange concept see it as an inevitable feature of all future microchips. Every computer, no matter how small, would be designed to be auctioning off any and all spare cycles, 24 hours per day. Billions of dynamically arrayed processors will power the deep compute cycles of even the largest industrial customers and provide the ultimate and infinite computing mesh that enables the Metaverse. Perhaps the only way for everyone to hear a tree fall is for everyone to water it.

Whatever the prospects for decentralized computing, there are still those who believe that the full vision of the Metaverse, imagined by authors such as Stephenson and Gibson and tech pioneers such as Carmack and Sweeney, is simply impossible until quantum computing is possible, reliable, and scalable. In contrast to typical computing, which processes information using conventional bits of data (i.e., 0s and 1s) according to rules broadly understood in the 1830s and codified by Alan Turing in the 1930s,17 quantum computing uses quantum bits and the more nascent field of quantum mechanics. “Qubits” can exist in multiple states simultaneously (superpositioned”), and experience quantum “entanglement,” in which the state of one qubit is dependent on another, even if they are a great distance apart.

The Sycamore Supercomputer in 2019

In 2019, the scientific journal Nature published a paper that argued Google had produced the first quantum computer to achieve “quantum supremacy”—the ability to solve a problem faster than any traditional computer. Specifically, Google claimed its Sycamore took 200 seconds to complete a task that would take the world’s most powerful traditional computer, the IBM-developed Summit at the Oak Ridge Laboratory in Tennessee, 10,000 years to complete.§ In 2023, Google unveiled an updated Sycamore whose quantum processor was reportedly 241 million times more powerful than its 2019 predecessor.18 However, the quantum computing industry still faces many obstacles—and the extraordinary cost to construct these systems.¶ Qubits are incredibly sensitive to their local environment and can change state due to noise, vibrations, temperature changes, electromagnetic radiation, contact with neighboring particles, and more. The result is “quantum error” that is not just difficult (and costly) to address but difficult to notice—because it would take 10,000 years for a world-class computer to solve the problem attempted by Sycamore, Google could not directly verify its full results, and instead used extrapolations and spot examinations of key areas.19 Now that’s some netcode.

  2. † The exception here is when a game is running well below the capacity of the GPU that’s supporting it—as would be the case if one played the Nintendo 64 version of Mario Kart on the Nintendo Switch, which released 21 years after the Nintendo 64.

  3. ‡ Neal Stephenson described this sort of technology and experience at length in Cryptonomicon, which was published in 1999, seven years after Snow Crash.

  4. § IBM later claimed it could perform the task in 2.5 days if given access to Summit, though this test exercise was never attempted, and even if executed successfully, Sycamore would still have achieved “quantum supremacy” by a roughly 99.9% margin.

  5. ¶ As Sycamore is an R&D project, it’s likely that even Google does not know the true cost to produce the quantum computer. In fiscal years 2015 through 2023, Google spent an average of $25 billion annually on R&D (Eric Sheridan, GOOG Financial Model Client Version, Goldman Sachs, updated February 2, 2023).

Chapter 7 VIRTUAL WORLD ENGINES AND PLATFORMS

A virtual tree falls in a virtual forest. The last two chapters explained what is required for the tree to be rendered, and for its fall to be processed and then made available to any observer. But what is this tree? Where is this tree? What is the forest? The answer is data and code.

Data describes the attributes of a virtual object, such as its dimensions or color. For Berkeley’s virtual tree to be processed by a CPU and rendered by a GPU, this data needs to be run by code. And if a user wants to chop down that tree and use its wood to build a bed or light a fire, that code must be part of a much broader framework of code* that operates the virtual world.

The real world isn’t altogether different. The laws of physics are the code that reads and runs all interactions—from the reasons a tree falls to how this produces vibrations in the air that travel to a human ear and cause nerves to relay information via electrical signal across various synapses. Similarly, a tree being “seen” by a human observer means it reflected light produced by (usually) the sun, light that is in turn received and processed by the human eye and brain.

But there is a key difference: the real world is fully preprogrammed. Humans can’t see X-rays or echolocate, but the requisite information already exists in the world. In a game, X-rays and echolocation require data and a lot of code. If a user goes home, mixes up ketchup and petroleum, and then tries to eat it or paint with it, the laws of physics take care of the results. For a game to manage the same interaction, it needs to know in advance what ketchup and petroleum do when they’re combined (and probably in generic ratios), or it needs to know enough about the two for the game’s logic to figure it out, assuming the game is capable. A virtual world’s logic might say that petroleum cannot be mixed with anything. Or that it can be mixed only with oil. Or that if it’s mixed with anything at all, it produces unusable sludge. But a more complicated result requires considerably more data and for the virtual world’s logic to be far more comprehensive. How much petroleum can be added to ketchup before it’s inedible? How much ketchup can be added to petroleum before it’s unusable? How do the resulting substance’s color and viscosity change based on the ratio of one ingredient to the other?

The fact that so many of these permutations have little value is hugely valuable to those who produce virtual worlds. Because the hero of The Legend of Zelda does not need to go to space, no space-based physics are required. Call of Duty’s players don’t need kayaks, enchantments, or baking ingredients; the game’s developer did not create the relevant code. Nintendo and Activision could focus more data and code on what their virtual worlds need and benefit from, rather than on infinite permutations that have limited practical value to their games.

For all its efficiency, this approach introduces obstacles to building Metaverse-like virtual worlds, and especially in establishing interoperability among them. In Microsoft Flight Simulator, a pilot can land a helicopter beside a football field, but there’s no football game he can then observe, let alone join. For Microsoft to offer such functionality, it would need to build its own football system, even though many developers have already done so and, with years of experience, are likely better at it, too. While MSFS could instead try to integrate these football-specific virtual worlds, each party’s data structures and codes are typically incompatible. In fact, it’s probable that the many developers who have built football-specific games, or have integrated football into their video games, couldn’t make much use of one another’s code, either, and must instead endlessly build and rebuild everything from the layout of a football field to the physics of a ball flying through the air. Not only is this disconnected work counter to the very idea of the Metaverse, but it’s also financially exhausting—especially as virtual worlds have increased in size, detail, and complexity. According to Nexon, one of the world’s largest video game publishers, the average number of staff credits for an open-world action game has grown from roughly 1,000 in 2007 to over 4,000 by 2018, with budgets growing by a factor of ten (roughly two and a half times faster).1

The previous two chapters of this book covered the networking and computing power required to share, operate, and render the Metaverse. The next two will focus on the code that will constitute and unite it.

Game Engines

The core of a virtual world’s code is typically contained in a “game engine,” a loosely defined term that refers to the bundle of technologies and frameworks that help to build a game, render it, process its logic, and manage its memory, among other functions. In a simplified sense, a game engine establishes the virtual laws of a virtual world’s universe—the ruleset that defines all interaction and possibilities.

For the first few decades, most developers created bespoke engines for their virtual worlds. But as summarized in Chapter 3, an alternative model emerged in the 1990s in which developers could license an engine, such as Epic Games’ Unreal Engine (1996) and, later, Unity Technologies’ Unity (2005).

Using these engines has a cost. Unity charges every individual developer that uses it an annual fee that ranges between $400 and $4,000 depending on the features required and the size of the developer’s company. Unreal typically charges 5% of net revenues.

Fees aren’t the only reason to build your own engine. Some developers believe doing so for a given game genre or experience, such as realistic and fast-paced first-person shooters, ensures that their games “feel better” or perform better. Others worry about the need to rely on another company’s pipelines and priorities, or fret that their vendor has such a detailed view into their game and its performance. Given the concerns, it’s common for large publishers to build and maintain their own engines (some, such as Activision and Square Enix, even operate a half dozen or more).

Most developers see significant net positives to licensing and then customizing Unreal or Unity. Licensing allows a small or inexperienced team to build a game with an engine more powerful and extensively tested than they might ever build—and that is less likely to break and can never run over budget.† Developers can also focus more of their time on what will differentiate their virtual world—level design, character design, gameplay, and so on—instead of the basic technology required for it to run. And rather than hiring a developer and then training them to use or build on a proprietary engine, a game maker can instead appeal to the millions of individual developers already familiar with Unity or Unreal and immediately put them to work. For similar reasons, it’s also easier to integrate third-party tools. An independent start-up that makes, as an example, face-tracking software for video game avatars doesn’t design their solution to work with a proprietary engine they’ve never used, but instead to work with those chosen by the largest number of developers.

A good analogy is designing and building a house. Neither the architect nor the decorator designs proprietary lumber dimensions, assembly hardware, measurement systems, blueprint frameworks, or tools. Not only does this make it easier to focus on the creative work, but it makes it easier to hire carpenters, electricians, and plumbers. If the house ever requires a renovation, another team can more easily modify the existing structure because they don’t need to learn new techniques, tools, or systems.

This analogy has a key shortfall. Houses are built once and in one place. Games, conversely, are designed to run on as many possible devices and operating systems as possible—some of which haven’t yet been released or even developed. As a result, games must be compatible with, say, different voltage standards (e.g., the UK’s 240 volts and the United States’ 120 volts), measurement systems (imperial and metric), conventions (aerial telephony wires and buried ones), and so on. Unity and Unreal build and maintain their game engines so that they’re not just compatible with every major platform but tailored to each platform’s strengths and shortfalls so that a developer can easily tap into each without needing to build to the lowest common denominator of computing power.‡

In a sense, one can think of independent game engines as a shared R&D pool for the industry. Yes, Epic and Unity are for-profit companies, but instead of every developer sinking part of their budget into proprietary systems to manage core game logic, a few cross-platform technology providers can concentrate a portion of their budgets into a more capable engine that supports, and benefits, the entire ecosystem. As the major game engines developed, another type of independent gaming solution emerged: live services suites. Companies such as PlayFab (now owned by Microsoft’s Azure) and GameSparks (Amazon) operate much of what a virtual world needs to “run” online and multiplayer experiences. This includes user account systems, player data storage, processing of in-game transactions, version management, player-to-player communications, matchmaking, leaderboards, game analytics, anti-cheat systems, and more, all of which work across platforms. Both Unity and Epic now have their own live services offerings, too, which are available at low to no cost and are not limited to their engines. Steam, the world’s largest PC game store and a key point of discussion in Chapter 10, offers its own live services product, Steamworks.

As the global economy continues to shift to virtual worlds and environments, these cross-platform and cross-developer technologies have become quietly ubiquitous and essential. And the next wave of virtual world builders—not game makers, but retailers, schools, sports teams, construction companies, and cities—are particularly likely to use these solutions, rather than build their own. This places the companies that own them in a favorable strategic position. Most obviously, they become a sort of standard feature, or lingua franca, for the virtual world—think of them as the “English” or “metric” of the Metaverse. Just as it is likely that the average reader of this book uses some English and some knowledge of the metric system when traveling internationally, odds are that if someone is building a virtual world today, they are using—and paying—one or more of these companies. More broadly, who better to establish common data structures and coding conventions across virtual worlds than the companies that govern their logic? Who better to facilitate exchanges of information, virtual goods, and currencies among these virtual worlds than the companies that power the same inside them? And who better to create an interconnected network of these virtual worlds, as ICANN does for web domains and IP addresses? Chapter 8 will return to these questions, but first, it’s helpful to examine a path some think of as the easier, and best, way to build out the Metaverse.

Integrated Virtual World Platforms

As both independent game engines and live services suites developed over the past two decades, other companies combined these approaches into a new one: integrated virtual world platforms (IVWPs), such as Roblox, Minecraft, and Fortnite Creative.

IVWPs are based around their own general-purpose and cross-platform game engines, similar to Unity and Unreal (Epic’s Fortnite Creative, like Fortnite, runs on the company’s Unreal Engine). In this case, though, they are further “productized” so that no actual “coding” is required. Instead, games, experiences, and virtual worlds are built using graphical interfaces, symbols, and objectives. As an analogy, consider the difference between using the text-based MS-DOS and visual iOS, or designing a website in HTML versus creating one in Squarespace. In short, the IVWP interface enables users to create more easily and with fewer people, less investment, and less expertise and skill. As Roblox enthusiasts know, many of the game’s creators are kids, and nearly ten million have created and distributed their virtual worlds on Roblox’s platform.

In addition, every virtual world built on these platforms must use the platform’s entire live services suite—its account and communication systems, avatar database, virtual currency, and more. All of these virtual worlds must be accessed through the IVWP, which therefore serves as a unified experiential layer and a single installer file. In this sense, building a world on Roblox is more like constructing a Facebook page than a Squarespace website. Roblox even operates an integrated marketplace for developers where they can upload anything they custom-made for their virtual world (e.g., a Christmas tree, a snowed-on tree, a barren tree, a pine-bark texture) and license it to other game makers. This provides developers with a second source of income (developer-to-developer rather than just developer-to-player), while also making it easier, cheaper, and faster for others to build their virtual worlds. The process also drives further standardization of virtual objects and data.

Though it’s easier for a developer to build a virtual world using an IVWP than a game engine like Unreal or Unity, it’s harder to build an IVWP than a game engine in the first place. Why? Because for an IVWP, everything is a priority. An IVWP wants to enable creative flexibility while also standardizing underlying technologies, maximizing interconnectivity among everything that’s built, and minimizing the need for training or programming knowledge on the part of creators. Imagine if IKEA wanted to build a country as dynamic as the United States, but force all buildings to use IKEA prefabs. Additionally, IKEA would be in charge of the new country’s currency, utilities, police, customs, and more.

One way to understand the difficulty of operating an IVWP comes via Ebbe Altberg, a former CEO of Second Life. In the mid-2010s, one of the platform’s developers created a business selling virtual horses, alongside a subscription to virtual horse feed. Later, Second Life upgraded its physics engines, but a bug resulted in horses sliding past their feed whenever they tried to eat it. As a result, the horses starved and died. It took time for Second Life to even know this bug existed, and more time still to fix it, then to provide the appropriate redress to those affected by it. All the same, these sorts of events disrupt Second Life’s economy, while also producing distrust in the market, which harms both buyers and sellers. Finding a way to constantly improve functionality, while continuing to support old programming and doing so without errors, is an extraordinary task. Game engines also face a version of this problem. Consider that when Epic updates Unreal, it is up to every developer to deploy this update, and they can do so at the time of their choosing, after extensive testing, and without worrying about how that update affects their interactions with other developers. When Roblox pushes an update, it automatically reaches all of its worlds.

At the same time, the fact that a “virtual IKEA” is built on programming, not particle board, means that its potential is bound not by literal physics but by the nearly boundless potential of software. Anything made in Roblox by the Roblox Corporation or its developers can be endlessly repurposed or copied at no marginal costs. It can even be improved upon. Every developer in an IVWP is effectively collaborating to populate an ever-expanding and increasingly capable network of virtual worlds and objects. As this network improves, it becomes easier to attract more users and more per-user spending, which leads to more network revenue, enabling more developers and investment, clearing a path for further improvements to the network, and so on. This is the benefit of pooling not just engine R&D but, well, R&D for everything.

But what does this look like in practice? The Roblox Corporation offers the clearest example, as Fortnite Creative is managed by Epic Games, which remains private, and Minecraft’s financials are not disclosed by its owner, Microsoft.

Start with engagement. By the middle of 2023, Roblox was averaging 5.4 billion hours of usage per month, up nearly a billion year over year and four times the average of early 2019.2 These remarkable figures do not include time spent watching Roblox content on YouTube, which is the world’s most used video site and reports that gaming content is its most watched content category, and Roblox its second-most-popular game (Minecraft, another IVWP, ranks first).3 The top three Roblox games, Brookhaven RP, Adopt Me!, and Blox Fruits, come from independent developers with little to no prior experience and staffs that consist of fewer than 10 to 30 people and started with only one or two. To date, these titles have been played 30 to 45 billion times each.4 In a single day, they’ll reach half as many players as Fortnite or Call of Duty—and half as many as titles like The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild or The Last of Us do in their lifetimes. And as for populating the platform with a wide range of virtual objects? In 2022, Roblox’s users created over 15,000 worlds each day,5 up from 14,000 a year earlier,6 and designed 170,000 virtual clothing/accessory items,7 up from 70,000.8

Part of Roblox’s surging engagement is driven by its growing userbase. From Q4 2018 to Q4 2023, average monthly players increased from an estimated 75 million9 to nearly 355 million (or +375%),10 while average daily players grew from around 13.7 to 71.5 million (or +425%).11 Note that average daily players grew more than the monthly userbase over this period, and engagement grew by an even larger degree.

Additional evidence of Roblox’s network effects can be seen in its financials. Roblox’s revenues are up over 650% from Q4 2018 to Q4 2023, while its payments to on-platform world builders (i.e., developers) have grown 950%.12 In other words, the average Roblox user is spending more per hour than ever before and generating revenues faster than ever before, and with growth in these two metrics exceeding the already impressive growth in users, which is then exceeded by the growth in compensation to developers. Furthermore, Roblox’s growth has been disproportionately concentrated among older audiences. At the end of 2018, 57% of daily users were under 13. Five years later, only 41% were. Put another way, Roblox now boasts close to five and half times as many players over 13 as the service had under 13 in 2018.13

The most impressive aspect of Roblox Corporation’s flywheel may be its investments in R&D. In the first quarter of 2020, the last before the COVID-19 pandemic, the company generated $162 million in revenue and invested $49.4 million in R&D.14 That means 30 cents of every dollar spent on Roblox went back into platform improvements. By Q4 2023, quarterly revenues had grown to $750 million (+365%), with the company investing $341 million in R&D (+590%)—equivalent to 45% of revenues and more than twice the company’s quarterly pre-pandemic revenue.15 In 2023, total R&D exceeded $1.25 billion.16

As points of contrast, consider Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto V (GTA:V) and Red Dead Redemption 2 (RDR2). GTA:V is the second-best-selling game in history, with over 200 million copies sold (Minecraft ranks first with nearly 300 million). RDR2 was the best-selling title made for the eighth generation of consoles (i.e., PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch), with 65 million copies sold. The two games are also believed to be among the most expensive game productions ever, with final budgets estimated at $250–$300 million and $400–$500 million, respectively, which includes more than half a decade of development each, plus extensive marketing and publishing costs. Or compare Roblox’s R&D budget to that of Sony’s PlayStation group, which was estimated at $2.17 billion in 2023 and spanned close to a dozen gaming studios, its cloud gaming division, live services group, and hardware division (including VR).17 In 2019, the last year for which data is publicly available, Epic Games’ Unreal Engine generated less than $100 million in revenue (it’s likely this figure is considerably higher in 2024).18 Unity’s engine brought in much more but still came short of Roblox’s R&D spend.19

Roblox’s R&D investments are diverse, spanning improvements in developer tools and software, server architecture to synchronize high-concurrency simulations, machine learning to detect harassment, artificial intelligence, rendering for virtual reality, motion capture, and more. That Roblox can invest so much into its platform is astonishing. In theory, every additional dollar enables developers to produce more compelling virtual worlds, which attracts more users, leading to more revenue—which enables more R&D not just by Roblox but also by the independent developers who make these worlds, investment that again drives more user engagement and spending on Roblox, leading to more R&D by the company.

Many Virtual Platforms and Engines, Not Many Metaverses

Chapter 4 provided a “full-spec” description of the Metaverse: “A massively scaled and interoperable network of real-time-rendered immersive virtual worlds that can be experienced synchronously and persistently by an effectively unlimited number of users with an individual sense of presence, and with continuity of data, such as identity, history, entitlements, objects, communications, and payments.” Some might read this description and consider Roblox to be an imperfect, but still fairly close, match. It cannot be experienced synchronously and persistently by an effectively unlimited number of users; no real-time-rendered virtual world can, at least for now. And when that does become possible, it will surely be true for Roblox. And yet Roblox is unlikely to meet my definition in one key way: most virtual works will exist outside of it.

But could Roblox eventually become the Metaverse? What if Epic’s IVWP Fortnite Creative, game engine Unreal, and live services suite Epic Online Services, along with its other special projects, were all combined—would the result be the Metaverse? If one squints, it’s possible to imagine these companies, or one like it, subsuming all virtual experiences, thereby becoming a Metaverse-sized Metagalaxy. And it is notable that some form of this process is how the Metaverses of Snow Crash and Ready Player One come into existence.

The current state of technological progress suggests another outcome. Why? Because as fast as these virtual giants are growing, the number of virtual experiences, innovators, technologies, opportunities, and developers are all growing faster.

While Roblox and Minecraft are among the most popular games in the world, their reach is modest when considered in the broadest terms. These two supposed titans have but a small fraction of the global internet population of 4.5–5 billion. In effect, they are still at the ICQ stage of virtual worlds; billions of users and millions of developers have yet to even try them. It’s easy to assume that Roblox or Minecraft will be the sole or at least primary beneficiaries of this growth. History provides reason for optimism.

When Microsoft acquired Minecraft in 2014, the title had over 25 million monthly active players. By mid-2020, this playerbase had more than quintupled—even though Minecraft’s primary competitor, Roblox, had seen its usership grow from fewer than 5 million to more than 200 million over that same time, and many other IVWPs had launched to success, too. In 2018, Fortnite launched FNC, and throughout the decade, Rockstar had progressively transformed its 2013 title Grand Theft Auto V into the makeshift IVWP in Grand Theft Auto Online.

As long as there are billions, or even tens of millions, of players left to adopt IVWPs, more will come to market and traditional games will launch their own creative modes, just as Fortnite did in 2018, with Free Fire following suit in 2021. It’s likely that GTA 6, which is expected to release in 2024 or 2025, will incorporate many of the lessons learned from the success of Roblox, Minecraft, and FNC. Rockstar’s August 2023 acquisition of a leading GTA and RDR2 “modding platform,” Cfx.re, which converted Rockstar’s combat-based games into “role-playing” simulations enabling complex role-playing, is a case in point.20 It was not long ago that Rockstar had been calling the role-play companies—including Cfx.re—“[violators] of our terms of service,” whose products were “designed to facilitate piracy.” According to some reports, Rockstar even sent private investigators to physically shut down servers operated by these supposed malfeasants.21 But as markets change and customer behavior evolves, even the most successful of platforms need to evolve, too.

Many new IVWPs are being developed around different technical premises, too. At the end of 2022, even the largest of the blockchain-based IVWPs, including Decentraland, The Sandbox, Cryptovoxels, Somnium Space, and Upland, had less than 0.05% of Roblox’s and Minecraft’s daily active users. But by allowing users greater ownership over their in-world items and even giving them a say in how the platform is governed and a right to share in its profitability, these blockchain IVWPs will be able to grow far more quickly than traditional IVWPs (more on this theory in Chapter 11). In early 2024, Krafton, which makes the blockbuster title PUBG, and Naver, another South Korean digital media giant, are expected to launch an NFT-based IVWP titled Overdare, which will run on its own blockchain, Settlus.22

Facebook’s Horizon Worlds is not limited to immersive VR and AR, but it is focused in those areas, which contrasts with Roblox, which is available in immersive VR but prioritizes traditional screen interfaces, such as an iPad or PC screen. Upstarts such as Rec Room and VRChat are also centered on immersive VR world creation, are rapidly accumulating users and boast orders of magnitude more users than Horizon Worlds—even on Facebook’s own Quest line of devices. Niantic, the maker of Pokémon Go, is working on its own augmented reality and location-based virtual world platforms.

These would-be alternatives to Roblox, Minecraft, and Fortnite might falter, but it’s more likely that they will grow alongside and potentially displace current market leaders. Take Facebook as an example. The social networking giant entered 2010 with more than half a billion monthly active users, but has failed to subsume any of the hit social media platforms which emerged in the decade. Snapchat launched in 2011, with Facebook launching its own Snapchat-like app (or “clone”) in 2013, called Poke, which was shuttered a year later. In 2016, Facebook launched Lifestage, its second Snapchat clone, which was also closed after 12 months. That same year, Facebook’s Instagram app also copied Snapchat’s signature “Stories” format, with Facebook’s main app adding the feature the following year. Then in 2019, Instagram launched its own dedicated Snapchat-like app, Threads from Instagram, though almost no one noticed. Facebook Gaming, the company’s Twitch competitor, launched in 2018, as did Facebook’s TikTok competitor, Lasso. Facebook Dating released in 2019, with Instagram adding a TikTok-like feature named “Reels” in 2020. Facebook’s efforts have undoubtedly curbed these services’ growth, yet each service is larger than ever and still expanding. By the end of 2021, TikTok had more than a billion users and was reportedly the most visited web domain of the year, with Google and Facebook rounding out the top three.

Though the top integrated virtual world platforms are mighty and fast-growing, they also represent a far smaller portion of the gaming industry than Facebook does in the social web. In 2021, the combined revenues of Roblox, Minecraft, and FNC represented less than 2.5% of gaming revenues, and reached fewer than 500 million of an estimated 2.5–3 billion players. Moreover, they’re dwarfed by the major cross-platform engines. Roughly half of all games today run on Unity, while Unreal Engine’s share of high-fidelity 3D immersive worlds is estimated at between 15% and 25%. Roblox’s R&D expenditures may exceed those of both Unreal and Unity, but this ignores the billions in investment made by licensors of these engines. The two most popular games in the world, excluding low-fidelity casual titles such as Candy Crush, are PUBG Mobile and Free Fire, both built on Unity. Most important may be the reach of Unreal’s and Unity’s developers. While millions of users have made a Minecraft mod or a Roblox game, the number of active semiprofessional and professional developers using these IVWPs is more likely to be around 100,000.23 Epic and Unity count millions of active and skilled developers. And scores of proprietary engines, such as Activision’s IW (Call of Duty) and Sony’s Decima (Horizon Zero Dawn and Death Stranding), continue to receive investment and the games that use them are more popular than ever.

The growing value of virtual worlds and the Metaverse increases the incentives for a developer to insource their technology stack, as this approach provides a greater opportunity for technical differentiation and greater control over their technology overall, reduces their reliance on third parties who might become competitors,§ and increases profit margins. Of course, many of these developers will still use Unreal or Unity as a game engine, or GameSparks or PlayFab for live services. These providers enable a developer to “pick and choose” what they like, and also to customize much of what they license. Unlike IVWPs, they also allow a developer to manage its own account systems and operate its own in-game economies. These services are also much cheaper. Roblox pays a developer less than 25% of the revenue a player spends on their game.¶ As mentioned, Epic’s Unreal Engine, conversely, takes only a 5% royalty on revenues. The total cost of Unity’s engine is likely to be less than 1% of a successful game’s revenue. Roblox does take on additional expenses for its developers, such as costly server fees, customer service, and billing, but in most cases a developer will still have higher profit potential by building a stand-alone virtual world, rather than one inside an IVWP. As such, one should assume that no matter how much more successful Roblox or Minecraft become, they will power only a minority share of all games. While games and game engines are central to the Metaverse, they don’t come close to encompassing it. Most other categories have their own rendering and simulation software. A typical example is Pixar, which builds its animated worlds and characters using its proprietary RenderMan solutions. Most Hollywood studios and production companies, meanwhile, use Autodesk’s Maya software. Autodesk’s AutoCAD, along with Dassault Systèmes’ CATIA and SolidWorks, are the primary solutions used to build and design virtual objects that will then be made into real-world ones. Examples include cars, buildings, and fighter jets.

In recent years, Unity and Unreal have made inroads into nongaming categories, including engineering, filmmaking, and computer-aided design. In 2019, as discussed earlier, the Hong Kong International Airport used Unity to build a “digital twin” that could be connected to myriad sensors and cameras throughout the airport to track and evaluate passenger flows, maintenance, and more—all in real time. The use of “game engines” to power such simulations does make it easier to produce a Metaverse that spans both the physical and virtual planes of existence. To be sure, the success of the Hong Kong airport endeavor and other simulations like it means more competition, as Autodesk, Dassault, and others respond by building their own real-time simulation functionality. And just as Unreal and Unity don’t provide all the technology required to build or operate a game, they’re not sufficient in other domains either. Many new software companies are emerging that take the “stock” editions of these engines and “productize” them for civil and industrial architects, engineers, and facility managers, while also adding their own custom code and functionality. One example is Disney’s Industrial Light & Magic (ILM) special effects division. Since using Unity to film Disney’s The Lion King (2019) and Unreal for the first season of the TV show The Mandalorian (2019), ILM has developed its own real-time rendering engine, Helios. The fact that even the most avid Star Wars fans failed to notice any impact from the switch from Unreal to Helios for The Mandalorian’s second season further suggests how many different rendering solutions and platforms will be built in the years to come.

As measured by the number of assets created, the fastest-growing category of virtual software may be those that scan the real world. Matterport is a multibillion-dollar platform company whose software converts scans from devices such as iPhones to produce rich 3D models of building interiors. Today, the company’s software is primarily used by property owners to create vivid and navigable replicas of their real estate on sites such as Zillow, Redfin, and Compass, affording would-be renters or homebuyers, construction professionals, and the like a better way to understand the space than is allowed by blueprints, photographs, or even live tours. Soon such scans will be used to determine the best placement of a wireless router or household plant, to test out a selection of different lamps (each one purchasable through Matterport), or to operate an entire smart home, including electricity, security, HVAC, and more. Another example is Planet Labs, which scans nearly the entire earth via satellite each day and across eight spectral bands, capturing not just high-resolution imagery but details including heat, biomass, and haze. The company’s goal is to make the entire planet, in all its nuances, legible to software and to update its data on a daily to hourly basis.

Given the number of virtual worlds that will compose the Metaverse, and given their diversity and the technical difficulty of constructing them, it’s likely that there will be dozens of major virtual world platforms, with many more underlying technology providers. This is good; there is danger to having a single virtual world platform or engine operating the entire Metaverse.

Recall Tim Sweeney’s warning about the scope of the Metaverse: “This Metaverse is going to be far more pervasive and powerful than anything else. If one central company gains control of this, they will become more powerful than any government and be a god on Earth.”

Though Sweeney’s remark is exaggerated, there is already widespread worry about the ways a handful of big-tech companies shape modern existence—from what their users buy to what they do, how they feel, and even what they believe to be true. As the Metaverse emerges, a growing share of human time, labor, leisure, friendships, memories, and spend will exist or occur in virtual space, rather than just be transmitted through it as with Zoom or Instagram today. Moreover, the Metaverse will help guide, inform, capture, and power the physical world, rather than just bring it online. It is hard to imagine any outcome in which this does not increase big tech’s control, and it is easy to fear one in which a single tech company not only defines the virtual laws of physics but also serves as landlord, treasurer, judge, and customs officer.

But if the Metaverse is to have many underpinning platforms and rival technologies, then there needs to be a way to interoperate among them.

In addition, the version of Fortnite which is so popular today—its “battle royale”—was not the original version of the game. When the title launched in July 2017, it was a cooperative survival game in which players worked to defeat zombie hordes. It wasn’t until September 2017 that Epic added its battle royale mode, which closely resembled that used by the hit game PUBG, which, notably, licensed the Unreal Engine. The publisher behind PUBG subsequently sued Epic for copyright infringement. The suit was later settled on confidential terms, so it’s unclear if any money changed hands. (See https://smcarthurlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/Dkt-100-order-granting-settlement.pdf.) In 2020, Epic launched its own publishing arm to release games made by independent studios, thereby placing the company in even greater competition with some of the publishers that occasionally licensed Unreal.

  5. ¶ There is some flexibility here—and most analysts expect this payout ratio to go up over time. More on this topic in Chapter 10.

Chapter 8 THE TECHNOLOGIES, PHILOSOPHIES, AND ECONOMICS OF INTEROPERABILITY

It is common to hear the phrase “interoperable assets” when discussing the Metaverse, but no such thing exists, because virtual assets don’t exist. Only data does. And it’s here—at the very start—where the problems of interoperability begin.

Consider the “interoperability” of physical goods, such as a pair of shoes. The manager of an Adidas store in “the real world” could decide to prohibit a customer from wearing Nikes in their store. This would be a business decision, and obviously a poor one—and also one that would be almost impossible to enforce. A customer wearing Nikes can get inside an Adidas store by opening its door. This is because physics is universal, so atoms are “Write once, run everywhere.” That Nike shoes physically exist means that they are automatically compatible inside any Adidas store. The Adidas store manager would need to write a policy covering the wearing of non-Adidas shoes in the store, create a system to implement that policy, and then enforce that system.

Virtual atoms do not work like that. For virtual goods from a virtual Nike store to be understood in a virtual Adidas outlet, the latter would need to admit information on these shoes from Nike, operate a system that understood this information, and then run code to operate the shoes in the manner specified. Suddenly, the admission of sneakers has changed from passive to active.

Today, there are hundreds of different file formats used to structure and store data. There are dozens of popular real-time rendering engines, most of which have been fragmented further through various code customizations. As a result, almost all virtual worlds and software systems are incapable of understanding what each considers a “shoe” (data), let alone being able to use that understanding (code).

That such enormous variation could exist might surprise those familiar with common file formats such as JPEG or MP3, or who know that most websites use HTML. But the standardization of online languages and media stems from how late “for-profit” businesses came to the internet. Apple didn’t unveil iTunes until 2001, nearly 20 years after the Internet Protocol Suite was established. It was impractical for Apple to reject the standards already in wide use, such as WAV and MP3. Gaming is a different story. When the gaming industry began to emerge in the 1950s, no standards for virtual objects, rendering, or engines existed. In many cases, the companies producing these games were pioneering computer-based content. Apple’s Audio Interchange File Format (AIFF) is still the most common audio file format used to store sound on Apple computers; it was created in 1988 and was based on the general-purpose Interchange File Format standard devised by game maker Electronic Arts in 1985. Furthermore, video games were never intended to be part of a “network” like the internet. Instead, they existed to run on a fixed and offline piece of hardware.

Timing is not the only reason online virtual worlds have considerable technical diversity compared to the rest of the internet.
