Another critical factor is the intense computational, networking, and financial demands of modern simulations, which in turn encourages developers to code to their immediate needs and build whatever proprietary tech might better support their ambitions. In this sense, fragmentation is often essential, as the needs of AR and VR experiences, 2D and 3D games, realistic and cartoon-styled worlds, high-concurrent-user and low-concurrent-user simulations, high-budget and low-budget titles, and 3D printers can be quite different. As such, full standardization would likely mean underserving one application, falling massively short on another, and so on—and in totally unpredictable ways.

The challenge of interoperation goes beyond file formats and approaches questions that are more ontological. It’s relatively easy to agree on what an image is—it’s only two-dimensional and it doesn’t move (with video files being simply successions of images). But in 3D, especially with interactive objects, agreement is far harder. Is a shoe an object, or is it a collection of objects? If the latter, how many? Are the caps on a shoelace part of the shoelace or separate from it? Does a shoe have a dozen individual eyelets, each of which can be customized or even removed, or are they a single interconnected set? If shoes seem hard, just imagine avatars—would-be representations of real people. Forget trees—what is a person? Beyond visuals, there are other attributes that must be examined, such as motion or “rigging.” The bodies of the Incredible Hulk and a jellyfish should not move in the same way, but this means that the creator of these avatars needs to enshrine them with code detailing their movement, code that another platform can understand. To permit third-party objects, platforms will also need data that describes a good’s appropriateness (e.g., nudity, penchant for violence, language). A game for toddlers needs to differentiate between a PG-rated swimsuit and an R-rated one. Similarly, a gritty war simulator will want to know the difference between a sniper wearing a shrub-like ghillie suit and a “sniper” that’s actually an anthropomorphic bush. All of this requires data conventions—and probably additional systems. A 2D game will want to be able to import a 3D avatar but then restyle it according to its own logic. And vice versa. To support this functionality, a suite of interoperable standards, conventions, and systems are required. But these are still not enough.

To have a virtual goods economy, there must be mechanisms that record who owns various goods, support the sale of these records between users and their use across independent platforms, and can be modified or edited by both users and platforms. The difficulties involved are immense, which again reflects the difference between goods in the virtual and physical worlds (or between code and atoms).

In the “real world,” money can be exchanged physically with no intermediary; neither party is obligated to update their private ledgers for the transaction to be successfully completed. Digital payments involve and require a record but do not require the literal transfer of a specific dollar. Venmo does not operate individual bank accounts for each of its users but instead manages a series of corporate accounts that hold all user funds with an associated database recording how much of that pool is owed to each user. And when one Venmo user sends $100 to another, Venmo simply updates its record to reduce that user’s entitlement by $100, while the other is increased by $100. Interbank transfers are more complicated, but they too are bundled with and then netted against other inbound and outbound payments. Sending $1,000 from one bank to another may not, in fact, involve that sum leaving one bank and going to another, and certainly not the specific dollars in the account. This is possible because dollars are fungible; no one dollar is worth more than another and is instead fully substitutable with another.

When physical goods are sold, again, no intermediary is required, and the process involves one person’s literal dispossession of the good and another person’s literal acquisition of it. And while records are sometimes used—such as a house title or deed—they help affirm ownership but do not actually ensure it, nor are they required to use the asset.

Digital assets and ownership rights—that is, data—are trickier. While the internet enables a digital good to be transferred worldwide in a matter of seconds, there are no protocols that manage the ownership rights to that good. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that transmission results in the creation of duplicates—every device, server, and even network that is touched by the transfer gets a copy, and there is no record of provenance that autonomous owners or platforms might use to validate the “true owner” and ensure the value of the “true copy.” There are, of course, many permission-based services, but they manage access to a stored file; they do not enable the authoritative copy to be taken to a third-party service.

The only exception to the above is the internet’s domain system, which is managed by ICANN. It established the 1,500 or so top-level domains such as.com and.org; some 2,500 domain registrars, which have overseen the registration, purchase, and sale of close to 400 million second-level domains such as google.com or facebook.com; and a series of “dispute resolution providers” to manage ownership conflicts and rights. However, email domains are fairly basic (alphanumeric alternatives to IP addresses rather than executable code), are modest in transfer volume (roughly one every two seconds, mostly of low-value addresses), require the use of an intermediary to be completed, and cannot be altered by the owner.

Given these limitations, the rights to virtual goods are exclusively managed within a platform. Roblox effectively uses the Venmo model, managing which users own a Roblox asset; those assets are managed on Roblox’s servers and bought and sold using Roblox’s own currency, which is also stored on their servers. Not only does the Metaverse require the ability to send the sole copy of a good off of Roblox to a platform such as Minecraft, it must also be possible for the latter to then trade or customize it, with Roblox then able to reflect these changes.

To get a clearer sense of the challenge, imagine a user purchasing a good on Platform A and then attempting to use it on Platform B. Does Platform A provide Platform B access to an ownership record and asset maintained on Platform A’s servers, or transmit both to Platform B and then delete its own records? The latter method seems needlessly complex, as the user might then take the good to Platform C or sell it to a user on Platform D. But if Platform A maintains control, how is it compensated for this service? Who is going to pay for the related costs of storage, various transactions, and various legal risks? Keep in mind, the volume of requests to Platform A can be quite high, as they would come not just from Platform B but also hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of other platforms and independent worlds. Moreover, Platform A would also need to allow third-party platforms to modify this record and facilitate the sale of its underlying product to another user. And what if the user who was using an item from Platform A on Platform B wanted to sell it to a Platform B user who didn’t have an account on Platform A—then what happens?

The typical response is that some form of digital storage-locker service offered by virtual world producers and independent companies will emerge. These lockers might charge monthly fees, usage fees, or transaction-based fees or monetize through ads and data collection and arrange to permanently house and provide access to a user’s virtual goods. The issue with a “Metaverse storage locker” is that it’s a bit of a brand-based handwave. While it presumes more bespoke technology to support its supposed functionality, it doesn’t address the problems involved, nor ensure adoption. In addition, these wallets still need to be able to transfer items to other wallets (otherwise a user’s ever-growing investments would forever be stuck in and controlled by said operator) and receive them from various platforms.

Finally, there are the financial requirements of interoperability. Any platform that enables the exchange of valuable goods must comply with state-to-state “Know Your Customer” (commonly known as KYC) regulations, which help governments mitigate money laundering and ensure income is reported to tax authorities. Many virtual worlds also generate at least part of their revenue from the sale of virtual goods. Often, they operate complex in-game economies that use these goods, too. As a result, these virtual worlds’ makers and operators tend to tightly manage in-game economies by fixing prices and exchange rates, limiting what can be created, sold, or traded; and almost never allow users to “cash out” into real-world currency. For the developers of these worlds to put their businesses at risk, let alone allow third parties to modify their creations, they will need forms of compensation that ensure, not just pitch, considerable income from doing so.

Interoperability Is a Spectrum

Given the many enormous challenges to interoperability, some doubt that the Metaverse will ever come into existence. Instead, its ideas will be limited to independent virtual worlds and virtual world platforms, such as Roblox, Fortnite, Nvidia’s Earth 2.0, and Google’s geospatial platform. There are both economical and historical reasons for optimism. But first, a little nuance is required.

Interoperability in the Metaverse is not binary. It is not about whether virtual worlds will or won’t share or whether standards exist. It’s about how many worlds share, how much is shared, when, where, and at what cost, with what standards and how many. This dynamic is not unique to the Metaverse.

Think about a piece of apparel in the real world. All belts are presumed to work with all pants. Exceptions exist, of course, but overall, most belts are compatible with most pants, irrespective of the year they were bought, the brand, or the country they’re from. At the same time, not all belts fit all pants equally well. And while there are common standards for pants and belts, a 30 × 30 pant from J.Crew, as an example, may fit differently from a 30 × 30 pant from Old Navy or any other apparel retailer—and dress sizes are known to vary even more widely. These standards vary globally too, hence those shoe labels that list several size categories—typically those of the United States, the UK, and Europe. Indeed, many differing technical standards exist, such as those for residential voltage, and for measurements of speed, distance, or weight. It’s also common for these rival standards to be intermingled. The UK uses miles for distances and pints for milk and beer but the metric system for most other measurements, while Canada uses proportionally more metric but continues to use feet and inches. The result of this measurement mixture is frustration or, more seriously, occasional errors and even losses.

In some instances, new equipment is required for a foreign device to be used in a local environment (as in the case of an electrical outlet adapter). In other instances, a government will require updates or replacements to a given part to ensure that it is locally compliant (e.g., updating a car’s exhaust system to meet tighter emissions regulations).

Even where compatibility is technically simple, friction and prohibitions remain. Pants work everywhere, but not every location will admit someone wearing jeans. Movie theaters allow almost any clothes and accept most forms of credit, but not outside food or drink. One can carry a shotgun in much, but not all, of the American outdoors, but rarely in cities and almost never in a school. Cars work on all roads in the United States, but to drive on a golf course a person needs to rent a golf cart (even if they privately own one, too). Not every business accepts every currency, but currencies can be exchanged for a fee. Many stores support some, but not all, credit cards and a few accept none. Most of the world now embraces trade, but not all of it, nor for all things, in all quantities, or for free. Identity is even more complicated. There are passports, credit scores, school records, legal records, employer IDs, state IDs, and more. Which of them are used for what, which of them are available to outside parties or can be affected by outside parties—it all varies, sometimes based on where a person is at a given time.

Though premised upon interoperability, the internet isn’t exhaustively interoperable, either. There are still public and private networks (and even offline ones) and sundry networks, platforms, and software that admit the majority of common file formats—but not all. While the most popular protocols are free and open, many are paid and private.

No interoperable system or standard is perfect in its design or complete in its adoption. Yet the arc of all global technologies is to interoperation and standardization, both of which typically strengthen or expand network effects and reduce costs. The aforementioned “protocol wars” are a great case study. From the 1970s to the 1990s, few believed that the many competing networking stacks would be replaced by a single suite, least of all one steered by nonprofit and informal working bodies. Instead, those who wanted to trade emails, files, or other data would need to contend with a “cyberspace divided.” Eventually, the utility and economics of a unified global networking suite proved too great.

Another example comes via credit scores. Banks and other financial institutions did not always share customer credit data—it was seen as far too valuable. In time, it became clear that pooling their data would be to their collective benefit, as every bank would have a fuller picture of a customer’s creditworthiness, including their history of payments and defaults and their outstanding liabilities. Competing homestay marketplaces Airbnb and Vrbo are now partnering with a third-party data provider to prevent guests with a history of poor behavior (loud noise, property damage, other rule violations) from making future bookings. Although this harms the individual offenders, all other guests see lower prices and better inventory as a result, while hosts limit their risk of rental incidents. Meanwhile, the two platforms face reduced legal liability and can offer more reliable income streams to their partners.

The top case study is language, one of humanity’s first and core technologies. By the early 2010s globalization had led many of the world’s largest corporations to mandate English as their official corporate language—including Rakuten, Japan’s largest e-commerce company; Airbus, an aerospace giant that counts the governments of France and Germany as its two largest shareholders; Nokia, the fourth-largest company in Finland; and Samsung, South Korea’s largest company. A 2012 poll by Ipsos found that 67% of individuals whose professional dealings involved communications with people based in other countries preferred to conduct their work in English. The next closest language was Spanish, at 5%. Crucially, 61% of respondents said they did not use their native language when working with foreign partners.1 As such, English’s reported dominance does not stem from its noncommercial popularity. In fact, the language dominates despite the fact that fewer than one in ten people globally have English as a first language. Globalization has also driven standardization of currencies (the US dollar and the Euro, the latter itself a unification of nearly two dozen regional currencies), units (the metric system), and the import/export of goods (the intermodal shipping container).

The March to Interoperability

When it comes to virtual worlds and 3D assets, there are many theorized drivers of interoperation and standardization. There is also observable progress.

For more than a decade after online console gaming emerged in the mid-2000s, the leading video game console, Sony PlayStation, refused to support so-called cross-play. Sony’s policy meant that even if one friend had the PlayStation version and another owned the Xbox version of the same title, they would never be able to play together, no matter how technically similar or compatible each title’s code was or the efforts by the developer to connect the two. Even if a single player bought two copies of the same game (say, one for their PlayStation and another for their laptop), their in-game currencies, in-game purchases, and in-game achievements would remain siloed in one or the other. In industry terms, Sony prohibited not just “cross-play” but “cross-purchasing,” “cross-progression,” and “cross-communications” with outside platforms, which also meant there were no cross-platform identities, either.

Critics of the policy argued that Sony’s stance was clearly a consequence of its dominant market position. If users didn’t need a PlayStation to play with other PlayStation users—which typically outnumbered those on rival consoles such as those of Nintendo and Microsoft—they’d be less likely to buy a PlayStation in the first place, and might abandon it even after they did. Sony’s president of interactive entertainment tacitly admitted as much in 2016 when he said “the technical aspect could be the easiest” part of opening up access to its PlayStation Network for cross-play.2 And lo and behold, Sony launched full cross-play two and a half years later.

Sony did not change its mind because of internal preferences, financial straits, declining PlayStation sales, or customer feedback. Instead, it was effectively forced to do so by the success of Fortnite, which came from a company, Epic Games, that, not coincidentally, was built around an engine that could run on as many platforms as possible.

Fortnite had a number of rare attributes when it launched. It was the first mainstream AAA game that could be played on nearly every major gaming device globally, including two generations of PlayStation and Xbox as well as the Nintendo Switch, Mac, and PC; the following year, Epic expanded to iPhone and Android. The title was also free, so players didn’t have to buy multiple copies to be able to play on multiple platforms. Fortnite was also designed as a social game; it became better as more of a player’s friends used it. And it was built around live services rather than a fixed narrative or any offline play: the game’s content never ended and was constantly updated. This, plus superb creative execution, helped Fortnite become the most popular AAA game globally (excluding China) by the end of 2018. It was also generating more revenue per month than any game in history.

From the start, Sony’s console competitors opted to support cross-platform capabilities for Fortnite. Nintendo had negligible online networking business and therefore little concern about defending it, and there was little evidence that its handheld Switch platform was in direct competition with the PlayStation line anyway. In contrast to Nintendo, Xbox was in direct competition with PlayStation and had a thriving online multiplayer and services business—widely believed to be far superior to that of PlayStation. Despite this service leadership, Microsoft had long been an advocate of cross-platform gaming—after all, a majority of its customers were on its open Microsoft Windows platform, not the closed Microsoft Xbox. Microsoft also wanted to open up gaming for the very reason Sony had resisted doing so—to weaken PlayStation’s player lock-in and to give Xbox users the ability to play with all of their friends (a plurality or even majority of whom were on PlayStation). PC and mobile devices, meanwhile, had never blocked cross-platform functionality as neither were dedicated gaming services, to say the least. Moreover, these devices, unlike consoles, were not sold at a loss that necessitated video game purchases for recoupment.

As the entire market embraced cross-platform gaming with the exception of Sony, its PlayStation offered the “worst” version of the game—yes, the PlayStation version had better graphics than that of Nintendo Switch, Apple iPhone, or Android, but it could be used to play with only a subset of a player’s friends. What’s more, PlayStation owners could play the cross-platform version of Fortnite from nearly any other device in their home—and as the title was free-to-play, they didn’t even need to pay another dollar to do so. This dynamic placed Sony in a tough spot. The company’s historical decision to block cross-play might have cost it the incidental sale—a PlayStation user whose friends all had Xbox might have skipped buying a $60 copy of the PlayStation edition of Call of Duty as a result—but it was better than enabling its competitors. Now, though, PlayStation was missing out on most of the revenue from the highest-grossing title in history and driving many players to competing platforms. Sure, PlayStation offered a better technical experience than the iPhone, but most players valued the game’s social elements more than its average specs. And on at least three occasions, Epic had “accidentally” activated cross-play on PlayStation—proving Sony’s lack of support was just a company preference, not a technological impediment, and prompting many PlayStation owners to demand Sony “open up.”

All of these factors led Sony to change its policies—and to the long-term benefit of the entire video gaming ecosystem. Today, most hit games can be accessed by nearly all computing devices globally—and so can be played by anyone, anywhere, anytime—without users needing to repay or to fragment their identity, achievements, or player networks. Furthermore, cross-platform play, progression, and purchasing means that every console competes primarily on hardware, content, and services, not rent-seeking. Even so, PlayStation is thriving, with the console generating over 45% of total Fortnite revenues and continuing to outsell Xbox by a ratio of more than three to one.3

Crucially, Sony’s decision to open up its closed platform also provides a view into potential economic solutions to the challenge of interoperability. In order to avoid “revenue leakage,” Sony required Epic to “true up” its payments to the PlayStation store. If a Fortnite player spent 100 hours playing on PlayStation and 100 hours on Nintendo Switch (i.e., 50/50) but spent only $40 on PlayStation compared to $60 on Nintendo Switch (40/60), Epic would have to pay Nintendo a 25% commission on its $60 share (as per usual), and PlayStation a 25% commission on its $40 share (again, as per usual), and then pay PlayStation 25% on $10 that didn’t happen on its platform, but its share of time suggested the platform was owed. In other words, Epic pays twice on $10. It’s not clear whether this policy is still applied in 2024—the public knows it ever existed only because of leaked legal filings. Regardless, the model is an example of how the proliferation of cross-platform gaming aids all market participants.

Even after Fortnite opened up various cross-platform services across the major gaming ecosystems, some limitations remained. One console’s player network (say, Xbox Live) could not friend a player on another (PlayStation Network), except when adding them inside a specific game such as Fortnite. For similar reasons, players on each system could talk to or message one another only when inside a game. While this approach worked well enough when two players knew which single game they wanted to play before logging on, it didn’t work well for unstructured hanging out or enjoying ad hoc play, and it meant that players had to use alternative communications suites (chat, email) to communicate when they were not inside their gaming app of choice. The more central gaming was to someone’s lifestyle, the less this patchwork solution suited them.

Discord, an instant messaging and voice over IP platform founded in 2015, began to fill the gap that the major gaming ecosystems refused to fill. Unlike the social systems of PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo, and Steam, Discord was available on all major computing platforms—PC, Mac, iPhone, and Android—thereby enabling every single gamer to talk to every other gamer, irrespective of the game they were playing or their gaming device of preference, while also building an overarching social graph that superseded every game and device, and that even included occasional and lapsed gamers, too. Though Discord’s functionality was imperfect, users flocked to the service, which has since grown to have a larger and more active userbase than any other gaming platform. And crucially, there is no way for the platforms to stop users from using Discord in lieu of platform- or game-based communications suites, because users can and almost certainly do “second-screen” the app on their phones while they play.

As Discord became more essential to game discovery, many publishers began to integrate Discord application programming interfaces (APIs), sometimes even replacing their native communications suite with those of Discord. By 2022, Xbox and PlayStation announced native integrations of Discord in their closed platforms—a move that created a new “interchange” solution for their player networks, communication services, and socializing online.

The next steps for cross-play and identity are emerging. One such step harkens back to credit histories and homestay scores. Online toxicity is an unfortunate part of all social platforms and gaming services. Most of these platforms spend millions (sometimes tens of millions) a year on human moderators who review user reports of abuse and harassment, and ban severe or serial offenders. But there are key limitations to these operations. If Activision’s Call of Duty bans a user for abusive or racist language, that user can then go on to troll on Epic’s Fortnite—or just create a new account on Call of Duty. No gaming company wants to share their customer data with competitors, nor take on additional risks of losing this data—but no developer or player benefits from toxic behavior, and everyone is negatively affected by it. In that spirit, efforts are underway to build cross-publisher account-reporting systems and child-safety protocols.

There are also growing efforts to establish frameworks that would enable users to take an avatar or item from one virtual world to another. This area of interoperation is sometimes lampooned with reference to the apparent mismatches of the various titles, as in “Who wants to wear Fortnite’s anthropomorphic banana skin ‘Peely’ while playing Call of Duty?” Now to be fair, a giant, comically styled anthropomorphic banana doesn’t make much sense in Call of Duty, or in a virtual classroom, for that matter. But it is equally obvious that some users want some items, such as a Darth Vader costume, a Lakers jersey, or a Prada purse, in many different spaces. And they certainly don’t want to buy these items over and over again. They might be reluctantly willing to do so today, but virtual clothing is still in its infancy. By the end of the decade, billions of people will be sitting on numerous (effectively) duplicated outfits across their many previously played games—and will doubtless resist buying those outfits again. Liberating purchases from a single title will, the theory suggests, lead to both more purchases and higher prices. Put another way, would Disney sell more or less merchandise if it could be worn or used only in its theme parks? How much would someone pay for a Real Madrid jersey that could only be used in Santiago Bernabéu Stadium? Or how much lower would user spending be on Roblox if a player’s outfit was limited to a single Roblox game?

It’s likely that consumer spending today is constrained by the profound truth that no game lasts forever. Think of the many objects bought during a vacation that aren’t expected to make the trip home—a boogie board, a water bottle, a costume for Día de los Muertos—and how that fact affects the price that might be paid for these goods. Expected obsolescence always limits spending.

Enabling interoperable virtual goods is technically distinct from providing users with true “ownership” over these items, including the right to freely buy, sell, or trade them, but these functionalities largely follow from the enabling of interoperation; the ability for a user to move (or access) goods across independent account systems and platforms makes it impossible to prevent gray market sales. Fortunately, the right of resale (and profit) should increase the commercial value of virtual goods, as should clearer ownership rights. In early 2021, the South China Morning Post reported that Tencent “sued a game item trading platform to determine who owns the in-game currency and items.” Specifically, the company argued that these assets had “no material value in real life” and that in-game coins bought with real money were “effectively service charges.”4 The result was outrage, with many gamers feeling mistreated and/or demeaned and understandably discouraged from making further investments.

One point of potential progress comes via Facebook, which is adding “interoperable avatars” to its Facebook Connect set of authentication APIs. Facebook Connect is better known to the public as “Log in with Facebook,” which allows Facebook users to substitute their Facebook log-in for a website or app’s own account system. Most developers would prefer that users create a bespoke account, as it provides the developer with greater information about the user and means that the developer controls this information and account (and not Facebook). However, Facebook Connect is far simpler and faster, and therefore it is the preferred solution for most users. As a result, developers benefit from an increase in the number of registered users—which beats having mostly logged-out anonymous ones. A comparable value proposition will exist for Facebook’s avatar suite, and the same is true of Snap’s Bitmoji and Apple’s Personas. If customized avatars are essential to user expression in 3D space, then few users will want to create a new, detailed avatar for every virtual world they use. It’s also unlikely that every platform—let alone the average platform—will boast avatar tools, or outfit choices, as capable as those of the big-tech giants. If so, the services that embrace cross-platform avatars will likely benefit, while also driving the standardization process.

Epic Games, meanwhile, is working to pioneer data standards that allow a single in-game “asset” (really, a right to data) to be repurposed in multiple environments. After acquiring Psyonix in May 2019, Epic Games announced that the publisher’s hit game Rocket League would go free-to-play in September 2020 and move over to the company’s online services suite, known as EOS, which would also allow the title to access Fortnite’s social graph.

To commemorate the free-to-play launch, Epic also unveiled the first of several two-week “Llama-Rama” crossover events in which Fortnite players could complete challenges in Rocket League that would unlock exclusive outfits and achievements that could be worn in and across either game. A second and third Llama-Rama began in March and December of 2021 and although there were no follow-ups in 2022 or 2023, Epic was at work expanding upon the model.

In March 2021, Epic bought Tonic Games Group, maker of Fall Guys and dozens of other games, as part of its investments “in building the Metaverse.”5 Eight months later, Epic acquired Harmonix, the music-focused video game developer that owned Rock Band, with Epic’s news release declaring, “As we work to build the metaverse, [Harmonix’s] expertise is needed to reimagine how music is experienced, created and distributed.”6 And then in April 2022, Epic announced that KIRKBI, the family-owned holding and investment company behind The LEGO Group, had invested $1 billion in Epic as part of a shared effort to “shape the future of the Metaverse” and “create new social entertainment exploring the connection between digital and physical worlds.”7

Epic’s many behind-the-scenes efforts began to publicly converge in 2023. In March, the company unveiled an update to Fortnite Creative entitled Unreal Editor for Fortnite (or UEFN), which enabled developers to build FNC using the PC-based Unreal Editor typically used by Unreal developers, rather than through Fortnite’s more simplified (and child-focused) in-game editor. Using UEFN, developers could create fully custom sounds and textures, as well as inject custom code into their worlds to govern non-playable character AI, alter physics, and use a visual style that had little resemblance to Fortnite: Battle Royale. Epic also announced that independent developers would receive up to 40% of total Fortnite revenue based on an (unshared) equation spanning the total time spent playing FNC worlds, the purchasing behavior of its players, and the degree to which those worlds attracted net new players to the platform, among other measures.8 Despite the increase in variety, users would still be able to wear their typical Fortnite avatars across all UEFN worlds (unless the developer behind this world prohibited it). To support Fortnite’s expansion toward the type of worlds and players typically found on Roblox, Epic also began to break its avatars down into more separable elements. For example, an avatar that previously included a holstered gun and belt of ammo would appear inside a PG world without its weapon and munitions, whereas some outfits were blocked altogether, thereby establishing a de facto system and taxonomy for avatar ratings and appropriateness.

On November 3, 2023, Epic launched Fortnite OG, a month-long event in which Fortnite’s original 2017 maps were brought back, prompting tens of millions of lapsed players to return too. On its second day, Fortnite OG hit a new record for Epic, with more than 44.7 million players logging on (including an estimated 33%–38% of all active PlayStation and Xbox players that day).9 To commemorate the end of the mini-season, Epic held a live-in-game event featuring rapper Eminem that transported players across several different, never-before-seen Fortnite realms—all of which were about to debut. On December 7, Epic launched a new free-to-play game mode inside Fortnite, LEGO Fortnite, a sort of mash-up of Fortnite’s gameplay mechanics with the aesthetics and construction focus of Minecraft and real-world LEGO bricks. As with UEFN, players could continue to wear their Fortnite avatars in LEGO Fortnite—but now they would do so using a LEGO-styled version of that avatar. On December 8, another free mode was added, Rocket Racing, a spin-off of Psyonix’s Rocket League but focused on the kart-racing genre popularized by Mario Kart, alongside the ability for players to buy cars, decals, and wheels that could be used inside Fortnite: Battle Royale, Rocket League, Rocket Racing, and eligible UEFN titles. On December 9, Epic premiered its final free new mode, Fortnite Festival, which reimagined Harmonix’s classic musical rhythm game Rock Band. Epic also began selling virtual instruments, as well as popular songs that users could play inside Rocket League and Rocket Racing cars or while driving a car or dancing in Fortnite.

By the start of 2024, Epic had yet to integrate Fall Guys into Fortnite—a move that seemed likely, but was technically difficult and time consuming. The seemingly rapid integration of Rocket League was aided by the fact Psyonix had built the game on Unreal.* In contrast, Fall Guys was built on Unity. As such, integration required Epic to either rebuild the title on its engine (while ensuring it “felt” and “played” the same), and/or invest in a series of translator tools—and do so while sustaining (if not growing) Fall Guys player base and defending against many copycat competitors that emerged after the title became a hit. Regardless of when (or whether) Fall Guys relaunches as part of Fortnite, it appears that through its cross-title assets and achievements model, Epic is trying to set a precedent similar to the ones it established in cross-platform gaming. The company believes that there are benefits—that is, more profits and players—to reducing the friction to accessing different games, making it easier for players to bring their friends and items across these games, and giving them a reason to try out new games. Players will then spend more time gaming, with more people, across a greater diversity of titles, spending more money along the way. If so, an ever-expanding network of third-party games will want to connect to Epic’s virtual identity, communications, and entitlements systems (which are a part of Epic Online Services), which helps to make Epic’s various offerings the standard. And only two months after the launch of LEGO Fortnite, Epic’s ostensible strategy received external validation: The Walt Disney Company agreed to invest $1.5 billion into Epic as part of a broader partnership that would involve the creation of a “new, persistent, and interoperable universe” connected to Fortnite.10 In its promotional artwork, Disney displayed a network of worlds based on franchises and films such as A Nightmare Before Christmas, Avatar, Marvel, Monsters, Inc., and Star Wars, as well as brands like Disney Cruise Line, ESPN, and 20th Century Studios, while promising fans would be able to “play, watch, [and] shop,” as well as “create their own stories and experiences.”11

In support of these efforts, Epic had a lower-profile but potentially more significant product launch in December of 2022, Verse, a new programming language “designed for the Metaverse” that Epic also open-sourced.12 Speaking to developers about Verse at the 2023 Game Developers Conference, Sweeney said it “is about solving the larger problem of the metaverse.”13 “When you release an app, you use a bunch of [different code] libraries. But you compile one piece of code, you ship it, and it doesn’t change again until you release a new version,” he remarked, but “the Metaverse, we think, will be the combination of millions of objects written by millions of different developers—a lot of code, a lot of content that’s constantly being updated—in which vehicles from one developer, together with characters from another developer, have to work together, even if those programmers have never met each other or never tested their content before [and use different engines].”14 To address this, Sweeney argued the Metaverse needed a “special kind of programming foundation”—one that was designed to be easy to learn, could better detect errors before being implemented into a live experience, was modularized, backward compatible, and widely interoperable, could scale to billions of users in a single simulation, be correctly interpreted by different clients just as different web browsers agree on the look and functionality of a webpage, and could support a decentralized open economy.15 Following Fortnite’s December 2023 expansion, Sweeney declared that the sixth version of Unreal Engine was effectively “Unreal Engine 5 + Verse + rough deployment parity into Fortnite and into standalone products + metaverse economy + standards + ?? magic TBD.”16 In addition to driving asset and economic interoperability, Epic is also driving the “interoperation” of competing intellectual properties, which is a philosophical, rather than a technical, problem (cross-platform gaming is a reminder that this is the harder of the two challenges). As virtual platforms like Fortnite, Minecraft, and Roblox have grown into culture-defining social spaces, they’ve become an increasingly necessary part of consumer marketing, brand building, and multimedia franchise experiences. Over its first five years, Fortnite has produced experiences with the NFL and FIFA; Disney’s Marvel Comics, Star Wars, and Alien; Warner Bros.’ DC Comics; anime hits Dragon Ball and Naruto; Lionsgate’s John Wick; Microsoft’s Halo; Sony’s God of War and Horizon Zero Dawn; Capcom’s Street Fighter; Hasbro’s G.I. Joe; Nike; and Michael Jordan, Travis Scott, and on and on. But to participate in these experiences, brand owners must embrace something they almost never allow: unlimited-term licenses (in-game outfits are kept by players forever), overlapping marketing windows (some brand events are mere days apart or overlap entirely), and as good as no editorial control. In sum, this means it’s now possible to dress as Neymar while wearing a Baby Yoda or Air Jordan backpack, holding Aquaman’s trident, and exploring a virtual Stark Industries. And the owners of these franchises want this to happen. By 2023, it was common for many blockbuster games—even those which ostensibly prioritize realism, such as Call of Duty or PUBG: Battlegrounds—to incorporate and intermingle popular IP.

To counteract the adverse effects of interoperable goods, several solutions have been proposed. One idea is “programmed degradation”—that is, for virtual goods to wear out with use or time or transfer, which would help keep such goods “scarce” and provide creators (or underlying license owners) with enduring price and supply power. An alternative approach would involve royalties paid to an item’s creator every time a trade occurs. Developers can (and would) also produce virtual goods that are not interoperable, cannot be resold or traded, or are altered when transferred. Keep in mind, too, that enabling interoperable assets does not mean embracing all of their functionality. An avatar that is able to fly in one virtual world is not automatically capable of doing so in another—the latter’s code would need to support it. Such qualifications ensure that no game or environment is “broken” through interoperability.

Beyond Virtual Goods

Most of the narrative around an interoperable Metaverse focuses on the objects described above—avatars and in-game items. The more important area of standardization and interconnection is at the 3D tools and design layer, which also happens to be developing more rapidly, too.

Take 3D assets. Over the past 30 years, the cost of developing an AAA video game has grown from single-digit millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. There were many causes for this increase, including the increasing use of motion-capture performance, recorded dialogue, and engine development, but a large portion stemmed from greater scale, diversity, and visual fidelity of a game’s virtual world.

In the 1990s, the average AAA open-world title might require only tens of megabytes (the 1998 Nintendo 64 title The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time), with the largest reaching perhaps 1.5 GB (the 1997 PlayStation title Final Fantasy 7, which required three CD-ROMs). By the late 2010s, the smallest of these titles would be 15 GB (2017’s The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, which supported only 30 fps and 1080p) and the largest passing 100 or even 200 GB (2016’s Final Fantasy XV, up to 240 fps and 4K).17

To aid the growing cost of virtual assets and the growing number of these assets used in a virtual world, new businesses and business lines emerged that were dedicated to producing assets for third-party licensing; there also arose a lucrative trade in marketplaces to aggregate those assets and sell their rights. The two largest such stores, which are operated by Unity and Epic Games, span several million assets. Many of these assets were originally designed for first-party use, but their developer later made them available for sale to help recoup the up-front investment in these assets. In 2019, Epic also made a trio of acquisitions intended to help build out its store. 3Lateral and Cubic Motion were used to create Epic’s “MetaHumans,” a sort of hyperrealistic avatar maker that can also be mapped to a smartphone camera or even professional-grade tracking solutions, while Quixel equipped the Epic’s asset store with “Megascans” of real-world environments that capture entire fjords and mesas down to every slab of stone, pebble, and scrape.

If asset stores are helpful when constructing fictional virtual worlds, they’re invaluable when making real ones. Few companies on earth could have produced Microsoft Flight Simulator save for Microsoft, which not only boasts the world’s second-largest cloud computing business but is also a market leader in the mapping and geospatial services that own and commission millions of satellite and aerial photos of the planet, in part for their use on its own Google Street View alternative, Bing Streetside. Despite this, neither MSFS nor Bing are entirely based on Microsoft’s proprietary data set. It also licenses traffic data, weather data, and supplementary maps covering topography and particularly remote regions of the world. The company also makes extensive use of OpenStreetMap, a free and open geographic database that spans thousands of underlying licenses. But even if companies such as Microsoft and Tesla can afford to build complete three-dimensional models of the world—or, say, specific large cities—such investments would be extraordinarily expensive and never ending because the world is constantly changing. This need, in turn, has led to assets stores, licensors, and marketplaces for the “real world.”

An example is Cesium, which manages and integrates a large pipeline of geospatial data (environmental scans, point clouds, photogrammetry data, and renders) from various sources (e.g., open libraries, its own database, private client clouds, dedicated mapping and licensing organizations). These data sets can then be cloud-streamed via any proprietary engine to create real-time visualizations using the 3D Tiles open standard. This allows any “developer” (a city, construction company, game maker, events company, etc.) to leverage simulations as part of its everyday work, such as site planning, measuring environmental change, tracking drivers in Le Mans, or launching a satellite.

Another area where economics are leading to 3D standardization is in game engines. Although the opportunity in virtual worlds has never been as large as it is today, that means that reaching the entirety of this market has also never been so difficult. In the 1980s, a developer might make a game for just one console and, in doing so, reach 70% of potential players; supporting two would mean reaching the entire addressable market. Today, there are three console makers, two of which operate consoles in two different console generations, plus a series of cloud-based consoles that use their own technology stacks, including Nvidia’s GeForce Now and Amazon’s Luna. There are also two PC platforms, Mac and Windows, that span dozens to hundreds of different hardware builds, and two dominant mobile computing platforms, iOS and Android, that span many more operating system (OS) versions, GPUs, CPUs, and other chipsets. Every additional platform, device, or build requires code that is unique to a specific set of hardware, but creating and supporting all this code is costly, time-consuming, and arduous—unless the developer writes it so generically that the title’s performance on any platform is constrained by the capabilities of any other one. Another option is to just ignore a large part of the market altogether (i.e., various OSs).

This challenge, when combined with the ever-increasing complexity of virtual worlds, is why cross-platform game engines such as Unity and Unreal have proliferated. They emerged partly as a response to fragmentation, and they don’t just solve the problem but do it at a low cost. Imagine a developer trying to pick a smartphone OS for their next game. Apple’s mobile ecosystem has 60% of smartphone share in the United States—80% share among teenagers—and over two-thirds of mobile gaming revenues globally. In addition, a developer can reach nearly 90% of iOS users by writing to only a dozen iPhone SKUs. The remainder of the global market is split among thousands of different Android devices. Forced to choose between these two platforms, a developer would always pick iOS. Unity lets the same developer easily publish their game across all platforms (including web), thereby increasing their revenue potential by over 50% at little incremental cost. In the abstract, Apple might prefer more exclusive games and games fully optimized for their own hardware, but it’s better for everyone, including iOS users and the App Store, that most mobile developers use Unity. By making more money, developers can build more and better games, prompting even more user spending on mobile devices.

The standardization of assets and the standardization of engines are intertwined processes. The availability of millions of detailed, diverse, and low-cost assets makes it harder for any virtual world builder to invest in—let alone develop or contribute to—fringe file formats or engines. But the potency of these parallel and intersecting processes might best be told through a specific example outside gaming.

The Happiest Place(s) in Any Galaxy

Traditionally, films relied exclusively on non-real-time rendering software such as Autodesk’s Maya, Pixar’s RenderMan, or SideFX’s Houdini, rather than real-time alternatives such as Unreal or Unity. There were several rationales for this choice. First, real-time solutions were not designed for the levels of fidelity expected of IMAX-grade feature films and, until recently, struggled to produce such quality. Second, there was no need to produce a frame in milliseconds, and instead, it made sense to spend anywhere from a few seconds to several hours to render a frame if that extra time produced a more realistic or detailed image. And the goal of the computer graphics department was to virtually produce an already-known image (that is, one based on a storyboard). This means that there was no need to build assets for real-time usage—such as a model of the Avengers Tower in New York City that had the requisite detail to be viewed from any perspective, rather than just in a fixed position in a camera shot from a half kilometer away, or that might respond to any alien fire or attack instead of just those Joss Whedon had specified in his script. Building an entire, or even partial, model of Manhattan made even less sense.

The focus on non-real-time assets and rendering did come with a cost: a film or TV show’s digital models were almost always “single use”—even if a subsequent production would end up making a nearly identical model later on. Studios knew that this was theoretically wasteful, but there was no clear business case to make for additional investments in the hopes of later reuse, and later productions that might want to use those assets might use a different rendering software anyway. By contrast, Hollywood’s cost-benefit approach to physical sets, costumes, and items is typically just a matter of storage costs and there’s no worry of whether a sword from one Roman epic might be physically compatible with another. As such, it’s common for everything from a sword to a rock to a Victorian headpiece to be reused across scores of unrelated productions.

There will always be financial trade-offs between creating single-use assets for a given production and investing in detail/metadata that can more easily support future ones, and similarly, between creating new assets and repurposing or updating old ones. However, advances in real-time simulation and related hardware, the increasing value of transmedia franchises, and the growing importance of computer-generated imagery are collectively reducing the costs of developing real-time assets while increasing the return from investing in them.

The blockbuster 2019 Disney film The Lion King provides an illustrative use case. Although the entry looks like one of the company’s live-action remakes, such as Mulan or Beauty and the Beast, nearly all of the film’s sets and all of its characters are computer-animated. To provide the film with an “ultrarealistic, documentary-style” aesthetic, rather than just photorealism, director Jon Favreau had most of the film’s virtual set designed in Unity’s real-time game engine.† This provided Favreau with an unprecedented ability to understand and test the film as it was being produced. In many cases, Favreau would put on a VR headset to explore as its many characters performed their roles, which experience enabled him to alter camera angles, lighting, blocking, and other aspects of the set. If he wanted to know what a scene would look like from the back of a gazelle or at night rather than day, he need not wait nor invest in potentially wasteful VFX work—the answer was available within seconds because nearly all objects and environments were in real time. The Lion King went on to gross $1.7 billion globally, more than any other film produced in the history of Walt Disney Pictures.

Only a few months after The Lion King’s release, Disney debuted Disney+, arguably the company’s most important single product launch in its nearly century-long history. And the service’s signature launch title? The Mandalorian, the first-ever live-action Star Wars TV series, which also happened to have Favreau as its creator and one of its key writers. Unlike The Lion King, The Mandalorian mostly starred human performers and made extensive use of practical effects and sets—but although the series spanned forests, deserts, and icescapes, every minute was shot on a single Manhattan Beach soundstage. This soundstage was also designed for game engines—Epic’s Unreal Engine this time—not green screens. The performers and physical sets of The Mandalorian were surrounded by a 20-foot-tall, 75-foot-wide, and 270-degree LED screen that projected, in real time, the show’s fantastic world, including its backdrops and some of its epic monsters, using the Unreal Engine. This technical approach meant that everyone inside the LED “volume” could experience what Favreau did in a VR—but without wearing a headset. It also meant that “real people” could be seen inside the environment too—rather than everyone just watching preplanned animations of Timon and Pumbaa. In addition, the cast could be affected by the volume’s LEDs; the light shining down from a virtual sun would recolor an actor directly and provide them with an accurate shadow, which would then not need to be applied or corrected in postproduction. A set could have the perfect sunrise year-round—and years later, that exact same setting could be summoned in a matter of seconds. The Mandalorian went on to receive an Outstanding Series nomination at the 2020 Primetime Emmy Awards, the first time a Star Wars entry was nominated for the highest creative honor in TV. It has remained the most popular original title for Disney+ across its first four years.

Hollywood’s adoption of “virtual production” doesn’t just make it easier to film a sequel—it makes it easier to make all derivative works. It’s no coincidence that Disney’s Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge theme park attractions run on the Unreal Engine, and when the company adds AR and VR functionality to its parks, Unreal will be the likely choice then as well. By standardizing around Unreal and the associated asset formats and metadata conventions, it becomes easier for the company to repurpose existing models, such as those of Din Djarin’s Razor Crest or Nevarro City, and impractical to change technology stacks that require reconstructing these assets. And if Peloton wants to sell a course set on the Death Star or the Avengers Campus, it can repurpose (i.e., license, pay for) much of what Disney has already made—thereby saving money that, at a minimum, will make the resulting courses more affordable to Peloton’s customers, if not financially practical in the first place. If Tinder wants to offer virtual dates on Mustafar, the same logic applies. Instead of playing blackjack via the video-based iCasino, why not play on Canto Bight? Rather than launch a Star Wars integration in Fortnite, Disney will just populate its own miniworlds on Fortnite Creative using what they’ve already built. The many video game publishers that license Star Wars IP, too, might reconsider their own engine choices if using Unreal means access to the hundreds of millions in assets Disney has already developed. This is how standardization happens—decisions that were once made in isolation, such as a CTO’s preference for Old Technology A or New Technology B, are instead shaped by the activities of the broader market.

The network effects around engines and assets are particularly profound when it comes to real-world simulations. As an example, take the 56-acre, 20-building, multibillion-dollar redevelopment of Water Street in Tampa, Florida. As part of this project, Strategic Development Partners enlisted the XR real estate software company Imerza to produce a 17-foot-diameter, 3D-printed, modular scale model of the city, which was then supported by twelve 5K laser cameras that projected 25 million pixels atop this model, based on city data feeds for weather, traffic, population density, and whatever else.18 All of this was run by an Unreal-based real-time-rendered simulation that could be viewed through a touchscreen or VR headset.

A Real-Time Simulation of Tampa Using a 3D Printed Model, XR Projectors, and Unreal Engine

The perks of a real-time 3D simulation are difficult to describe in writing for the very reason that SDP saw value in building a physical model and digital twin in the first place. However, SDP’s investment enabled the city of Tampa, prospective tenants of the Water Street development, investors in the project, and construction partners to better understand and plan for it. It was possible to see exactly how present-day Tampa would be affected by not just the construction process but also the completed project. How would a five-year build affect local traffic? How would the effects be different from those of a six-year build? What would happen if a given building were replaced by a park? Or if its floors were reduced from 15 feet to 11? How would the views of other buildings and parks in the area be affected by the development, including through refracted light or radiated heat—and at any time or day in the year? How would these buildings shape emergency response times in the area? Might it necessitate a new police, fire, or ambulance station? On which sides of the buildings should fire escapes be built? All of these answers could be simulated, tested, and tweaked, ad infinitum.

SDP’s Water Street development was intended to aid the design process while also enlisting greater municipal and commercial support for the project. But that is just the beginning. The long-term goal of such simulations is to live-operate the resulting buildings, inclusive of the many businesses within them, and their relationships with the city. These simulations can support myriad use cases, from something as small as helping to manage the flow of shoppers in a retail mall to aiding evacuation procedures, and helping the local municipality operate a more comprehensive and intelligent traffic light network. For this to be possible, each collaborator must have common code types, structures, and mechanisms for exchange, as discussed throughout this book. They must also have similar models. It makes little sense for every participant to build such a model from scratch, if and when that’s even financially possible. What’s more, these duplicated yet isolated efforts would doubtless produce errors and lead to avoidable underlap. And while Tesla might be able to generate most of San Francisco, including its live and historical traffic, it needs third-party sources for weather, and its ability to predict travel stoppages is limited by the time it takes its network to know what the city does minutes, hours, or even weeks in advance. And if Tesla needs outside data support, so too does every other developer looking to build AR and location-based experiences.

This need is already producing technical solutions. In August 2023, Amazon, Facebook, Microsoft, and navigation company TomTom, in partnership with the Linux Foundation’s Joint Development Foundation, also announced the formation of the Overture Maps Foundation. The purpose of Overture is to develop the world’s largest open-mapping suite and database, all of which will conform to common data structures and conventions, with the intent of fostering interoperation rather than closed ecosystems. Overture was not just prompted by the expanding importance of 2D and 3D geospatial data and the need for developers to intermingle their geospatial services, but also in response to the confines of the services offered by market leaders Google and Apple. Google Maps APIs, which are among the most widely used globally, do not allow developers to provide more than 20 search results per user query or the storage or caching of any information, which effectively blocks the developer from performing rich user analytics and degrades the user’s experience.19 Developers must also pay Google for every thousand uses of the Google Maps API. Apple Maps is ostensibly free of charge to iOS app developers, but it requires these developers to distribute through Apple’s App Store, which charges 15%–30% on all eligible transactions and also intermediates the developer’s billing relationship with the user and restricts many of the developer’s other commercial and technical decisions, including which data they collect. If a developer opts for a browser-based experience—or just offers it alongside their native app—the developer must pay Apple every time their map API is called. And should the developer want to build a native app for platforms other than Apple, such as Android, they are effectively forced to use another mapping solution. As such, the developer’s choice is really between using Google Maps on all platforms, or building a technology stack that uses both solutions, which leads to greater technical complexity, experiential variability, and costs.

It will take time for Overture to offer mapping detail comparable to Google’s and Apple’s mapping suites, and the foundation’s tools are unlikely to be as easy to use or “productized” either, but it is fully free and unrestricted in legal usage, and can be integrated into every computing platform in the world. To seed Overture, Facebook and Microsoft contributed nearly 60 million geospatial “points of interest”—buildings, monuments, lakes, businesses—as well as an unspecified number of transportation routes and boundaries.20 In February 2024, Niantic joined the Overture Maps Foundation as a contributor member and promised to contribute geolocation data to the group.21

No matter the forces of standardization pipelines, assets, and engines, there will always be fragmentation in the Metaverse because there will always be specialty simulations, new software, and unforeseen use cases that require rich customization. Nvidia’s Omniverse, which launched in 2020, is one of several “interchange” platforms that address this problem. An automotive company might be able to bring its Unreal-based cars to an environment designed in Unity and have those cars interact with objects made in Blender, all the while testing the results against weather conditions simulated by Nvidia’s Earth 2.0. Omniverse doesn’t support all engines, file formats, metadata structures, and functionality, but its shortlist still drives the standardization process, while also making the Metaverse more possible specifically because it allows companies to participate without refactoring their entire 3D business.

Notably, Omniverse is built around Universal Scene Description (USD), a file format that was developed by Pixar in 2012 to detail the geometries, materials, physics, and behaviors of 3D worlds.22 In 2016, Pixar open-sourced the format and in the years that followed, USD saw widespread adoption across industries such as architecture, robotics, and mechanical engineering, with Apple’s ARKit also choosing the derivative USDZ format as its standard for user scans of real-world objects.23 Following the release of Omniverse, Jensen Huang declared USD the “HTML of the Metaverse”—a format that would serve as the declarative specification of the contents of a virtual world.24 In 2023, Pixar, alongside Adobe, Apple, Autodesk, Nvidia, and the Linux Foundation’s Joint Development Foundation, formed the Alliance for OpenUSD (AOUSD), a nonprofit standards body that would steer the newly designated “OpenUSD” format and foster the development of its surrounding ecosystem. Cesium, Epic Games, IKEA, SideFX, and Unity joined the AOUSD as general members upon its release.

A year before AOUSD, nearly three dozen companies—including competitors such as Meta, Microsoft, Epic Games, Unity, Adobe, and Nvidia, plus organizations such as the World Wide Web Consortium and Khronos Group—had come together to create the Metaverse Standards Forum, an organization intended to facilitate the creation of various standards groups such as OpenUSD. By its first anniversary in June 2023, MSF had amassed over 2,400 member organizations, prompting hope that Pixar would not be the last company to give away control of its proprietary technologies for the collective benefit.

  1. * Not only were LEGO Fortnite, Rocket Racing, and Fortnite Festival all built on Unreal, they were designed specifically for the Fortnite platform.

  2. † The final rendering was still produced in Maya, non-real-time animation software published by Autodesk.

Chapter 9 HARDWARE, HMDS, AND THE HARDEST TECHNOLOGY CHALLENGE OF OUR TIME

For many, the most exciting aspect of the Metaverse is the new devices that might be used to access, render, and operate it. A great deal of attention focuses on head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are typically categorized in three ways. First are virtual reality (VR) headsets, which typically include a pair of one-to-two-inch displays directly in front of a user’s eyes which show a purely synthetic 3D environment. To aid immersion and visual clarity, the user’s eyes are usually fully surrounded by the headset, which thereby blocks out their peripheral view of the “real world.” In a simplified sense, a VR device is like watching a smartphone only an inch from one’s eyes and in landscape orientation, while wearing visual blinders and using head, eye, and other bodily motion to operate the device and potentially handheld controllers too. VR users are almost always stationary when using the device. While VR replaces “the real world,” augmented reality (AR) adds information on top of it. An analogy might be viewing the world with live and digital annotations, such as a virtual signpost that identifies an in-view statue and enables the user to press a digital button that plays an audio recording and perhaps a visual animation of the individual. There are two core methods of AR. In the first, the user sees through glass that is selectively illuminated to render AR information (“optical AR”). In the second, the user is looking at a live video of the real world that their device has captured and subsequently annotated (“passthrough AR”). As with VR headsets, AR devices are typically controlled, at least in part, by tracking a user’s hands, eyes, or body.

The last HMD category is mixed-reality (MR) devices, which are similar to AR but involve more direct interaction with the real-world environment. So a user might be able to play virtual tennis with the virtual ball, bouncing off both the real-world floor and the nearby wall, or collect fairies that have been programmatically placed throughout one’s home, hiding in drawers and flying around household plants. AR and MR devices are intended for both stationary and mobile use.

Many AR and MR headsets can also offer VR experiences by filling in all available pixels and using no visual inputs from the real world. Most, though not all, companies investing in VR, AR, and MR consider the ultimate goal to be a pair of lightweight MR glasses (not a “headset” or “goggles”) capable of sophisticated MR experiences, though such a device would not necessarily replace dedicated VR or AR devices, just as smartphones have not replaced the occasional need for a PC. As of yet, this goal is well behind schedule.

In 2016, Mark Zuckerberg repeated his belief that within a decade, “normal-looking” AR glasses not only would be a part of everyday life, but the devices would often displace the role of a smartphone for calls, sharing photos, and browsing the web.1 A big-screen TV, meanwhile, would be replaced by a “$1 app” that would place an even larger AR screen on a family’s living room wall.2 That same year, Tim Sweeney predicted that within five to seven years, VR devices would be as powerful as the PCs of 2016 yet a fraction of the price and shrunk down into glasses the size of Oakley sunglasses.3 When Google unveiled its Google Glass smart glasses hardware in 2012, the company suggested that annual sales could reach tens of millions by 2015 and eventually appeal to the nearly 80% of people who wear glasses daily.4 Instead, Google Glass became one of big tech’s most infamous flops, with sales failing to crack 100,000 units. In a similar vein, most estimates show that fewer than one million AR headsets or glasses have been sold in the decade since that market misfire. VR has performed better, with roughly 50–60 million in lifetime sales,5 but many buyers stop using the device within weeks of purchase.6 In October 2022, a few weeks before the Quest 2’s second anniversary since release, the Wall Street Journal reported that barely a third of the 20 million devices sold by Facebook were used monthly.7

These poor results are not for lack of effort. In the nine years after acquiring Oculus VR in March 2014, Facebook has spent roughly $53 billion on its Reality Labs division. This spend spans marketing, manufacturing, and device subsidies—most Quests are sold below cost—but also includes investments into software, R&D, and M&A, some of which relates to devices, technologies, or experiences that have yet to see release, with another portion relating to products Facebook has since discontinued or shuttered. The resulting revenues are estimated at $7 billion, producing a $46 billion lifetime division loss, with roughly 20 million Oculus/Quest devices shipped over that same period. In 2021, Facebook partnered with Ray-Ban to release several models of co-branded glasses that enabled users to take photos and listen to music from the device, among other features. The Wall Street Journal has reported that 300,000 units were sold over the first eighteen months, with fewer than one in ten purchasers using them monthly.8 In April 2022, Facebook was reportedly “rushing” to release its first AR glasses by the end of 2024,9 but by February 2023, the company had pushed its target release date to 2027—11 years after Zuckerberg had predicted it would take less than a decade for the form factor to become quotidian.10

Despite the swift public rejection of Google Glass in 2014, Google released an updated business-focused model in 2017, with another update following in 2019, and only halted sales in March of 2023.11 Between 2020 and 2023, Google spent an estimated $1–$2 billion acquiring start-ups such as North, which designed AR glasses and interfaces,12 and Raxium, which produced MicroLED displays for AR glasses.13 In 2022, the company announced that it was publicly field-testing a new AR glasses device (without the Google Glass branding), with The Verge reporting that Google had targeted a consumer release for 2024.14 In January 2023, this device was canceled as part of Google’s cost-cutting efforts, prompting Clay Bavor, an 18-year veteran of Google who reported directly to CEO Sundar Pichai, and oversaw both the company’s HMD division and its Area 120 group (most famous for overseeing Google’s “20% time”), to depart the company.15 Not long after, Mark Lucovsky, who was hired by Google in 2021 to lead its AR glasses initiative and was previously the GM of operating systems at Oculus, announced he was resigning from the company.* In an interview with Business Insider, Lucovsky said, “The recent changes in AR leadership and Google’s unstable commitment and vision has weighed heavily on my decision.”16 While Google’s AR efforts received comparably more press, the company’s investments in VR have arguably been even more significant and disappointing.

Google’s first foray into VR, Google Cardboard, came in 2014 with the express goal of inspiring interest in immersive virtual reality. For developers, Google produced a Cardboard software development kit (SDK), which helped developers create VR-specific apps built in Java, Unity, or Apple’s Metal. For users, Google created a $15 foldout cardboard “viewer” into which users could place their iPhones or Android devices in order to experience VR without needing to buy a new device. A year after Cardboard was announced, Google unveiled Jump, a platform and ecosystem for VR filmmaking, and Expeditions, a program focused on providing VR-based field trips for educators. The top-level numbers achieved by Cardboard were impressive: over 15 million “viewers” were sold by Google in five years, while nearly 200 million Cardboard-enabled apps were downloaded, and over a million students took at least one Expeditions tour within the first year of release. However, these figures proved to be evidence of consumer intrigue rather than sustained interest in viewer-based VR. In November 2019, Google shut down the Cardboard project and open-sourced its SDK, with Expeditions being discontinued in June 2021.

In 2016, Google launched its second VR platform, Daydream, which was intended to improve on the foundation established by Cardboard. The improvements started with the quality of the Daydream viewer. The $80–$100 headset was made from foam and covered in soft fabric (available in four colors) and, unlike the Cardboard viewer, could be strapped to a user’s head rather than requiring users to hold it up in front of them when in use. The Daydream viewer also came with a dedicated handheld remote control, and had a near-field communication (NFC) chip that could automatically put the phone into VR mode, instead of requiring users to do so themselves. While Daydream received positive reviews from the press and led companies including HBO and Hulu to produce VR-specific apps, consumers showed little interest in the platform. Google canceled the project at the same time it terminated Cardboard.

Fourteen years after the 2010 start of HoloLens, Microsoft has sold fewer than a half million units across its two models, which were released in 2016 and 2019. Less than a year after the US Army awarded Microsoft a contract worth up to $22 billion for customized HoloLens devices and software, Congress duly rejected the army’s request for $400 million to purchase another 7,000 models. This denial followed an internal army finding that the HMD had failed four of six operational tests, with 80% of users experiencing mission-affecting physical impairments such as headaches, eyestrain, and nausea within three hours of use. In addition, the HMD could only augment roughly 20% of a wearer’s total visual field and the army reported that the glow of its display could give away a soldier’s location even at great distances.17 Instead, Congress provided the army with $40 million to fund the development of a new model, with the army paying Microsoft an additional $125 million out of previous congressional appropriations to further R&D and purchase more test units.18

Between its founding in 2010 and 2022, mixed-reality start-up Magic Leap raised upwards of $3.5 billion from investors including AT&T, Alibaba, Andreessen Horowitz, Google, Kleiner Perkins, Qualcomm, and NTT Docomo, achieving a peak valuation of nearly $7 billion.19 In January 2023, reports emerged that Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund had taken majority control of the company following a $450 million equity-and-debt deal, suggesting that the company’s valuation had under a billion dollars, possibly down to even half a billion—a fraction of the cash Magic Leap had raised and invested over its lifetime.20

Amazon began development of its Echo Frames smart glasses in 2017, with the first model released in 2019 and an updated model following a year later. Both editions were limited to audio-only augmentations and lacked a digital display. Neither seems to have sold well. Snap, which was valued at roughly $15 billion throughout 2023, has spent an estimated $1.5 billion acquiring companies such as Vergence Labs, which designed AR glasses, WaveOptics, an AR display manufacturer, and NextMind, which developed AR-focused neurotechnology sensors, over and above the billions spent on internal R&D. These investments supported four different models of Snap Spectacles sunglasses released between 2016 and 2021, with cumulative sales estimated at less than a million. In 2022, the company announced it was deprioritizing its AR glasses initiatives to instead focus on its AR software for smartphones. Most of the employees working on its devices were let go.

Despite the missed release dates, poor sales, and nearly $50–$100 billion in total industry investment, many technologists and tech companies remain hopeful that the era of HMDs is nearby. Even primitive AR devices are seeing sustained increases in deployment in vocational training, surgery, and engineering—and these uses are quite literally saving lives. Though user retention remains poor, the 2020 Meta Quest 2 outsold the 2019 Quest 1 by a factor of more than ten over its first 12 months, with lifetime sales reaching $20 million. A particular bright spot is the recently released Apple Vision Pro. Apple has a quarter-century history of being a relatively late entrant to categories as diverse as MP3 players, smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches but nevertheless cracking those categories open through innovations in both form factor and interface. Often, Apple discards features and functionality that prior entrants considered necessary, while embracing those that others had ruled out. The company also excels at branding and marketing, boasts the world’s largest and most valuable developer ecosystem, and mobilizes over 500 retail stores and 30,000 retail employees to help explain and sell its devices. But while Apple’s arrival seems to herald the start of a new computing category, its first device also suggests that mainstream use remains far out. At release, Apple Vision Pro was priced at US$3,500, with sales tax adding the equivalent of roughly US$450 in Canada and $700 in the UK—each figure more than the price of Facebook’s Quest 2—while users that require eyeglasses also need to purchase custom lenses that cost $99 to $149. This total price point, which excludes optional accessories, places it well outside the reach of the average person and suggests a lengthy path to widespread adoption. The Apple II, which was one of the first-ever commercially successful consumer computers and Apple’s first hit product, retailed for $1,300 at its 1977 release (equivalent to over $6,500 in 2024), and it was decades until the average American had such a device and longer still for the average person worldwide to own one.
