The largesse of this spend reiterates the criticality of default position, too; in the typical year, Google’s payment to Apple is equivalent to a third of its net income and increases Apple’s by a quarter. Some regulators view these payments as directly anti-competitive, as they discourage Apple from launching its own rival search product (as it did with Maps, Mail, Music, etc.), making it difficult for any other engine to gain share. The total advertising revenue of Microsoft, which operates the second-most-used search engine, Bing (3% market share), is barely half of what Google pays Apple annually—and a 16th of Google’s own ad revenue.39 Whether or not such sums do test antitrust laws, it’s clear they do not improve Google Search, nor do they benefit users or those who fill the World Wide Web with worthwhile content. Instead, Google’s defensive position enables it to layer ever-more ads into its product without worry of losing customers.

The Web3 community believes that software built on blockchain can avoid the pernicious outcomes and competitive stagnation that have characterized the internet of the past two decades and instead ensure that competition remains intense, innovations frequent, and advances widely shared. This is possible not just because blockchains are run by a decentralized network, and these networks run dapps, but because they also maintain most of the “data” considered valuable on the internet today.

Start with identity. To use a Web 2.0 application, users must typically sign up for an account operated by that application or otherwise connect an account that’s operated by another Web 2.0 application (such as Facebook or Gmail). In contrast, Web3 users “connect” their crypto wallet, which is operated by the blockchain and controlled exclusively by the user, to a dapp. The user’s assets (images and videos), social graph, and data (transaction history) would also be stored “on chain,” with the user in control of when and how this information is exposed to a given dapp. Furthermore, much of the user’s interaction with the dapp would be stored on chain, too, including their transactions, likes, and so on. As a result, every dapp must be relentlessly and endlessly focused on offering the best possible experience, price, product, and array of services—or else an existing competitor or new entrant will come along to take their business. An example helps to bring this theory to life.

Uniswap was one of the first Ethereum dapps to gain mass adoption, having launched in 2018 and pioneered the automated market maker model that enabled users to exchange cryptocurrencies without the use of a centralized exchange or bank. Uniswap’s business model involved a 0.05% cut of all transactions while offering those providing liquidity—the supply of tokens available for exchange—a 0.25% spread on the market rate. In 2020, a competitor called Sushiswap emerged that had copied Uniswap’s predominantly open-source and straightforward code. But Sushiswap needed more than functional code to operate—it also needed cryptocurrency owners to make their holdings available for exchange and in such volumes that the exchange rate offered by the marketplace could be competitive with Uniswap. Undercutting Uniswap’s fees to users was impractical—even if Sushiswap waived its 0.05% fee, few users would even notice such savings, and the value of these savings would be dwarfed by the moment-to-moment changes in exchange rates that would be caused by insufficient liquidity on the exchange. Instead, Sushiswap announced a smart contract that would issue “Sushi tokens” to anyone willing to “stake” their cryptocurrencies on the exchange. This provided Sushiswap market makers with two means of generating a profit, an exchange fee per transaction and appreciation in the exchange itself, compared to just the former when using Uniswap. Later, Sushiswap announced an incentive that would specifically reward cryptocurrency owners for shifting their stake tokens from Uniswap to Sushiswap, which naturally increased its supply while also decreasing that available to the incumbent. This targeted offer was impossible for Uniswap to block, as records were publicly available on various blockchains, and easy for Sushiswap to provide, for the same reason. To defend its business, Uniswap announced that it would issue its own token, while also retroactively rewarding prior providers.

User-beneficial “arms races” are typical in dapps, and they often place the product on a path to progressive decentralization in which the community owns the product, rather than just its creators, and indeed directs it, too.

A View to the Future

The vision of Web3 is compelling. It imagines a version of the internet that not only is decentralized in its operations and protocols but is literally run through that same network. This internet also enables users to store their identity, payments, and data on that network, instead of forcing it into databases under the control of massive for-profit corporations. In doing so, optimists believe that the internet can return to the principles of openness upon which it was founded—and forever stay that way. Chris Dixon, a crypto-focused venture capitalist at Andreessen Horowitz, is fond of saying that if the dominant ethos of Web 2.0 was “Don’t be evil,” Google’s de facto motto from the early 2000s until 2015,40 then the slogan of the Web3 era will be “Can’t be evil,”41 adding that “the only API you should trust is one controlled by a blockchain.”42

Even if the benefits would be widespread, rebuilding the internet and its many applications is not going to be easy. Precedents also suggest that it’s unlikely. Free, open-source, and community-run technologies have been available for decades—and they almost always offer a more fair and prosperous future to developers and users alike. Despite this, these technologies tend to lose to paid, closed, and privately owned alternatives because the companies that operate those alternatives can afford enormous investments in services and tools, engineering talent, customer acquisition, and exclusive content. Such investments lead to an ineluctable feedback loop in which more users leads to more developers and vice versa. Once this feedback loop becomes powerful enough, developers and users are financially, creatively, or technically locked in—if not all three.

Blockchains can’t disassemble the Web 2.0 flywheels, but they do provide a mechanism through which significant and diverse resources—from wealth to infrastructure and time—can be easily aggregated by independent groups on a scale that contends with the mightiest of the private companies. Furthermore, these mechanisms have a baked-in economic model to compensate those who contribute to its success or ongoing operations, rather than relying on their altruism and empathy, as is the case with most open-source projects. And while the precise value of this compensation is not always known and is never guaranteed, it increases with the success of any given project. As such, early supporters can receive rewards commensurate with the risks they undertook, which are often competitive with the high salaries and certainty of traditional tech jobs. By the end of 2023, New Hampshire, Utah, and Wyoming had all legalized DAOs,43 with some technologists imagining it as the Metaverse-era version of the LLC (limited liability corporation) or 501(c)(3) (nonprofit organization)—a new structure that would forever alter (and ease) capital formation while enabling billions of otherwise disenfranchised individuals to participate in the high-growth tech economy.44

Blockchains have also operated at extraordinary scale. In 2021 and 2022, more than $14 trillion in value was processed by the Bitcoin and Ethereum blockchains, several times the sum of Stripe, PayPal, Square, Shopify, and WeChat combined.45 All of these transactions took place without the need for a central authority, a managing partner, or even a headquarters. Also, the payments were made across dozens of rival wallets (rather than limited to a tightly controlled network, as is the case with peer-to-peer rails such as Venmo or PayPal), could be made at any time (unlike automated clearinghouses and wire transfers), were completed in less than a minute (unlike ACH), and required neither sender nor receiver to establish a bank account, let alone negotiate a long-term agreement with any specific blockchain, blockchain processor, or wallet provider. Many of these payments were programmed to automatically run applications, cast votes, lend money, fund projects, grant users access to a club, or trigger any number of other activities. Or payments were caused by these events. For this reason, the Web3 community argues that supposed “digital payment rails” such as PayPal, Venmo, and WeChat, as well as Apple’s IAP and Apple Pay, are little more than facsimiles of legacy ones. And unlike these rails, blockchains cannot be used to control users, extract added fees, or force the use of other products.

All of the benefits of a Web3 internet apply to the Metaverse. Many are amplified. On top of these points, the blockchain is often seen as the only way to solve many of the Metaverse’s most intractable problems, such as its insatiable need for computing power. In 2017, long before the crypto boom of 2021, Tim Sweeney said that people will “come to the realization that the blockchain is really a general mechanism for running programs, storing data, and verifiably carrying out transactions. It’s a superset of everything that exists in computing. We’ll eventually come to look at it as a computer that’s distributed and runs a billion times faster than the computer we have on our desktops, because it’s the combination of everyone’s computer.”46

NFTs are a particular area of optimism, with advocates seeing the potential to solve many of the interoperability issues reviewed in Chapter 8. Consider the adage “Possession is nine-tenths of the law.” Under centralized server models, a user can never truly take ownership of a virtual good. Instead, they are simply provided access to a good that’s held, via digital record, on someone else’s property, such as a server. And even if the user takes that data off that server and puts it onto their own hard drive, that’s not enough. Why? Because the rest of the world needs to acknowledge that data and agree on its use. Blockchains can do this by design; anyone who reads it sees the owner and the underlying structures. The sense of possession is augmented by another key property right: the unrestricted right to resale. When a user buys an NFT from a given game, the trustless and permissionless nature of blockchain means that the game’s maker cannot block the sale of that NFT at any point. They’re not even actively informed of it. Similarly, it is impossible for a developer to “lock” blockchain-based assets into their virtual world or technically prevent them from being used elsewhere—the reverse of the typical problem with virtual entitlements.

Token structures also solve for economic models. The blockchain would store assets, rather than individual servers, with network validators compensated for its incorporation into various apps and with crypto wallets consolidating a user’s assets across these many apps. The NFT model also ensures that even if a duplicate version of this virtual good is minted, the original remains distinct and “original”—like a signed and dated painting listed as one of one. Then there are smart contract–based royalties, which enable those who create an NFT to profit in perpetuity from their works and therefore also from their usage by outside developers. In January 2022, Ethereum’s Buterin also began development of a new form of NFT, “soulbound” NFTs, which can never be transferred and so will encourage the collection of NFTs for reasons beyond financial speculation.47

Present Reality

If the vision of Web3 is so positive and capable, what accounts for the widespread skepticism of and resistance to blockchain technology? For one, critics of the blockchain correctly point out that the supposed benefits often gloss over its limitations, drawbacks, and impossibilities. It’s also true that the crypto boom from 2020 through 2022 benefited from a poor understanding of these same issues, and many of the field’s greatest achievements are not technical innovations but legal or financial ones. To evaluate such arguments, it’s necessary to, again, start with database operations.

Irrespective of how transactions are validated (e.g., proof-of-work, proof-of-stake, or any other consensus system), it will always take more time and effort for multiple parties to validate a single financial transaction or nonfinancial record change than for a single entity to do so. Given the scarcity of computing resources today—and especially the needs of the Metaverse—even small inefficiencies have great costs. And modern blockchains are very inefficient by traditional measures. While Visa boasts that its network can process more than 24,000 transactions per second (TPS), the Bitcoin blockchain can manage only 7 TPS, while the proof-of-work version of Ethereum was limited to roughly 10 to 15 TPS.48 Given this, transactions can take 15 seconds and five minutes to confirm, while Bitcoin averages ten minutes.49 The fee for this work is also high and variable. During 2021, Ethereum’s gas fee averaged more than $5 and shot up to tens of dollars during periods of peak congestion—sums impractical for most daily purchases and many NFTs. That same year, Bitcoin averaged between $0.50 and $2.50, but was also prone to spikes that crossed the $40 mark (more to the point, these surges were typically caused by heavy volatility in bitcoin’s price, which meant that the ten-or-so-minute delay in a transaction could cost users dearly). And high though these gas fees could be, the price would be even greater if users wanted to bid their way up the transaction queue.

There is technical progress underway to address each of these issues. Ethereum’s 2022 merge increased transactional capacity to an average of 25 TPS, but in 2023, fees still swung as high as $40.50 Buterin believes that various proposals to Ethereum 2 could increase TPS to between 2,000 and 3,000 within a few years,51 with his current roadmap for Ethereum ending with 10,000 TPS.52 Such promises seem fantastical, but keep in mind that work on Ethereum’s PoS network began before the PoW version of Ethereum even debuted, and the merge occurred 20 months after the test network launched—all of which is to say, preparations are long-running.

Many of Ethereum’s scaling solutions already help to reduce its congestion, costs, and speeds, too. Polygon, an Ethereum Layer 2, regularly achieves 7,000 TPS and claims to be capable of roughly ten times that, with fees in 2023 averaging less than $0.02.53 Then there are the alternatives to Ethereum. Solana, a “high-performance” Layer 1 alternative to Ethereum, claims to have hit 65,000 TPS on its test network and regularly achieves 800 to 8,00054 due to its novel proof-of-stake and proof-of-history architecture (though when normalizing its methodology to Ethereum, Solana’s TPS is more likely between 400 and 80055).

Yet even if 100,000 or 1,000,000 TPS is achieved, the Metaverse will need many billions to operate “on chain” and, despite the need for distributed networks of computers to validate these transactions, to do so in tens of milliseconds, not ten seconds or two minutes. As Tim Sweeney tweeted in January 2021, blockchain technology “is going places” but the “state of the art is far from the 60Hz transactional medium needed for 100M’s of concurrent users in a real-time 3D simulation.”56 Some doubt that blockchains will ever get there.

One common problem faced by all blockchains is the “trilemma,” so coined by Buterin in 2017, which refers to the interconnect trade-offs required for a blockchain to achieve “scalability” and “security.”57 A blockchain can increase its scalability (high TPS count) by reducing decentralization or reducing security, but one of the two must give. And increased security means less scalability, as does greater decentralization.

Polygon has a capped validator network of only 100, and the top 10 holders (mostly the blockchain’s founders, foundation, employees, and advisors) own roughly 66% of total token supply.58 In contrast, there are more than 500,000 Ethereum validators—who can join permissionlessly—and the top 10 holders own less than 10%.59 In 2022, a prominent investor alleged that Polygon’s “admin key” is controlled by a multisignature contract that requires approval from only five of the eight eligible signees (four of whom founded the network, with the remaining four selected by the foundation) and could therefore be used to hijack billions in tokens.60 In 2021, Polygon paid a $2 million bounty to a white hat hacker who identified a security exploit that would have enabled a hacker to steal $850 million. Solana’s network has averaged roughly 3,000–3,500 validators since Q1 2022,61 with the top ten holders estimated to own roughly 10%62 (though some investors sued, alleging that de facto ownership is as much as 48%63). In part due to Solana’s low fees to validators, the network crashed more than half a dozen times between September 1, 2021, and September 30, 2022, with the longest outage lasting 20 hours.64 In March 2022, hackers stole over $600 million from wallets stored on the Ronin sidechain, which had been developed by Sky Mavis so that Axie Infinity could support high volumes of low-cost transactions, despite being based on Ethereum.65 But Ronin operated with only nine validators, four of which were run by Sky Mavis, whose centralized server was hacked. Unfortunately, one of the five independent validators had loaned their key to Sky Mavis in order to speed up transactions as the game’s userbase spiked; this was enough to give hackers control of over half the network and the ability to validate fraudulent transactions.66

It’s also essential to note that TPS is not the only constraint to rapid transaction speeds, as TPS measures throughput, not the time required to establish consensus. The larger a validator network is and the more spread out it is globally, the more time is required—the speed of light endures as a constraint. This could be addressed by establishing local validator networks, but consistent with the blockchain trilemma, such a model would decrease network security as it makes it easier for said validator network to collude and harder for each validator to remain anonymous and thus unknown to would-be hackers.

Due to the many limitations of modern blockchains, dapps continue to place most of their data and operations “off chain.” Games, for that matter, simply must; there is no way to run a game engine, much less a multiplayer service, on a decentralized validator network. But with its reliance on centralized databases, critics maintain that much of the blockchain ecosystem remains under centralized control.

Recall from Chapters 7 and 8 that for data to be used, it must be run by code. An NFT may provide a user with immutable ownership of a Michael Jordan avatar, but this doesn’t assure that a game will always recognize this avatar or any of its properties. Even the game that issued that NFT might change its rules unilaterally so that the user’s ability to use that NFT is limited or effectively disabled. Take Sandbox, the crypto-focused integrated virtual world platform owned by blockchain conglomerate Animoca Brands. Section 4(a) of Sandbox’s terms and conditions lists 22 “Prohibited Activities.” Section 4(b) warns that:

“If we reasonably believe that you are engaged in any of the category b prohibited activities, in addition to our right to immediately suspend or terminate your user account and/or delete your premium NFT’s images and descriptions from the platform, we also reserve the right, at our sole and absolute discretion, without notice or liability to you, to take any of all of the following actions: (a) to deem any transaction that look place via or as the result of such activities to be void ab initio; and/or (b) to immediately confiscate any premium NFTs (including their underlying NFTs) that were purchased or acquired as the result of such activities.”67

While the terms of use list specific “prohibited activities” whose potential harm is evident (such as distributing viruses), at least in theory, Sandbox could change that list tomorrow to prohibit any conduct it so chooses. Certainly, Sandbox does not benefit from taking such steps, but the mere fact that it has the legal right to take those steps, even to the point of confiscating an NFT, makes the technical distinction between decentralized NFTs and centralized assets seem trivial—either way, it’s trust, not “immutability,” that keeps the system together. Some virtual games are constantly changing how their code interprets various NFTs so that their games can stay fresh and reward new forms of play. This was the approach used by Sky Mavis, which frequently alters the skill sets or powers of its Axies and tweaks what they can earn, too. It’s hard to say ownership is immutable if one’s ability to use a good that one owns is so easily and fundamentally changed.

Applications such as Sandbox and Axie Infinity also point to the limits of dapp-versus-dapp competition, such as that between Uniswap and Sushiswap. These latter two apps boast little custom code, have negligible server costs, and involve no proprietary IP, with the business primarily concerning assets developed by outside parties. But the code of Sandbox and Axie Infinity is protected, the costs of operations are high, and their IP cannot legally be repurposed even though their NFTs can be read by other developers. Building a comparable offering with a comparable userbase is not easy. In this regard, competing with a hit blockchain game is not much different from, nor much easier than, competing with those of Activision Blizzard or Warner Bros. Interactive—yes, a developer could offer a game that’s “better” or “cheaper” or that “offers better rights,” but that’s just part of the challenge.

These examples expand into DAOs, as well. When CityDAO passed a motion to reduce voting stakes to the rounded-down square root of the number of tokens held, it forcibly diluted 12.3% of the other members of its DAO—and by varying degrees! A member that had 25 votes was diluted to 5, a net loss of 80%, whereas a user that had 4 diluted to 2, a net loss of 50%. And while CityDAO’s developmental lease for its Colorado site is clear that the DAO maintains the deed and right to rescind the NFT, such clauses show that the NFT is primarily ceremonial and, more often than not, subordinate to classical property law.

Consensus-based actions that target or disadvantage individual users or even groups are not uncommon in crypto. In May 2023, a group of Decentraland users put forward a motion to mark a given district as “stolen” on the platform’s marketplace, which would prevent its owner from selling the district on Decentraland and impair the price they might receive on third-party marketplaces.68 The petitioners argued that the user who owned “District X,” RobL#4045, had contributed less than 0.1% of the district’s total real estate, gained control over the entire district through governance failures, removed the rights of all other contributors to the district after gaining control over it, then refused to provide financial disclosures relating to the district income and instead sought opportunities to sell it for personal gain in the “7 figures.”69 The motion was denied, even though 37 users voted in favor, only 16 voted no, and 2 abstained. The problem? The nays had an average “voting power” that was 3.1 times higher than the yays.70

Blurry Seas

In some cases, dapp owners and users alike will target the rights of a minority group—and in doing so, potentially imperil the overall future of Web3. The best example here might be in NFTs.

Although many consider the royalty model of NFTs to be one of its most important features, these payouts are not programmatic or trustless, unlike the smart contract that operates the NFT and executes the transfer of an NFT. Instead, when an NFT is minted to the blockchain, code is included that specifies what portion (typically 5%–10%) of all subsequent sales of that NFT should be paid out to a wallet other than that of the seller. For years NFT marketplaces ensured that whenever they facilitated a transaction, these royalty payments occurred.

In October 2022, the Solana NFT marketplace Magic Eden announced that it would be shifting to a “royalty-optional” model, with sellers able to choose whether they would like to honor the royalty or instead keep all (or half) of it themselves. Though this policy shift angered NFT creators, few of whom knew that royalties could be ignored and many of whom launched NFTs precisely in order to reap these very payments, Magic Eden was responding to problems in its own market. Six months earlier, new competitors had emerged that used “royalty-optional” sales to differentiate from Magic Eden, which held 90% market share. And compete they did. By early September, Magic Eden’s market share had fallen below 80%, and by the time of its policy change, it was under 60%.71 Stephen Hess, Magic Eden’s then CEO, defended his move by pointing out that enforcing royalties on his marketplace would have “little effect” if the blockchain ecosystem continued to support marketplaces that did not72 and reminded critics that three months earlier, his company had touted an in-development NFT standard that would have guaranteed royalty payments, but had found little support.73 Perhaps, Hess speculated, the future of NFTs would be multi–asset class—spanning untradable soulbound NFTs, royalty-optional NFTs, royalty-mandated NFTs, unchangeable NFTs, and so on.74

A week after Magic Eden dropped its royalties, the Ethereum-only NFT marketplace Blur launched with the hopes of displacing market leader OpenSea, which supported NFTs across five different blockchains and had maintained 50%–90% market share among Ethereum NFTs throughout the crypto boom and crash.75 Like Magic Eden, Blur enabled sellers to skip royalties. It also took no sales commission, undercutting OpenSea by 2.5%, and, like Sushiswap, announced it would issue $BLUR tokens to users based on their trading volume.

Within a month of Blur’s mid-October debut, OpenSea had lost 15 points of market share to Blur, which had just hit the 20% mark.76 In response, OpenSea announced it would no longer enforce royalties for all NFTs—only those which were minted (or updated) to use its “Seaport protocol,” which would prevent these NFTs from being sold on marketplaces that did not honor royalties. “Make no mistake,” OpenSea’s CEO, Devin Finzer, wrote in a blog post, “technical decisions like this involve trade-offs: enforcing creator fees on chain requires sacrificing some of the censorship-resistant and permissionless nature of NFTs.” Finzer’s language was similar to that of Hess’s months earlier, who had written, “Royalty-enforcement solutions have trade-offs. Adopting them requires us to rethink what ‘ownership’ means. The concept would have to become more conditional, where creators would retain some rights to alter an NFT’s functions depending on user behavior.… In order for protocol-enabled royalty enforcement to work, a trend toward centralization will also need to occur. One key trade-off is that holders may not be able to freely transfer the NFT, [especially] as wallets don’t support these new technologies or standards at the outset.”77

Days after OpenSea announced its blocking code, Blur announced that it would offer its own blocking tools, while also offering more $BLUR tokens to traders who chose to pay full royalties. By the end of the year, Blur provided an update that disappointed NFT creators—their token incentives had underperformed and most sellers were still not supporting full royalties. As a result, the marketplace would mandate royalties, but only at 0.5%—a tenth of what the average NFT specified—though Hess said he would try to slowly increase that rate to 1.0%, 1.5%, 2%, and so on should the market support such increases.78 Blur continued to enforce full royalties on collections that were updated to include (or for newer releases, were issued with) marketplace-restrictive protocols or express permission lists.

By January 2023, Blur and OpenSea were consistently tied in market share at 40%–50% each. By February 2, Blur discovered a way to integrate OpenSea’s Seaport protocol into its marketplace, thereby allowing NFTs blocked from Blur to be sold there nevertheless (though Blur committed to enforcing full royalties for relevant collections).79 A week later, Blur completed the first drop of $BLUR tokens, netting some users millions of dollars as a result.80 Blur’s market share spiked to 75% by mid-February—all at OpenSea’s expense.81

Not long after, Blur alleged that OpenSea “automatically sets royalties to optional when they detect trading on Blur,” which “forced” creators to choose between the two platforms. As such, Blur was updating its policy once again—this time to a four-category system.82 The first category covered NFTs that were written to block OpenSea. In these cases, Blur would ensure full royalties. The second category covered NFTs that blocked neither OpenSea nor Blur, but did block royalty-optional marketplaces. These, too, would receive full royalties when sold on Blur. But if an NFT used the Seaport protocol to try to block Blur (and other royalty-free marketplaces), Blur would continue to use its workaround to make these NFTs available for sale on its marketplace, and these NFTs would receive only a 0.5% royalty. The last category was NFTs with no blocks whatsoever, which would also be limited to a 0.5% royalty. In response, OpenSea announced it would shift to a minimum of 0.5% royalty on all NFTs that did not use Seaport (or like substitutes), while removing Blur from its Seaport blocklist.83

In August 2023, OpenSea finally admitted defeat. In a blog post that was widely criticized online—even by OpenSea investor Mark Cuban—Finzer announced that his marketplace would no longer enforce royalties. “[Blocklists] depended on support from everyone in the ecosystem to be successful,” Finzer wrote, “and that just didn’t happen.” He was right. Over the previous 12 months, the effective royalty rate paid on NFTs across all major blockchains and marketplaces had fallen from a more or less stable 5% to around 0.55%.84 In response, Yuga Labs, the maker of Bored Ape Yacht Club, announced that it would update its Bored Ape NFTs to block sales on OpenSea, having blocked Blur in January 2023.85 Since 2021, the company had netted over $175 million in royalties but had seen the share of Bored Ape buyers that paid full royalties fall from 100% to 5% between August 2022 and February 2023.86

While Blur is often blamed for the end of NFT royalties, its fight with OpenSea masks other truths. For one, there is no consistent evidence that dapp-versus-dapp competition is always good for the marketplace. And to that end, it’s notable that the d in “dapp” stems from the fact that they run on a decentralized network, not that their ownership structure is decentralized. In most cases, the dapp’s founder or founding team will hold a large portion of the dapp’s tokens out of the natural belief that the dapp will succeed and its tokens will therefore increase in value. As such, these individuals may have the ability to alter the dapp at will, or at least play a strong (and potentially blocking) role in its development over time.

The fight over NFT royalties also reveals the limitations of immutability and the realities of human commerce. That NFTs could be updated to prohibit various marketplaces or trades is proof that their much-touted code-based ownership rights are fewer than believed and that even when using decentralized records, customers are at the mercy of centralized entities. There are potential solutions to this issue, but none is enviable. The first requires NFTs to be minted without the ability for updates (or “upgrades”). This functionality has existed for years, but it’s rarely adopted because of the cost of permanence. If an NBA Top Shot, as an example, cannot be modified, then a moment that captured a 2D version of a Michael Jordan dunk could never be upgraded to VR—and only new NFTs could offer that sort of experience. Similarly, this NFT could never be transformed with use, or modified to unlock a product, experience, or any other sort of capability that had yet to be imagined at the time it was minted. Now, the owner of this “locked” NFT could be issued a new NFT, which provides the above functionality based on ownership of the original NFT but is essentially the same problem: the utility and value of the core NFT depends on the actions of a centralized entity.

Royalty enforcement faces similar challenges. While the market may eventually adopt a new NFT standard that does force royalties, workarounds will always exist. A user could sell an NFT worth $1 million, which would generate a $50,000 royalty, for $10 in exchange for a $999,990 transfer. Though this puts the buyer at risk, the two could write a smart contract, or form a DAO, to achieve the same effect.

As Sandbox and others demonstrate, the usage rights for (and thus also the value of) an NFT might always be modified, constrained, or otherwise affected by the original rights owner, whether it’s a nonprofit DAO, a for-profit Web 2.0 concern, or a Web3 company. Similarly, ownership of an NBA Top Shots NFT does not automatically give an independent developer the right to incorporate these NFTs to make an NBA game (just as buying a physical Disney costume does not give the buyer the right to make commercial films starring as or featuring Iron Man or Elsa).

The limitations of supposed “true ownership” are extensive. Sandbox’s terms of services specifies that “By using the Services, you grant TSB a worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-free, perpetual, irrevocable, sub-licensable (through multiple tiers), transferable right and license to use, reproduce, publicly display, distribute and adapt the publicly shared Assets and Games for the purposes of developing, distributing, providing, improving, and promoting the Services, our activities, and your publicly shared Assets and Games. You further grant TSB the right to use your name and trademarks, if any, in connection with our use of your publicly shared Assets and Games.” In short, users might “own” the token associated with Sandbox items, but such ownership requires users to provide effectively unlimited (and alterable) rights back to Sandbox, including the right to reproduce the item and advertise its “owner,” and at no cost.87

Crypto optimists believe that over time, the market will reward those companies that fully decentralize their ownership structures, provide the greatest rights to users, and exhibit the best behavior, forcing Web 2.0 operators to convert and/or exit the market altogether. This may still happen. In the interim, though, these forces do not appear to be at work. Instead, individuals, businesses, and organizations of all kinds operate under laws—hence terms of service, and government registrations—calling into question the purpose of partial decentralization. Trillions of dollars of value are exchanged annually through centralized databases that are more efficient and just as reliant on the law for enforcement.

The law provides a way to support the budding Metaverse. Epic Games’ Unreal license to developers is written such that licensees have indefinite rights to one specific Unreal Engine build.88 Epic can still change its license for subsequent builds and updates—and giving away such a right would be financially impractical and probably harmful to developers over the long run. But the result of this policy is that developers need not worry that by choosing to use Unreal, they’re forever reliant upon the whims, desires, and leadership of Epic. And as the Unreal Engine license allows developers nearly free rein for customizations and third-party integrations, developers can choose not to use future updates and instead build their own in lieu of whatever Epic adds in future releases.

In 2021, Epic made another important modification to its Unreal Engine license: it gave up the right to terminate that license, even in instances where a developer had failed to make an outstanding payment or violated the agreement outright. Instead, Epic would need to take its customer to court to mandate payment or win an injunction that would allow it to suspend support of the developer’s app.89 This makes it harder, slower, and costlier for Epic to enforce its rules, but the policy is designed to build trust with developers, which Epic hopes will be good business overall, while placing pressure on “powerful companies” that use “termination of contracts to exert control” and act as “judge, jury, and executioner.”90

Blocking and Tackling

By the start of 2024, venture capital funds, private equity firms, and hedge funds have invested over $80 billion directly into crypto and blockchain start-ups since 2012, a sum that excludes the purchase of NFTs, DAO and dapp tokens, and cryptocurrencies that were made through secondary trading platforms, marketplaces, and exchanges such as Coinbase, OpenSea, and Uniswap; retail investment is similarly excluded.

Expecting world-changing solutions from such world-changing figures is reasonable, though these sums need to be put in context. Over half of crypto investment occurred after December 2021, and at the start of 2024, barely one in six dollars has been at work for more than four years. Rebuilding the internet, and society with it, takes time. Eighty billion dollars is probably close to Facebook’s and Apple’s combined Metaverse investments, which likewise have yet to take off or, in some cases, debut. At the same time, there is not much evidence that the next great technology companies are emerging from the Web3 community—let alone those which might rival and force change from giants such as Apple and Google.

Some analysts now speculate that “tokenomics” may actually be a bug, not a feature, of crypto entrepreneurship.91 It’s possible that such structures reward hype and quick financial returns to the detriment of the quiet, long-term efforts that have, on balance, created the world’s most enduring corporations—and its most significant nonprofits, too. Another issue relates to market feedback. By providing early users, customers, and partners with large volumes of tokens, it’s theoretically easier for an entrepreneur to drive adoption and set in motion a “flywheel,” but it can also be hard to determine how much of their product’s usage reflects “product-market fit” versus speculation from those who don’t even care what the product does or doesn’t do, or why.

It’s also clear that tokenomics alone cannot differentiate a platform—and might not start its flywheel, either. Integrated virtual world platforms such as Decentraland (which opened publicly in February 2020, with parcels available for sale since 2017) and The Sandbox (2021 and 2017) promised that their blockchain foundations would allow them to rapidly accumulate users and developers and ultimately outmaneuver Web 2.0 giants such as Roblox and Minecraft. In 2022, Sandbox reported that it had 1.3 million total players throughout the year, with an average of 200,000 monthly players, and 30,000 to 40,000 daily players, while Decentraland claimed 57,000 average monthly users.92 As Apple’s iOS, Microsoft’s Xbox, Nintendo’s Switch, and Sony’s PlayStation all prohibit crypto, blockchain IVWPs face a lower user ceiling than non-blockchain IVWPs. Even so, the gap between these services and Web 2.0 IVWPs is astounding—in 2022, an average of 39,000 users logged on to Roblox each minute.93 Reports also suggest that most of those that log on to Sandbox and Decentraland do so not to play these titles but instead to access their wallets or trade game-related NFTs and other tokens.94 Developer investment is equally lackluster (and partly responsible for the poor user numbers). In March 2024, Sandbox announced more than 1,000 user-generated experiences were available on the two-year old platform.95 In contrast, Fortnite Creative had added nearly 100,000 new worlds in the previously year alone, reaching an average of 600 each day.96 And during 2022, Roblox reported it was growing by 15,000 experiences per day.97

In 2024, most enthusiasm for the blockchain now focuses on financial use cases, which are broadly termed “DeFi,” as in “decentralized finance.” There are obvious benefits to reducing the cost of capital formation and improving payment delivery. At the same time, regulators spent much of 2023 arguing that many token offerings are securities—including those of major Layer 2s like Polygon and centralized Layer 1s such as Solana and Top Shot maker Dapper Labs’ Flow—alongside many of the tokens used to fund or participate in dapps and DAOs, and even some NFT collections.98 Securities that are available to the public require their issuers to register their offerings, provide various public disclosures, agree to audits and oversight, and face legal consequences for misrepresentations and other gaps. These issuers, and those that sell these supposed securities, such as Robinhood or Coinbase, must also ensure that they “know their customer” to comply with federal provisions designed to limit money laundering and facilitate tax collection, and cannot sell some of these securities to unaccredited investors. In turn, Web3 proponents (among others) point out that these requirements often benefit the already wealthy and discriminate against the poor, represent a roadblock for start-ups trying to raise money, and are out of date in the digital era (especially in the case of crypto). In either case, at least part of DeFi’s scale reflects regulatory arbitrage, if not outright legal violations, rather than a technical unlock. Furthermore, the lack of oversight has had consequences.

From 2020 through 2023, more than $80 billion was verifiably laundered using cryptocurrencies, according to Chainalysis.99* At least $35 billion was verifiably stolen via hacks (primarily by attacking DeFi protocols) and through scams in which the quasi-anonymous founders or ringleaders of a DAO, dapp, or DeFi project raise money and then abscond with the proceeds.100 North Korea perpetrated at least $3.4 billion of this theft101—a sum made even more remarkable when contrasted to the country’s $25–$30 billion GDP,102 inclusive of less than $150 million in annual exports.103 At least $15 billion in customer funds has been lost as a result of legitimate organizations that, perhaps due to operating outside of typical financial regulations, mismanaged the funds.104

Scant regulations are also said to have inflated many of crypto’s shocking sales figures. Some studies have found that as much as 70% of cryptocurrency trades may be “wash trades”105—those in which the buyer and seller are the same person, or otherwise affiliated—as are 45% of NFT sales.106 Washing has been illegal for nearly a century in the United States due to its distortive impact on trading volumes and prices and its role in tax evasion.107

Due to the risk of theft (or immutability of mistakes), need for regulatory compliance, general difficulty of blockchain systems, high and unreliable gas fees, and transaction times, most cryptocurrency trading continues to occur through “centralized exchanges” (CEXs) such as Binance, Coinbase, and Robinhood, in addition to traditional banks such as Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase, rather than “decentralized exchanges” (DEXs) like Uniswap and Sushiswap, which run on the blockchain. Between January 1, 2021, and September 1, 2023, close to $44 trillion was traded through CEXs, with DEX volumes less than $3 trillion (or 6%).108 CEXs effectively defeat the purpose of blockchains in the first place, as they manage user funds no differently than a traditional bank does US dollars or Euros—through centralized database entries that reallocate monies between users and accounts, rather than by shifting these resources to and from them. CEX trades also do not involve any updates to the blockchain—which is precisely why they are so fast, reliable, and low in fees. To protect its customers from fraud, stolen wares, and counterfeit NFTs, OpenSea has also launched various verification, banning, and “copymint” services—none of which are unreasonable solutions, but they too illuminate the limitations and problems of “trustless,” “permissionless,” and “immutable” code and the centralization that springs up to address them.

To the Moon, Back Down to Earth, and Then Maybe Back Again?

Having long been conflated with the Metaverse, crypto’s role in building it is now unclear. Though its systems continue to improve, blockchain funding has become scarce, many once-promising start-ups now languish, and users are hard to come by. Many blockchain advocates now exhibit disinterest, disappointment, or even disdain.

Not long after Jensen Huang declared in February 2022 that “blockchains [are] going to be here for a long time and [will] be a fundamental new form of computing,”109 he stopped mentioning the topic altogether. Throughout 2022, Facebook added the ability for select users to display, mint, trade, buy, and sell Ethereum, Solana, Flow, and Polygon-based NFTs on Instagram and Facebook.110 In March 2023, Facebook removed this functionality before it was even launched to most users, with the company stating that instead, it would focus on “areas where we can make impact at scale.”111 Having described blockchains as “the combination of everyone’s computer” in 2017, Sweeney pronounced in early 2021 that a “blockchain based underpinning for an open Metaverse … is the most plausible path toward an ultimate long term open framework where everyone’s in control of their own presence, free of gatekeeping,” though he called cryptocurrency investment “a wild, speculative mess.”112 Eight months later, Sweeney remained optimistic about the potential in blockchain, but was also discouraged by its misuse, declaring that Epic Games wasn’t “touching NFTs as the whole field is currently tangled up with an intractable mix of scams, interesting decentralized tech foundations, and scams.”113 After Steam banned games that used NFTs, Sweeney announced that “Epic Games Store will [continue to] welcome games that make use of blockchain tech provided they follow the relevant laws, disclose their terms, and are age-rated by an appropriate group. Though Epic’s not using crypto in our games, we welcome innovation in the areas of technology and finance.”114 By the end of 2022, Sweeney’s thoughts were best summarized by the one-word tweet “Craptocurrency,”115 which he quote-tweeted in early January 2023 with “Kleptocurrency.”116

To many in the crypto community, the retreat of big tech and “traditional finance” from Web3 is a mostly positive development. It reduces the influence of these companies, while revealing their talk of openness to be just that: talk. Going forward, development will be slower, less well funded, and less high profile, but it will continue and perhaps benefit from less day-to-day scrutiny.

Those who still believe in blockchain-based decentralized computing are right to point out that its technologies are immature. The first NFT debuted in 2014, with Ethereum launching in 2015, the first dapp following in 2016, and the modern NFT standard (ERC-721) defined in 2017. Most usage of these technologies has occurred since the start of 2021, as has two-thirds of funding, but there has been little change to underlying structures or protocols during this time. For that matter, it’s important to reiterate that the “best” technical solution rarely wins—those that are adopted do. It’s hard enough to create any interoperable entitlements system, let alone one that sees widespread usage and scales into trillions of transactions. Perhaps it’s better to prioritize deployment, rather than blueprint altogether new solutions that, if adopted, would be superior.

A number of Metaverse aspirants do still see the blockchain as the “most plausible path” to an open Metaverse. In December 2022, Activision Blizzard’s chief operating officer Daniel Alegre decamped to become president and COO of Yuga Labs, which the company said would “expedite its ambitious vision for blockchain gaming, metaverse development, and community-building.”117 Four months later, Mike Seavers, Epic’s executive vice president of development and Riot Games’ former chief technology officer, announced he was also joining Yuga Labs, taking the position as CTO.118 In 2019, Sam Altman, the cofounder and CEO of OpenAI, cofounded Worldcoin, which intended to provide online authentication to all of us humanity using iris scans that were secured and validated by its Ethereum-based Layer 2 blockchain, which also issued users with its namesake token in exchange for scanning their iris. By May 2023, Worldcoin had raised nearly $250 million from venture funds such as Andreessen Horowitz, MultiCoin, and Khosla Ventures, as well as individuals such as FTX cofounder Sam Bankman-Freid and LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, with the company exiting beta two months later.

And Neal Stephenson? In 2022, he announced that he was co-founding a new blockchain-focused company, Lamina1, with former Bitcoin Foundation chairman Peter Vessenes. The purpose of the company was to develop a Layer 1 blockchain that could serve as the “foundational layer” of an “open metaverse” that would enforce royalties, foster interoperability, resist the “cooptative” controls of “mega-platforms or corporations,” and be “owned by its citizens.”119
