Chapter 12 THE ROLE AND ACCELERANTS OF AI

Chapter 3 provided a brief timeline of artificial intelligence, from the philosophical theory of thinking computers in the 1930s to the emergence of transformer models capable of answering complex queries, crafting detailed images, and writing everything from short emails to sophisticated code and erudite essays in a matter of minutes.

One of the more overlooked pioneers in AI’s history is the American cognitive and computer scientist Marvin Minsky.* In 1959, Minsky co-founded the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory† with John McCarthy, who had coined the term “artificial intelligence” four years earlier and would debut his LISP programming language in 1960.1 Minsky’s 1969 book, Perceptrons, which was co-authored by South African mathematician and computer scientist Seymour Papert, is regarded as one of the foundational texts of the field of artificial neural networks. In the run-up to the book, Minsky had served as an advisor on Stanley Kubrick’s landmark 1968 film, 2001: A Space Odyssey; the character Victor Kaminski was named after Minsky.2 In Arthur C. Clarke’s novelization of the film, which expanded and updated his 1951 short story “The Sentinel,” Minsky is mentioned directly, with Clarke predicting that he would achieve breakthroughs in neural networks that led directly to the creation of HAL 9000.3

In the 1950s, Minsky developed‡ one of the first widely accepted definitions of AI—“the science of making machines do things that would require intelligence if done by humans”—which reflected what MIT Technology Review characterized as his belief that “the human mind was fundamentally no different than a computer.”4 Minsky’s definition was never universally embraced by AI researchers of his era, and contemporary computer scientists have largely discarded it. One issue is that tasks that were once viewed as evidence of or benchmarks for AI advances often become so routine that they are reclassified as mere “algorithms” or “computation,” rather than any form of “intelligence” at all—much less “human intelligence.” Examples here include playing chess against a human opponent or passing the Turing Test, but a particularly fun case is autocorrect.

Early versions of the autocorrect feature arguably lacked any form of “AI.” Instead, a word processor or email client simply looked up every would-be “word” a user wrote against a database of known words, identifying those that did not match any stored entries, and then listing off the entries with the greatest fit according to a ruleset that focused primarily on the number of letters shared between the nonword and a real one or the ordering of those letters. Later, spellcheck began to take into account common spelling errors, such as an ff that should have been a gh, which would otherwise mislead a correction system that was based purely on letter overlap and sequence. Still, this was not “intelligence” but a more sophisticated ruleset.

In 1993, Microsoft shipped Word 6.0, which included not just spellcheck, which had shipped with the very first edition of Word a decade earlier, but also “grammar check.” While this new feature understood various forms of “logic,” including syntax (the sequence of subjects, objects, and verbs in a sentence), conjugation (tense), and agreement (alignment among quantities and genders in a sentence), its system was still just following rules, albeit now against a more elaborate directory that included word classes (nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs), genders (in applicable languages), exceptions, and idioms. Over time, spellcheck continued to improve. By 1997, Microsoft Word could understand identity errors relating not to spelling per se but to homophones like using “accept” instead of “except.” This required the application to understand a word’s specific meaning and context in a sentence. Later, spellcheck added the ability to strive for “clarity” or “concision,” which involved understanding which words or phrases might be confusing or unnecessary. In the mid-2000s, autocorrect systems began to incorporate aggregate user behavior into their systems by measuring which words or phrases were typically selected when an error was identified—the word “lichens” might be closer to the misspelling “lichense,” but users were far more likely to pick “license” instead. This functionality enabled spellcheck programs to register and then use new words and slang, and eventually to recognize typos caused not by poor spelling but by the typical layout of a keyboard. By the 2010s, many spellcheckers could also “learn from” and then tailor their recommendations to individual users, which was particularly helpful to users writing in a nonnative language, were left-handed, suffered from a disability, or had poor typing methods, all of which tended to produce more fringe typos.

Although spellcheck might meet Minsky’s definition of artificial intelligence, few today consider it AI. Conversely, many do consider transformer models that power the large language models (LLMs) of OpenAI’s ChatGPT to be AI.§ These models have two core parts: an “encoder,” which processes, understands, and evaluates an input, and a “decoder,” which generates an output.5 When supporting an LLM, the initial work of an encoder looks similar to that of conventional language-processing models—it reviews a sentence word by word while assigning weights based on each word’s role and placement in the sentence. One of the key innovations of transformers is to then use “self-attention,” which involves reviewing all words in a sentence simultaneously to understand their internal connections and dependencies.6 The transformer model then generates a response on a word-by-word basis while paying attention to each word it generates. Given this, some analysts argue transformers are not “artificial intelligence” but “inference machines” or “reasoning engines” that deduce connections based on patterns rather than actual understanding.7 This lack of true knowledge (as a human would understand the term) also means that LLMs can sometimes “hallucinate,” as the recent lingo has it, by “generating outputs or recognizing patterns that don’t correspond to actual data or reality,” which it nevertheless believes are true.8 When this occurs, the LLM cannot be “convinced” or “taught” it is “wrong” and why. Instead, the user must alter their query to avoid generating a hallucinatory response or instruct the model to disregard specific (hallucinatory) “beliefs” or otherwise retrain the model altogether or adjust its architecture.10

Is 900 equal to 90% of 1000?

No, 900 is not equal to 90% of 1000.

To find 90% of 1000, you would multiply 1000 by 0.90.

1000 x 0.90 = 900

So, yes, 900 is actually equal to 90% of 1000. I apologize for the intial oversight.

The Limitations (and Benefits) of Self-Attention

This query, which was posed to OpenAI’s ChatGPT-4 on October 16, 2023, highlights the limitations, dynamics, and “intelligence” of self-attention models. GPT-4 understands that the user is looking to confirm whether a specified sum is the correct output from a basic mathematical problem. The model also recognizes that it has all of the information required to answer the query and correctly assembles the equation needed to do so. Despite this, GPT-4 provides the incorrect answer—one that most sixth-grade students could complete. Because “self-attention” models also make inferences from their own responses, the process of explaining its (incorrect) response then results in the model realizing it was incorrect, and providing the correct answer.

GPT-4 often fails similarly constructed equations (e.g., “Is 450 equal to 90% of 500?”) or problems (e.g., “If Hillary bakes ten cakes a week, but two full cakes are eaten each week and one goes rotten, how many does she have after three weeks?”). But if instructed to “take a breath” before answering, or “go step-by-step,” the extra iterations routinely produce more accurate answers.9 ChatGPT-4, Matthew Ball

Humankind and Machines of a Human King

The mechanics and limitations of modern transformer models highlight the second common argument against Minsky’s definition—that by using terms such as “intelligence,” “neural networks,” and “machine learning,” one is anthropomorphizing the concept of AI, which leads to misconceptions and misunderstandings regarding how these systems work, what they might achieve, and why.

Marc Benioff, the CEO and co-founder of Salesforce (which gave its LLM the name “EinsteinGPT”) has suggested “hallucinations” are just a euphemism for “lies” and that LLMs are “very convincing liars”—a problem made worse by the fact that these models don’t know they’re telling a lie and are instead quite convinced of their mistruth.11 One could argue that the propensity to lie and stick to that lie is, itself, evidence of some humanity. Sam Altman, who co-founded OpenAI and serves as CEO, purports that hallucinations are instead essential to generative AI systems—especially when they are applied to the most “human” of jobs. For example, Altman points out, early AI models have most strongly disrupted creative fields first (e.g., art, music, writing), instead of more menial and repetitive tasks, as was originally expected.12 This is only possible, according to Altman, because a generative AI model can look at existing data sets and then present this data in a new, sometimes unexpected way, adding that “if you want to look something up in a database, we already have good [technology solutions] for that.”13Andrej Karpathy, a founding member of the OpenAI team, has made similar points. In December 2023, Karpathy tweeted, “In some sense, hallucination is all LLMs do. They are dream machines. We direct their dreams with prompts. The prompts start the dream, and based on the LLM’s hazy recollection of its training documents, most of the time the result goes someplace useful. It’s only when the dreams go into deemed factually incorrect territory that we label it a ‘hallucination.’ ”14 In contrast, a search engine “takes [a user’s query] and just returns one of the most similar ‘training documents’ it has in its database, verbatim. You could say that this search engine has a ‘creativity problem.’ ”15 The solution, according to Karpathy, is not to eliminate LLM hallucinations, but to build assistants based on these same models that do not hallucinate.16

Not only is there disagreement on what constitutes AI in the first place, but even the ideas of “intelligence” and “humanity” prove uncertain—which is particularly problematic when one considers the development of so-called “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a computer program “that can perform intellectual tasks as well as, or better than, a human” (the core objective of OpenAI).17 Whereas Minsky defined AI based on whether human intelligence would otherwise be required, Larry Tesler, who pioneered human-computer interfaces at Xerox and PARC in the early 1970s and Apple in the 1980s, suggested that “intelligence is whatever machines haven’t done yet.”18 “Tesler’s theorem” is often paired with the “AI effect,” a term coined by John McCarthy to describe the “common public misperception, that as soon as AI successfully solves a problem, that solution method is no longer within the domain of AI.”¶19 To that end, Altman has said that ten years ago “a lot of people” would have said “something like GPT-4” would be AGI “[but] now, people are like, ‘well it’s like a nice little chatbot or whatever.’ ”20 In time, then, products such as GPT-3 and GPT-4, alongside DALL-E and DALL-E 2, will probably be reframed as smarter versions of “autocorrect” (i.e., probability engines) rather than AI.

Indeed, there is disagreement as to whether transformer models are the right pathway to AGI. In August 2022, the 3D graphics and VR pioneer John Carmack told Russian American computer scientist and podcaster Lex Fridman, “I am not a madman for saying that it is likely that the code for artificial general intelligence is going to be tens of thousands of lines of code, not millions of lines of code. This is code that conceivably one individual could write, unlike writing a new web browser or operating system.”21 Four months later, Carmack officially left his role as consulting CTO of Oculus at Facebook to found Keen Technologies, which, like OpenAI, aspired to build AGI. However, Carmack seems skeptical that transformer models and existing AI players will be able to build it.

In his first interview after starting the “fourth major phase of his career,”# Carmack told Dallas Innovates that the number of “billion-dollar off-ramps” for AI technologies has become a de facto obstacle to achieving true AGI.22 “There are extremely powerful things possible now in the narrow machine-learning stuff,” he said, “[but] it’s not clear those are the necessary steps to get all the way to artificial general intelligence.”23 “Most of what the mainstream is doing [this research and development is] because it’s fabulous, it’s useful … [but] there is this kind of groupthink,” Carmack went on, “that is really clear, if you look at it, about all these brilliant researchers —they all have similar backgrounds, and they’re all kind of swimming in the same direction.”24 In contrast, Carmack was optimistic about “a handful of ideas that are not the mainstream … some work from like the ’70s, ’80s, and ’90s that I actually think might be interesting, because a lot of things happened back then that didn’t pan out, just because they didn’t have enough scale. They were trying to do this on one-megahertz computers, not clusters of GPUs.”25 Even more radically, Carmack believes “the source code, the computer programming necessary for artificial general intelligence, is going to be a few tens of thousands of lines of code.”26 In contrast, the source code for the Chrome browser is 31 million lines, while Twitter is roughly 20 million, and operating systems can reach up to 100 million (depending on the definition of what’s in the operating system versus an application packaged with it).27 “You literally cannot type enough in your remaining life to write all of that code,” Carmack reported to Dallas Innovates, “but it’s my belief that I can really back up that the programming for AGI is going to be something that one person could write.”28

Synthetic Realities

Though “Tesler’s theorem” means AI is a moving target, and thus more a philosophical concept than an achievable state, it is the best way to understand the diffusion of these technologies and humanity’s shift to synthetic existence. Each year, the AI products once considered “magic” are normalized to the point that they’re considered unremarkable—even as they take on a greater role cataloging and directing human life. Meanwhile, the systems behind these AI are being created, maintained, and often updated in real time by those very same lives.

The most visible example is online recommendations. Search engines like Google, Yahoo, and WebCrawler once relied purely on “objective” data, including the number of sites linking to a given page or overall traffic, just as earlier cataloging methodologies used defined taxonomies (e.g., Dewey Decimal Classification) or alphabetization. Contemporary engines sometimes use this information, but it’s often secondary to what the engine knows about its user, including their favorite websites and their overall interests and antipathies—but always, crucially, in a comparative sense, assessing how that user compares to others making that same query. As such, the results provided by a search engine operate not by general-purpose rank-order systems but rather by AI-powered responses that target people as individuals. YouTube, Netflix, and TikTok operate similarly.

In 2024, there are myriad copies of every internet user’s personality stored on computers around the world. And though the “brain prints” established by these companies are based on pattern matching and inference, just like a transformer model, and are isolated from one another rather than cohesive, they are often a more accurate and detailed representation of how a user thinks than anything the user, their loved ones, or their psychiatrist might devise. A few years after Facebook launched, Mark Zuckerberg reportedly built a model that examined “friend relationships and communications patterns” that “could determine with about 33 percent accuracy who a user was going to be in a relationship with a week from now.”29 Facebook never confirmed the existence of this tool; if it existed at the time, it probably does not today. Yet an updated model would doubtless be more accurate—and more capable. Facebook would likely be able to predict not just which prospective mate a newly single individual would date (or at least the basics of what they’d look like) but also when and where the meetup might take place—all of which might be recommended and/or fulfilled by Facebook’s various services, in fact. And that’s before Facebook and others launch suites of devices that can track a user’s face and eyes, electrical signals skittering across their skeletal muscles, and eventually, even brain signals.

In addition to generating mental models of humanity, internet users are digitizing the real world. Facebook’s facial recognition software is based on users manually tagging their friends in billions of photo albums, a feature that launched in 2006. By 2010, Facebook was capable of automatically generating tags for users; in 2017, the social network’s facial recognition software was so accurate that it notified users whenever they were included in a photo uploaded by another user, even if that user didn’t manually tag them.30 Google first deployed facial recognition in 2008 through Picasa, with Google’s own Photos app adding the functionality in 2015 and Apple Photos doing so a year later.

In some cases, users have actively, but still unwittingly, trained AI. In 2009, Google bought the company reCAPTCHA, which used CAPTCHA challenge-response tests to validate whether an internet user was human in order to thwart bot attacks and spam. Most reCAPTCHA users did not realize that their inputs were also being used to help Google manually digitize old books and ingest its Street View scans, learn how to identify and properly orient boats, cars, and penguins, decipher human speech, and build autonomous (i.e., computer vision–based) vehicles.

Amazingly, the real-world photos that billions of users have uploaded, tagged, categorized, rotated, and transcribed also have enabled the creation of AI that can now create photographs of the real world that are more detailed than physics allow—and use these same photos to build detailed models of the real world, too.

A prominent example is high dynamic range (HDR) mode, which is available on nearly all smartphones in use today. A photo is assembled out of a series of other photos that are rapidly taken at different exposures, then scanned by a machine learning algorithm that recognizes and separates individual objects and depths, then merges these many inputs together to create a final “version” that has a better balance of highlights and shadows—plus greater detail and clarity. More recently, techniques known as Deep Fusion, Photonic Engines, and optical flow use onboard neural engines to process images on a pixel-by-pixel basis. Computer vision also allows camera applications to accurately and automatically focus on horizon lines or humans, separate foregrounds and backgrounds, alter lighting, reduce blur, and time shots to avoid human blinks and capture the “best” facial expressions.** “Night Mode” isn’t concerned with capturing what the human eye can see but rather what a smartphone’s camera can find despite the scarcity of photons.

The result is not just “better” photos but photos that are better than is possible. Unlike graphical and computing processors, which benefit from ongoing miniaturization in transistors, a process that produces more computing power per unit of space while consuming less battery and generating less heat, photographs cannot improve as light is reduced. This is why smartphone cameras remain so much thicker than the rest of the device’s body, and why smartphones choose to add a second or third camera, instead of “making the first one better.” And in contrast to cloud (or quantum) computing, there is no way for a camera in a remote location to capture more light in support. Remarkably, AI can enable a smartphone application to substitute for the data (i.e., light) it lacks to produce a photo that looks as good as, if not better than, those produced by cameras that are thousands of dollars more expensive, have lenses several times larger, and whose exposure lasts an order of magnitude longer.

The Meta Frontier

In the decades to come, AI will continue to construct increasingly detailed and multidimensional versions of human minds, identities, histories, and friendships, as well as those of society and the world at large. AI will also be instrumental in building and operating the Metaverse, and these contributions can, at least for now, be simplified into six categories: (1) Enabling a greater number of real-world items and environments to be virtualized, and at higher fidelity levels; (2) Enabling digital twins to perform more complex tasks and simulations, and for human operators to make better use of these capabilities; (3) Enabling a greater number of purely virtual items and worlds to be created, and with greater richness; (4) Enabling many Metaverse experiences to increase their fidelity, frame rate, responsiveness, and consumer usability by “beating” the laws of physics; (5) Enabling the Metaverse to be populated with highly sophisticated and responsive AI agents; and (6) Enabling greater interoperation without requiring fully standardized asset formats or codebases, or otherwise requiring developers and businesses to build a nearly infinite number of permutations for every world and item they create.

#1: Virtualizing the Real World

In recent years, photo-based neural models have progressed from the 2D memorialization of 3D experiences to reproducing and then maintaining them. Apple’s Object Capture, which debuted in 2021, enables iPhone and iPad users to convert real-world objects into ultrahigh-definition virtual ones by taking a series of photos from different angles. Neural radiance fields, or NeRFs, can convert a few dozen 2D images into highly detailed, comprehensive, and immersive models of rooms, facilities, and even outdoor spaces. In this case, a neural model “fills in” information not contained in input photographs, such as the underside of a table, a chair’s unseen legs, or the knobs on a stove, but can also generate the materials in that image (reflective versus matte wood, say) and their attributes (firmness versus softness). Without these sorts of capabilities, Apple Vision Pro would not be able to offer immersive “memories” unless a user owned a half dozen cameras and staged them around their family gatherings, and it would be both financially and operationally infeasible for most companies to produce, let alone maintain, precise digital twins of the real world. Microsoft Flight Simulator is testament to that fact—its 500,000,000-square-kilometer map, 2 trillion unique trees, and 1.5 billion buildings were generated through Microsoft’s machine learning and geospatial computing suites. Most companies don’t need such a model—just a twin of their factory, office tower, or retail store—but they have far fewer employees and profit than Microsoft, too.

#2: Improving and Using Digital Twins

Not long after the Metaverse hype cycle began in 2021, manufacturers of all kinds rushed to announce they were building their own digital twin—one that would enable both cost savings and productivity improvements, reduce jobsite injuries while growing throughput, revolutionize their industry but play to their existing strengths, and so on. Three years later, there’s little evidence of these achievements and considerably less chatter. Much of the disappointment stems from the fact that it takes humans far longer to learn how to effectively use a digital twin than to construct one (as is always the case with software). Another hindrance is the extent that the facility represented by the twin has sufficient capabilities (i.e., Internet of Things, or IoT, sensors and automation functionality) to make extensive use of this twin. The major constraint, however, is AI.

Unity Technologies describes twins as having five “levels.”31 Level One twins are little more than a virtual version of a physical miniature model—they reflect a “real-world” space, typically with inconsistent proportions and some limited functionality (e.g., the ability to shift a truck from one stall to another). In some cases, these exist purely for demonstration purposes—intended to prove that a technical group can build such a model or to demonstrate the company’s commitment to “the Metaverse” to shareholders. More useful versions exist to help humans understand and explore a physical space without setting foot inside it, or to plan for that physical space (think back to Strategic Development Partners, Imerza, and the Unreal-based Tampa Water Street project from Chapter 8). Regardless, the life span of Level One twins is usually short, as they represent a space at a fixed point in time; as that space changes, so does the utility of the model.

Level Two twins are “connected twins.” At this point, a virtual model receives and visualizes data from the real-world environment it represents. That data may be reflected through 3D assets (e.g., a truck may be represented as a 3D model placed in a stall) or labels (a digital placard indicating that a stall is occupied and by which truck) and may be generated through IoT devices and sensors, or submitted by human staff. Level Three twins are “predictive twins,” which are essentially models that use the data captured by connected twins to simulate what could happen, or (better) what is likely to happen, in the future. Such predictions can include predicting bottlenecks on a factory floor, daily productivity, overheating equipment, delays relating to late arrivals, and so on. Under some definitions or implementations, a predictive twin may deploy “AI,” whereas others might just be 3D representations of information that could be represented in a 2D Microsoft Excel spreadsheet.

Level Four twins are “prescriptive twins.” Here, AI makes recommendations as extensive as how a facility should be organized, prioritized, scheduled, or staffed; how to optimize its use of materials; and how to triage burgeoning problems like late shipment arrivals, slow unloading processes, mechanical malfunctions, and so on. It is at Level Four that the twin shifts from exclusively supporting human work to guiding it. The final level is an “autonomous twin,” which involves the AI in Level Four being provided with the ability to partly “run” the facility. In this case, the AI might dynamically assign parking stalls, alter production flows, or preemptively cool rooms based on the knowledge of how many people will eventually be in it, for how long, and doing what activity. There is a parallel continuum that is not mentioned in Unity’s framework but applies to each of its upper four levels: integration into other digital twins. These outside twins might represent the operations of the city in which the twin is situated, the productivity (vehicular fleets) of the twin’s customers or suppliers, global meteorological conditions, and so on, all of which can aid prediction, prescription, and autonomous decision-making.

The value of a digital twin increases with each level, and as it increases, so does the number of outside twins it connects to and the degree to which it does so. These augmentations also substantially increase the reliance upon AI. Without AI, Level Five can’t be achieved, only rudimentary versions of Levels Four and Three can be attained, and integration into other twins quickly becomes impractical. Human operators simply cannot process as many decisions as reliably and accurately as a computer system, nor can they as quickly translate these decisions into actions. Still, the minimum threshold for AI is high. Beyond optimizing a facility’s operations, AI must be able to minimize the risk of human injury (and intervene when necessary), effectively explain a decision to humans in real time, and respond to human suggestions and requests, too.

#3: Building Out the (Purely) Virtual World

The need for AI is also apparent when it comes to creating synthetic worlds that are entirely separate from the “real world.” With nearly six million virtual worlds made on Roblox annually, alongside the millions more created on Minecraft and Fortnite, it’s clear that the desire to create such spaces is widespread. Yet most of these worlds are basic in their functionality, detail, and scope and fall far short of the imaginations and aspirations of their creators. All great art, to be sure, requires extraordinary investments in training, experience, and, frankly, mental anguish. But the underlying elements of a virtual world are not as easily abstracted as a note, word, image, or number, nor as easily produced individually or assembled into a chord, sentence, picture, or spreadsheet. Moreover, the creation of a virtual world requires each of these other art forms—there is no point visiting a virtual world that has no music, imagery, or operations. Advances in generative AI, machine learning, computer vision, and semantic recognition will soon enable users to create, modify, and run entire virtual worlds in a matter of seconds and minutes using nothing but a few typed or spoken sentences (David Baszucki, Roblox’s founder and CEO, estimates that such functionality will arrive before 202832). The result will be an increase in the number of worlds in the Metaverse, and their quality will spike too.

AI’s ability to autonomously operate within the guardrails of a creator will enable further innovations. Hello Games’ 2016 title No Man’s Sky allows users to traverse a nearly infinite universe with up to 18 quadrillion unique planets, each one fully filled with its own geography, flora and fauna that can be named and harvested, and potentially the operating bases of other players. This scale—or anything remotely near it—is achieved only through procedural content generation that is capable of both generating incredible diversity and ensuring compatibility and coherence across these creations.

#4: “Beating” the Laws of Physics

As detailed throughout this book, the construction and operation of the Metaverse is in constant competition with the actual universe (at least as it’s known today). Yet using AI, it is possible to perform tasks faster than physics would allow, or using less equipment than physics might require, or to higher fidelity, and so on.

Take Amazon’s much-touted “Just Walk Out” (JWO) technology as an example. Using a network of cameras (as many as 300 per 1,000 square feet) and sensors, powered by AWS’s computer vision and machine learning suites, Amazon is able to track which items users, as they wander around its grocery and convenience stores, pick up and hold on to or pick up and put back down again—and then charge the customers without ever needing them to “check out” or scan their items.33 Crucially, its JWO did this without reliance on any facial scanning or biometric user data.34 Instead, JWO tracked customers based purely on their body size, gait, and paths.35 When it launched the first Amazon Go store in December 2016, Amazon reportedly hoped that as many as 2,000 stores would be using its JWO tools by 2026, including independent licensors of its technology.36 In 2018, Bloomberg claimed that Amazon’s target had increased to 3,000 by 2021.37 But fully two years after that target, JWO was being used in only 60 or so Amazon-owned stores, some of which the company announced would be closing.38 It turned out that Amazon’s computer vision technology was costly to deploy and still required substantial support from human staff. The Information reported that there were as many as “1,000 people in India working on Just Walk Out as of mid-2022 whose jobs included manually reviewing transactions”—with customer bills featuring appropriate adjustments—“and labeling images from videos to train Just Walk Out’s machine learning model.”39 In 2024, Amazon announced that newly constructed Amazon Fresh grocery stores would not offer JWO and that most of the company’s existing locations would be overhauled to “version two” stores that replaced JWO with “Dash Carts” that enabled customers to scan their grocery items for purchase as these items were placed into their shopping cart.40 Amazon’s smaller, convenience store-styled Amazon Go stores were expected to keep JWO.

Humans may not need JWO for grocery shopping, but such technologies are essential for factories and plants such as those used to assemble cars or produce laundry detergent pods. To do so, computer vision will need to improve in accuracy, even as it increases the size of the environment it’s tracking, but without simply increasing the density and quality of the cameras and sensors that support the facility. Starline, as reviewed in Chapter 3, shows what’s possible. By leveraging two years of advances in AI, Google was able to maintain Starline’s image quality and fidelity, even as it substituted 12 high-end cameras and sensors with just a “few standard”—a change that not only substantially dropped the cost of the device, it shrunk it from the size of a restaurant booth to that of a midsize TV sitting on a minifridge.

Other examples concern consumer-worn hardware such as lightweight optical AR glasses (which will become increasingly important to navigating a world run through AI-powered simulation). These devices will never be able to store enough referential information to recognize the entire world—or even a user’s typical environment—nor the attendant details of how to interact with its digital and AR inputs and controls. Instead, neural networks will be used to process the world in real time, with user “brain prints” helping the device predict what is and isn’t of use and prioritize computational resources to suit those conclusions. In the case of passthrough AR and MR, real-time artificial intelligence is already required to assemble and correct live video footage captured from various external cameras, each one facing a slightly different direction and from a different position, and to support foveated and varifocal rendering.

Another example harkens back to Chapter 6, which examined how game engines use “level-of-detail” and “occlusion” systems to constantly load and unload visual detail and even objects in order to minimize computational needs. Historically, these solutions have been purely rules-based—a tree’s bark texture would be loaded only if the player was within a given distance from the tree, and objects located behind an obstacle would be loaded only once the player changed position and could see them. The advent of hybrid cloud-local data storage has required applications like Microsoft Flight Simulator to predict where its users might go and preemptively download data to ensure its availability when needed. This model is similar to that used by many smartphone applications and digital assistants, which might pre-download a recommended video or preload the webpage leading to the second entry in a ten-item search result based on the expectation the user will select it, saving that user seconds in wait time. Some believe that device-side AI can also be used to improve frame rates and resolution fidelity without needing to transmit much (or any) incremental data to that device or construct it with far more powerful CPUs/GPUs. Imagine, as an example, playing a game of Call of Duty Mobile on a mid-range iPad that could render no more than 1K at 60 fps and whose asset information (e.g., a car, shrub, mountain) contained only mid-range-fidelity detail. As the user plays the title, computer vision might be scanning the entire rendered frame, determining what each individual item (the car, shrub, mountain) is likely to be, then generatively “upscaling” the detail. And after every rendered frame, the device’s processor(s) are generating (not rendering) another frame that is shown to the user before the next rendered frame and which sits in between the two renders, based on what is likely to happen in the interim. The result is a doubled frame rate, but effectively no increase in transmitted data or GPU rendering, and instead only a minor tax on largely unused CPU resources.

Finally, there are netcode algorithms, which were discussed in Chapter 5. Netcode is used to sustain online multiplayer gaming experiences in the event of spiking network latency or packet loss by predicting what would have happened and/or coherently resolving conflicting information. Unfortunately, modern netcode doesn’t scale well as the number of players, complexity of their inputs, or variability in latency increases—predicting the next second of a two-player 2D fighting game is much simpler than in fully immersive social venues, but some expect that transformer models or other solutions will improve these predictions and, in doing so, bring more users into the Metaverse.

#5: Populating the Metaverse with AI Agents

A related area of focus is “non-playable characters” (NPCs), with developers using transformer models to imbue these agents with rich and dynamic personalities, skills, and desires. In April 2023, researchers at Google and Stanford published a paper summarizing a two-day simulation designed to test the believability of virtual agents powered by large language models. Specifically, the researchers assembled a town equipped with houses and dormitories, colleges and offices, grocery stores and bars, and populated with 25 autonomous agents powered by large language models modified “to store a complete record of the agent’s experiences using natural language, synthesize those memories over time into higher-level reflections, and retrieve them dynamically to plan behavior.”41 During the simulation, characters organically formed routines, while also establishing friendships, sharing information learned, and developing professional interests. After researchers prompted one NPC to host a Valentine’s Day party, the NPC opted to invite her friends to the party, roping in customers at the café where she worked, too, and asked her closest friend to help them with decorating. The friend did so and revealed that she had a crush on another NPC, whom the NPC then also invited to the party. At the party’s scheduled 5 p.m. start, all five NPCs arrived on time, having rearranged their days to accommodate the event—including the crush, “Klaus.”

After the simulation concluded, each behavior of each agent was reviewed and evaluated for believability using common behavioral models (e.g., TrueSkill) and variance tests (Kruskal-Wallis). Each agent was also “interviewed” for “self-knowledge” (details on their life), “memory” (such as whom they met and what happened during the simulation), “plans” (what they will do and when), “reactions” (what they would do in case of a fire or upon seeing a friend on the street), and “reflections” (what inspires them or what they would buy for another agent’s birthday). Independent human “crowdworkers” were also hired and asked to watch each agent’s two-day experience and then role-play as these agents while answering the same questions. The Stanford/Google researchers found that the LLM agents consistently outperformed their human role-players and exceeded the believability benchmark.

The goal of the Google/Stanford simulation was not to prove that bots can be more human than human—nor did it. Instead, the intent was to see if LLMs could be used to create AI that could populate “metaverses,” operate socially capable robots in the real world, be used to “train people on how to handle rare yet difficult interpersonal situations” or “test social science theories,” create “non-playable game characters that can navigate complex human relationships,” or serve as a truly personalized digital assistant.42 The answer seems to be yes and the support these AI might provide continues to grow. In 2023, a pair of professors at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School ran a study to determine whether MBA students or ChatGPT-4 would devise, on average, better business ideas. To do so, 200 students were each asked to create an idea for “a new product or service appealing to college students that could be made available for $50 or less.”43 ChatGPT-4 was asked the same question, providing 100 total responses, after which the model was trained on a selection of successful ideas submitted by students in prior classes, and then provided another 100 ideas. The 200 human ideas took many human days of work to generate, whereas ChatGPT-4 took only an hour. Once all ideas had been tallied, the Wharton professors constructed a survey that asked potential customers how likely they were to purchase the related product. The average “purchase probability of a human-generated idea” was 40%, while the untrained GPT-4 ideas netted 47%, and the trained GPT-4 received a 49%. When considering only the ideas which were in the top 10% of purchase probability scores, only 5 were created by students, 15 came from the untrained GPT model, and 20 from the trained one.44

#6: Solving for Interoperability

Lastly, AI provides a pathway to overcoming one of the Metaverse’s most intractable problems—not scarce computational power, bandwidth limitations, battery life, or payment costs, but interoperability. Just as AI can recognize and create objects, while also intuiting their purpose and attributes, it is increasingly able to convert between file formats and conventions, fill in the information that’s lacking or discard that which unnecessarily burdens a CPU or GPU, separate parts of a single asset (e.g., a tie from a suit model), and individually customize them, too. Of course, AI can’t yet solve for the business models of interoperation, but mediating human disagreements and commercial incentives may forever remain out of a neural network’s digital grasp.

CONCLUSION

“Technology frequently produces surprises that no one predicts. But the biggest and most fantastical developments are often anticipated decades in advance.” These words opened this book, and the pages since have hopefully demonstrated why and how the Metaverse is likely to fulfill them.

I’m certain that the future will be increasingly centered around real-time-rendered 3D virtual worlds and networks. Global internet bandwidth, latency, and reliability will all improve, even if the speed of light will remain the Metaverse’s greatest adversary irrespective of submarine cables, low-orbit satellites, atmospheric drones and balloons, and advances in AI or neural networks. The amount of computing power will grow, and that power will enable higher concurrency, greater persistency, more sophisticated simulations, and altogether new experiences. The locational mix of this computing power (i.e., remote, edge, local) is less clear, as is the nature of its operations (centralized, decentralized, quantum, or more fanciful concepts such as biocomputing). No matter the answer, I’d bet the supply of computing power will fall well short of the demand for it.

Interoperability will be achieved slowly, imperfectly, and never exhaustively or without cost. While the market will eventually coalesce around a subset of standards, these standards won’t convert perfectly into one another or support every use case, and each will have drawbacks, too. And before then, scores of would-be standards will be proposed, adopted, deprecated, and forked. AI will be an essential accelerant but is no panacea—least of all where human incentives, competition, and preferences are concerned. In the same spirit, it’s likely that economic interoperation is achieved not through virtual worlds “opening up.” Instead, platforms will strike bilateral “trade deals,” just as the United States has different policies with Canada, Indonesia, Egypt, and Honduras, in addition to the European Union (itself a collection of agreements spanning a finite set of “worlds”).

It will take longer than hoped for HMDs and other mixed-reality wearables to see widespread adoption—and even longer for this equipment to displace existing devices and do everything that science fiction authors and readers have dreamed for close to a century. And yet there is no doubt that the field continues to mature and that, overdue, its era will one day arrive. Given the cost of these devices, there are concerns that their adoption will produce greater inequality—especially in fields such as education. I suspect this will be true, though only temporarily.

When it debuted in 2007, the iPhone retailed for $500 (or roughly $730 in 2024 dollars). In 2024, the cheapest model sold by Apple, the iPhone SE, is only $429—15% less in nominal terms and over 40% cheaper in real terms, even though it boasts several hundred times more computing power, a display that’s 67% larger and with 100% greater pixel density, front- and back-facing cameras that can produce images that have 3.5–6 times more pixels than the first iPhone’s sole rear camera and leverage AI and neural-network technologies, and so on.1 Though a comparison of computational specs shows that Samsung’s entry-level budget Galaxy devices are less powerful than the iPhone SE, as of Q4 2023, they were available for $1602 and each one could outperform a rack of Apple’s groundbreaking first smartphone.3 It is likely that it will take longer for HMDs to become affordable than it did for smartphones to do so, but this very slowness means that adoption of these devices and use of their revolutionary software will also take time.

We typically underestimate how much time is required for entrepreneurs, companies, and even tech giants to make use of advances in networking, computing, AI, interoperability, hardware, and so on. All of the technologies required to build Facebook were widely available years before Mark Zuckerberg created the social network in 2004. In hindsight, it seems that the holdup was Zuckerberg and his peers. It took a child of the 1990s internet—characterized by text-based message boards, chat clients, and web-hosting platforms—to build Facebook, and he relied on his similarly minded peers to populate it. An analogous story played out with Evan Spiegel, a child of the 2000s mobile internet, who founded Snapchat in 2011 based around “ephemeral messages” that would dispose of sexts and spicy texts—a use case millennials and Gen Zs embraced en masse. In Chapter 3, I recounted the rise of the iPad native generation and the way it closely mapped (i.e., fueled) Roblox’s growth. The oldest of users is just now turning 20—in between the ages of Zuckerberg and Spiegel at the advent of Facebook and Snapchat—and so the new wave of entrepreneurs may soon be upon us, propelled not just by Roblox but by VRChat (which debuted in 2014), Rec Room (2016), Pokémon Go (2016), and the first consumer-release Oculus (2016).

Even as the Metaverse’s underlying technologies become more popular and capable, skepticism will persist and often grow. In 1995, Clifford Stoll, an American astronomer and former systems administrator at the US Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, wrote the now-infamous book Silicon Snake Oil: Second Thoughts on the Information Highway. In an editorial for Newsweek around the book’s publication, he stated, “After two decades online, I’m perplexed … uneasy about this most trendy and oversold community. Visionaries see a future of telecommuting workers, interactive libraries and multimedia classrooms. They speak of electronic town meetings and virtual communities. Commerce and business will shift from offices and malls to networks and modems. And the freedom of digital networks will make government more democratic. Baloney. Do our computer pundits lack all common sense? … What the Internet hucksters won’t tell you is that the Internet is one big ocean of unedited data, without any pretense of completeness.”4 Three years after Stoll’s opinion piece, Paul Krugman, who would win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences a decade later, wrote an (unintentionally) ironically titled article, “Why Most Economists’ Predictions Are Wrong,” in which he stated: “The growth of the Internet will slow drastically, as the flaw in ‘Metcalfe’s law’—which states that the number of potential connections in a network is proportional to the square of the number of participants—becomes apparent: most people have nothing to say to each other! By 2005 or so, it will become clear that the Internet’s impact on the economy has been no greater than the fax machine’s.”5 Notably, Krugman’s prediction preceded the launch of nearly all of the internet’s enduring social platforms, such as Skype (2003), Facebook (2004), Roblox (2006), Twitter (2006), Snap (2011), and TikTok (2014), and the companies that indexed the billions of pages made by internet users, including Google (founded three months later in 1998). In December 2000, the Daily Mail published a news piece headlined “Internet ‘May Just Be a Passing Fad as Millions Give Up on It,’ ” backed by research that estimated Britain was set to lose 2 million of its 15 million internet users.6

Though skeptics will shape the discourse, I’d guess that by the end of the current decade, many if not most of us will agree that the “Metaverse” has begun (though even in hindsight, there will be no precise date of its start, nor will we be able to predict when it will arrive in full). Furthermore, the term “the Metaverse” will probably have been discarded—perhaps for the “immersive internet” or “spatial internet” or “3D internet.” Or maybe we just keep saying “the internet.” After all, the younger generations will be first to adopt “the Metaverse,” and they have no interest in what social 3D spaces are called—nor any other labels for their behavior. I’d guess that for decades to come, we’ll continue to use many of the digital and mobile products we do today—real-time 3D rendering is not the best way to perform many tasks or experience all forms of content—even when the products are supporting Metaverse use cases.

The financial impact of the Metaverse’s construction, development, and realization will be considerable. “Trillions” is a large, yet reliable, number. The internet and computer are among the most powerful platforms humanity has ever created—and both will evolve and be redesigned in support of the Metaverse. Estimating the actual value of the Metaverse, however, will never be possible—which makes current forecasts unfalsifiable and distracting. Although it’s common to refer to the “digital economy,” there is no agreed-upon, nor particularly important, answer to what, exactly, its size might be. The answer depends purely on allocation. Imagine, as an example, attributing a portion of the purchase price of this book to “digital” or “the internet.” What is the right share and how would you know? Presumably the allocation differs if it’s a physical book, audiobook, or e-book, but how much? How would the answer change if you found out about the book on social media versus browsing a bookstore? Or based on whether I wrote it on a local versus cloud-based word processor, or even physical paper? What matters is that the Metaverse will be one of the propulsive global forces in the coming decades, with companies emerging, growing, shrinking, or dying as a result.

The formation of the Metaverse will help regulators force the major operating systems to unbundle their stacks. Despite this, the companies that own these OSs and ecosystems will still thrive because their unbundled offerings are still market leading and the emergence of the Metaverse will increase the size and importance of most of these markets. Overall, the structure of the Metaverse is likely to resemble that of the digital world today—a handful of horizontally and vertically integrated companies will control a substantial share of the digital economy, with their influence even greater. This outcome is likely regardless of whether the Metaverse is built on centralized or decentralized technologies. The underpinnings of the World Wide Web are nearly all decentralized—and it grew to popularity at a time in which the devices used to access the web were “open,” such as Windows, Mac, and Linux PCs. Even so, consumer usage of the internet rapidly consolidated around the ecosystems of Microsoft, Google, and Facebook throughout the 1990s and 2000s. There are many nontechnological feedback loops that concentrate power, such as branding and IP, user habits, data-center investments, commercial partnerships and sister products, profit margins, and so on. The key concern for the Metaverse is not whether centralization or decentralization “wins”—neither can—but where along the spectrum it sits, and how that placement changes over time. And here, I’m hopeful.

Whatever one believes about crypto, there is a clear want for better user rights and openness. Many early leaders in the Metaverse are responding to this desire. When Mark Zuckerberg announced his Metaverse strategy in October 2021, he also announced the end of a year-old policy that required Quest users to have a Facebook account7 and committed to supporting WebXR, an open-source API collection for browser-based AR and VR apps, and OpenXR, an open-source API collection for installed AR and VR apps, rather than forcing its own proprietary alternatives.8 Zuckerberg also said Quest devices would continue to allow users to directly install apps, including third-party app stores, and that developers would be able to choose their own in-app payment solutions.9 A few weeks later, Facebook began to open up many of the APIs that it had closed a decade earlier, including those that enabled users to cross-post Instagram photos on Twitter and other social networks.10 A month after announcing its Activision Blizzard acquisition, Microsoft unveiled a new, 14-point policy platform for its Windows operating system, and the “next-generation marketplaces [the company] builds for games.” This included a pledge to support third-party payment solutions and app stores (and not disadvantage developers who choose to use them), the right for users to set these alternatives as default options, and the right for developers to directly communicate with the end user (even if the point of that communication is to tell the user they can get better pricing or service by cutting out Microsoft’s store or services suite), and the statement that Microsoft was “committed” to bringing these same principles to its Xbox console (though no details or timing was provided). Epic Games’ ecosystem and ambitions are still developing, but its controls remain few and its promises largely met despite the extraordinary costs.

It’s fair to argue that Facebook, Microsoft, Epic, and many proponents of the blockchain ecosystem are fans of openness because they are stymied by their closed competitors. Were any of these companies or their leaders in control of iOS or Android, or less affected by those same platforms, they might hold different views. The current support for openness may or may not be sustained, either. Prior to leaving Facebook, John Carmack admitted that Facebook had to increase the price of Quest 2 because the most popular games on the device were free-to-play titles that rarely monetized and were made by independent developers.11 When Microsoft vowed to open up Xbox, it offered no roadmap or timeline to doing so, admitted its business model could not presently support it, and offered no ruminations on how it might. With every service it gives away, Epic’s de facto control likely grows. During the 2021 trial between Epic and Apple, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers seemed sympathetic to many of Epic’s arguments, but also declared, “Let’s be clear. Epic is here because, if relief is granted, it could turn the multibillion-dollar company into maybe a multitrillion-dollar company. They aren’t doing it out of the kindness of their heart.”12

The Metaverse will intensify many of the societal challenges of the internet today—from the role of inscrutable algorithms in shaping human behaviors, to the incidence of online harassment, abuse, and unhappiness, data rights, data literacy, data security, and platform power at large. Not only will these problems intensify, the lessons learned over the past 20 years will not always apply. Moderating asynchronous texts is quite different from live and haptically integrated 3D gestures. When the Islamic State (also known as ISIS/ISIL) began to use social media in the mid-2000s, the terrorist group hoped to radicalize Muslims around the world and then recruit them to parts of the Middle East for training. In response, governments around the world restricted the ability of foreigners and even their own citizens to enter their countries after visiting various “hot spots.” Such an approach no longer applies when candidates are trained through immersive platforms running on decentralized networks. And Alexa listening for a keyword trigger is a lot less invasive than optical AR glasses that scan, digest, and simulate the real world around them.

I worry comparatively less about virtual isolation. This is not an endorsement of spending more time inside and less out in the world but, instead, a recognition of how we currently spend our time. Including naps and bouts of sleeplessness, the average American over 18 sleeps for 8.7 hours per day and works for 5.6 hours, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.13 Of the remaining 9.7 waking hours, more than half (or 5–5.5 hours total) is spent watching television, movies, and user-generated video online.14 Some of this time is spent multitasking—the viewer is cooking, on the treadmill, watching their kids, or surfing the internet—but at least two-thirds of viewing occurs without such distractions.15 Sixty percent of total viewing is also done on a solitary basis,16 and nearly 90% of viewing is done while sedentary.17 Shifting any of this time to social, interactive, and more engaged entertainment is likely a positive outcome, not a negative one, even if we’re all still indoors. This is particularly true for the elderly. The average senior in the United States spends 7.5 hours per day watching TV. Few among us dreamed of retiring and living long in order to spend half of each of our remaining days watching TV. The Metaverse may offer no substitute for physically sailing in the Caribbean, but captaining a virtual sailboat alongside old friends is likely to beat midday cable news and offer its own perks, too.

Spectators, All

What I cannot predict is exactly what life will be like in the Metaverse—what we’ll do after we wake up and when we come home from work; how our jobs, relationships, and beliefs will change; and so on. Any attempt to describe the Metaverse with such precision would fail. Vannevar Bush had an uncanny ability to predict the devices of the future and much of what they might do, and he also had shrewd insights into the crucial role of government in making them useful and for the collective benefit. At the same time, his Memex was desk-sized and electromechanical—physically storing and connecting all the content a user might request—and did but a fraction of what we ask for from our iPhones. In 2001: A Space Odyssey, Stanley Kubrick and Arthur C. Clarke imagined a future in which humankind had colonized space and sentient AI had emerged, but iPad-like displays were used for little more than watching TV while eating breakfast, and telephones were still dumb and required cords. Neal Stephenson’s Snow Crash has inspired decades of R&D projects and now guides many of the most powerful companies on earth. Yet Stephenson believed the Metaverse would emerge from the TV industry, not gaming, and Hollywood looks like it will be a mostly passive observer of this next great medium. Indeed, Stephenson imagined that socializing in the Metaverse would involve “people going to bars on the Street,” but “what we have now is Warcraft guilds” that go on in-game raids.18

Right now, we are at the least interesting and least diverse point of Metaverse software development. New ideas are focused on “What if App X or Service Y but in 3D” and the like. In time, entrepreneurs will learn how to take advantage of a world full of electromyographic sensors, volumetric screens, and passthrough displays. And consumers will respond to these creations, all the while revealing new use cases, wants, and needs to those same entrepreneurs. Eventually, a thing that seems trivial—a mobile phone, a touchscreen, a video game—becomes essential, and ends up changing the world in ways both predicted and never even considered. The iPhone is a brilliant demonstration of this point—and the last story I’ll tell in this book.

When he announced the first iPhone in January 2007, Steve Jobs described it as a revolutionary product. He was right, of course. But this first iPhone lacked an App Store and there were no plans to allow third-party developers to make apps. Why? Jobs told developers that “the full Safari engine is inside of iPhone. And so, you can write amazing Web 2.0 and Ajax apps that look exactly and behave exactly like apps on the iPhone.”19 But in October 2007, ten months after the iPhone had been unveiled and four months after it went on sale, Jobs changed his mind. A software development kit was announced for March 2008, with the App Store released in July of that year. Within a month, the million or so iPhone owners had downloaded 30% as many apps, in total, as the more than 40 million iTunes users had downloaded songs. Jobs then told the Wall Street Journal: “I would not trust any of our predictions because reality has so far exceeded them by such a great degree that we’ve been reduced to spectators just like you, watching this amazing phenomenon.”20
